docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 4 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Buddha–Jina Prabhā: Buddhist and Jain Traditions. It introduces the two great Śramaṇa traditions of India as knowledge systems — their teachers and scriptures, their philosophy and logic, their meditative and ethical disciplines, their cosmology and mathematics, their monasteries and libraries, and their art and literature. It is written for undergraduates and teachers in courses on Indian philosophy, religion and Indian Knowledge Systems, and for general readers who want a reliable single-volume account of both traditions.

The volume tries to be both respectful and historically careful. Dates are given according to current scholarship, with traditional dates identified as such; thus the Buddha is placed in the fifth century BCE (c. 480–400 BCE on the “short chronology”), as is Mahāvīra. Quotations from primary texts are limited to passages whose wording and reference could be checked, and claims that ancient texts “anticipated” modern science or mathematics have been avoided. Chapter 7 includes an account of the decline of Buddhism in India; Chapter 12 surveys Jain grammar, lexicography, astronomy, historical writing and literature; Chapter 13 describes how monks, nuns and lay people lived these religions in practice; and Chapter 14 discusses their interactions, art and literature, caste and gender, and modern history. A select bibliography of standard works is provided for further reading.

The book is an introduction, not a substitute for the specialist literature. Readers are encouraged to follow the references to the translations and studies on which it relies.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Two Śramaṇa Traditions
docs.text:
Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.

I go to the Buddha for refuge, I go to the Dhamma for refuge, I go to the Saṅgha for refuge.

— The Three Refuges (Tisaraṇa), Khuddakapāṭha 1

Namo arihantāṇaṃ, namo siddhāṇaṃ, namo āyariyāṇaṃ, namo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, namo loe savva-sāhūṇaṃ.

Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the teachers (ācārya), homage to the preceptors (upādhyāya), homage to all mendicants in the world.

— The Namokāra (Navakāra) Mantra, the principal Jain prayer

docs.title: 1.1 The Indian Intellectual Landscape
docs.text:
The Indian subcontinent has long been a fertile ground for philosophical thought, spiritual inquiry and systematic knowledge. The phrase jñāna paramparā — “tradition of knowledge” or “lineage of learning” — captures the idea that knowledge is handed down, tested and renewed from teacher to student. In most Indian traditions knowledge is not only an accumulation of facts or theories; it is also a disciplined practice (sādhanā) whose highest goal is liberation, variously called mokṣa, nirvāṇa or kaivalya.

Within this landscape two traditions stand out for the depth of their philosophical analysis, the rigour of their ethics and the breadth of their influence: the Buddhist tradition (Bauddha) and the Jain tradition (Jaina). Both took their historical form in the middle Ganges valley in the fifth century BCE, within the broad movement of wandering renunciants known as śramaṇas, and both have continued to develop for some two and a half millennia (Gethin 1998; Dundas 2002). Each also understands itself in its own terms: Buddhists see the Buddha as rediscovering a path taught by Buddhas of earlier ages, and Jains regard their teaching as eternal, proclaimed anew in each age by a Tīrthaṅkara, with Mahāvīra as the last of twenty-four and Pārśva as his historical predecessor.

This volume of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā is devoted to the knowledge systems of these two traditions. Its title, Buddha–Jina Prabhā — “the radiance of the Buddha and the Jina” — honours the two teachers around whom the traditions crystallised: Siddhārtha Gautama, who became the Buddha (the “Awakened One”), and Vardhamāna, who became Mahāvīra (the “Great Hero”), the last of the twenty-four Jinas (“Victors”) or Tīrthaṅkaras (“Ford-Makers”) of Jain tradition.

docs.title: 1.2 The Śramaṇa Heritage
docs.text:
The term śramaṇa (Pāli samaṇa, Prakrit samaṇa) derives from the root śram, “to exert oneself, to strive”. Śramaṇas were wandering ascetics who sought liberation through personal effort, renunciation and contemplative discipline, usually outside — and often in criticism of — the Brahmanical emphasis on Vedic sacrifice (yajña) and hereditary priesthood. Early Indian texts frequently pair “śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas” as the two kinds of religious specialist, and the edicts of Aśoka (3rd century BCE) use the same pairing (Bronkhorst 2007; Thapar 1961).

The Śramaṇa groups differed widely, but they shared a recognisable ideal. The aspirant renounced household life and its pleasures (tyāga), which were seen as sources of bondage, and sought liberation by his or her own discipline rather than by ritual performed by others. Restraint from harming living beings (ahiṃsā) was central, though its scope varied greatly from group to group. Action was held to have consequences extending across lifetimes, and in time communities of monks and nuns provided the institutional frame for the religious life.

Buddhism and Jainism are the two most enduring expressions of this heritage, but they were not the only ones. The early Buddhist and Jain texts mention many other teachers and groups, including the determinist Ājīvikas, the materialists (later called Lokāyata or Cārvāka), and sceptics.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Historical Context
docs.text:
The fifth century BCE in the Ganges valley saw the growth of territorial states (the mahājanapadas), the rise of towns such as Rājagṛha, Vaiśālī, Śrāvastī and Vārāṇasī (Kāśī), the spread of coinage and long-distance trade, and the emergence of new social groups. Many historians link the appeal of the Śramaṇa movements to these changes, which created audiences — merchants, town-dwellers, members of the ruling clans — receptive to paths of individual moral effort (Gombrich 2006; Chakravarti 1987).

The early Buddhist lists (for example Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.70) name sixteen “great realms” (mahājanapada): Aṅga, Magadha, Kāśī, Kosala, Vṛjji, Malla, Cedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Pañcāla, Matsya, Śūrasena, Aśmaka, Avanti, Gandhāra and Kamboja. The list is schematic rather than a map of a single moment, and by the Buddha’s lifetime Magadha and Kosala were absorbing their neighbours. Both the Buddha and Mahāvīra taught chiefly in Magadha, Kosala and the Vṛjji confederacy, the region shown in Figure 1.1, with Rājagṛha (modern Rajgir), Vaiśālī and Śrāvastī among their favourite centres. Both drew followers from several social strata — rulers and merchants, brāhmaṇas and people of low status, men and women — although the surviving texts suggest that the urban elite and the ruling clans were especially prominent among their patrons (Chakravarti 1987).

Figure 1.1. The middle Ganges valley: places associated with the lives of the Buddha and Mahāvīra, with the later monasteries of Nālandā and Vikramaśīla. Sites are plotted by their modern latitude and longitude; no rivers or boundaries are drawn, and the names of the realms (in small capitals) mark only their approximate location. Mahāvīra’s birthplace, Kuṇḍagrāma, lay near Vaiśālī; Pāvāpurī is the traditional site of his death, and Sammeta Śikhara (Pārasnāth hill) the place where Jain tradition holds that twenty of the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras attained liberation.

docs.title: 1.2.2 The Six Teachers
docs.text:
The Pāli Sāmaññaphala Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 2) describes six well-known teachers contemporary with the Buddha, each with a following, a reputation and a distinctive view (Table 1.1). Its accounts are polemical and compressed, but they illustrate the variety of the Śramaṇa milieu (Walshe 1995; Basham 1951).

Table 1.1. The six teachers of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta (DN 2) Teacher Characteristic view Position as reported in DN 2 Pūraṇa Kassapa Non-action (akiriya) Actions bring neither merit nor demerit Makkhali Gosāla Fate (niyati); Ājīvika All beings are purified by passing through a fixed round of births; effort is ineffective Ajita Kesakambalī Annihilationism The person is made of four elements and is destroyed at death; no fruit of good or bad actions Pakudha Kaccāyana Seven unchanging bodies Earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and the soul are eternal; no one truly kills Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta Evasion (“eel-wriggling”) Refuses to affirm or deny any proposition about the afterlife Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta Fourfold restraint Mahāvīra, presented as teaching restraint of the self in four ways

The inclusion of Mahāvīra — here called Nigaṇṭha (“free of bonds”) Nātaputta (“son of the Nāta/Jñātṛ clan”) — among these teachers is significant. It confirms that he and the Buddha were contemporaries and that each tradition was aware of the other from an early date. The Buddhist summary of his teaching is not accurate by later Jain standards (the “fourfold restraint” is associated in Jain sources with Mahāvīra’s predecessor Pārśva), a reminder that such reports must be read critically (Dundas 2002).

docs.title: 1.2.3 The Ājīvikas
docs.text:
The Ājīvikas, whose best-known leader was Makkhali Gosāla, were for several centuries a major rival of both Buddhism and Jainism. They held a doctrine of strict determinism (niyativāda): all beings pass through a fixed, immensely long but finite cycle of rebirths, after which liberation comes of itself. Buddhist texts treat this as the most pernicious of wrong views because it denies the value of moral effort. Jain texts describe Gosāla as a former companion of Mahāvīra who later broke with him (Basham 1951).

The Ājīvikas received royal patronage: Aśoka and his grandson Daśaratha dedicated rock-cut caves in the Barabar and Nagarjuni hills in Bihar — among the earliest rock-cut monuments in India — to Ājīvika ascetics. No Ājīvika scripture survives, and the tradition is known only through the writings of its opponents and through inscriptions. Tamil inscriptions mention a tax on Ājīvikas as late as the thirteenth or fourteenth century, after which they disappear from the record (Basham 1951).

docs.title: 1.3 Buddhism and Jainism: Parallels and Distinctions
docs.text:
Buddhism and Jainism agree on more than either agrees with the Brahmanical orthodoxy of their time. Neither accepts the Veda as revealed or the Vedic sacrifice as a path to liberation; both hold that liberation is reached by one’s own discipline rather than by ritual or divine grace; both treat karma as a law of consequence that operates without a divine judge; and both organised orders of monks and nuns supported by lay followers, admitting, in principle, people of any class (a principle that practice did not always match, as Chapter 14 shows).

Their deepest disagreement concerns the self. For the Buddha there is no permanent self (anātman) to be found in any of the constituents of a person; for Mahāvīra every living being is an eternal, individual soul (jīva). The difference shapes the rest of each system. Because Jainism understands karma as a fine matter that adheres to the soul, the removal of karma is in part a physical process, and austerity (tapas) is one of its principal means; non-harming must extend to the smallest beings, including those embodied in earth, water, fire and air, because any careless action draws in more karmic matter. Because Buddhism understands karma as intention (cetanā), its discipline is above all a discipline of the mind, and the Middle Way rejects the extreme austerities that the Jains made central. Table 1.2 sets out these and other points of comparison.

Table 1.2. Buddhism and Jainism compared Aspect Buddhism Jainism Teacher Siddhārtha Gautama, the Buddha Vardhamāna Mahāvīra, 24th Tīrthaṅkara Self No permanent self (anātman); a person is a stream of processes Eternal, individual souls (jīva), infinite in number Universe Many world-systems, arising and dissolving in cycles; in Madhyamaka, all things empty of intrinsic nature A single, eternal, uncreated universe (loka) of six substances Karma Intentional action (cetanā) A subtle matter drawn in by activity and bound to the soul by the passions Liberation Nirvāṇa: the ending of craving, suffering and rebirth Mokṣa: the soul freed of karmic matter, with infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy Non-harming Central; intention weighs heavily Rigorous; extends to the smallest beings and to elemental life Asceticism The Middle Way rejects extreme austerity Austerity (tapas) a principal means of shedding karma God No creator; gods exist but are within saṃsāra No creator; Tīrthaṅkaras are worshipped as exemplars, not as dispensers of grace Key method Dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) Many-sidedness (anekāntavāda); conditional predication (syādvāda) Canonical languages Pāli (Theravāda); Sanskrit and Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit (other schools) Ardhamāgadhī (Śvetāmbara canon); Jaina Śaurasenī (Digambara scriptures) Canon Tipiṭaka/Tripiṭaka; Chinese and Tibetan canons Śvetāmbara Āgamas (Chapter 8); Digambaras hold the ancient canon lost Orders and divisions Bhikkhu and bhikkhunī saṅghas; Theravāda, Mahāyāna, Vajrayāna Monks and nuns (Digambara nuns are āryikās); Digambara and Śvetāmbara, each with sub-traditions Geographical spread Pan-Asian, now global Mainly India, with a modern diaspora

docs.title: 1.4 The Knowledge Systems Approach
docs.text:
This volume follows the approach of the series as a whole. Rather than treating Buddhism and Jainism only as “religions”, it asks what each tradition claimed to know and how it organised that knowledge (Figure 1.2). Each had a theory of the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and an account of what there is — the dharmas of the Buddhist analysts, the six substances (dravya) of the Jains. Each joined these to an ethics of precepts and vows and to a discipline of meditation, and each placed human life within a cosmology of world-ages and realms of rebirth. The Jains added a sustained interest in number and measure, and both traditions built monastic institutions that organised learning and attracted royal and mercantile patronage.

Figure 1.2. The Buddhist and Jain traditions as knowledge systems.

The results under these heads were uneven, and this book does not pretend otherwise. The Buddhist logicians Dignāga and Dharmakīrti built a system of epistemology with which every later Indian school had to engage (Chapter 5); Jain authors developed a philosophy of many-sidedness, an elaborate cosmology and a tradition of mathematical classification that distinguished the numerable, the innumerable and the infinite (Chapters 9 and 10). Other claims made for the two traditions in popular writing — that they anticipated modern physics or set theory, or that their monasteries were universities in the modern sense — do not survive a reading of the sources, and the chapters that follow say so where the question arises.

docs.title: 1.5 Scope and Structure of This Volume
docs.text:
The volume is organised into fourteen chapters in three parts.

Part I: Buddhist Knowledge (Chapters 2–7) The life and teachings of the Buddha (Chapter 2); the canonical literature of the Tipiṭaka (Chapter 3); the three major streams of Buddhist thought — Theravāda (Chapter 4), Mahāyāna, with Buddhist logic and epistemology (Chapter 5), and Vajrayāna (Chapter 6); and Buddhist institutions of learning, including the monasteries of Nālandā and Vikramaśīla and the decline of Buddhism in India (Chapter 7). Part II: Jain Knowledge (Chapters 8–12) Mahāvīra and the Tīrthaṅkara tradition (Chapter 8); Jain philosophy (Chapter 9); mathematics in the Jain tradition (Chapter 10); Jain cosmology and ethics (Chapter 11); and Jain grammar, lexicography, astronomy, historical writing and literature (Chapter 12). Part III: Practice and Shared Heritage (Chapters 13–14) Religious life in practice: the discipline of monks and nuns, the history of the Buddhist order of nuns, and the gifts, rites, worship and pilgrimage of lay Buddhists and Jains (Chapter 13); and the interactions between Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical traditions, their art and literature, questions of caste and gender, and their modern history (Chapter 14).

Several topics touched on here are treated more fully elsewhere in the series: the Buddhist and Jain schools among the Indian philosophical systems in Volume 3 (Darśana Darpaṇa), Buddhist tantra and its Tibetan schools in Volume 6 (Tantra–Āgama), Jain mathematics in Volume 11 (Gaṇita), and Buddhist psychology and the monastic centres of learning in Volume 22 (Manas and Śikṣā).

docs.title: 1.6 A Note on Sources and Terminology
docs.text:
The primary texts of these traditions are in Pāli, Sanskrit and several Prakrits, with vast later literatures in Chinese, Tibetan and the regional languages of India and Asia. Translations of Pāli texts quoted here follow, or are adapted from, the standard modern translations (Walshe 1995; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Bodhi 2000, 2012), with K. R. Norman’s versions of the Dhammapada and Sutta Nipāta (Norman 1997, 1992); Pāli glosses follow the Pali Text Society’s dictionary (Rhys Davids and Stede 1921). Jain canonical passages are cited from Jacobi’s classic translations and later scholarship (Jacobi 1884, 1895). References to Pāli suttas use the conventional abbreviations DN (Dīgha Nikāya), MN (Majjhima Nikāya), SN (Saṃyutta Nikāya), AN (Aṅguttara Nikāya), Sn (Sutta Nipāta), Dhp (Dhammapada), Khp (Khuddakapāṭha) and Thig (Therīgāthā). For names, texts and terms not explained here, readers may consult the standard reference works (Buswell and Lopez 2014; Silk 2015; Jacobsen et al. 2020).

Transliteration follows the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). Technical terms are given in the original language at first occurrence with an English rendering. Where a Pāli and a Sanskrit form both exist (nibbāna/nirvāṇa, dhamma/dharma), the Pāli form is generally used for Theravāda contexts and the Sanskrit form elsewhere. Tibetan names and terms, which are few, are given in a simplified phonetic form with the Wylie transliteration in parentheses at first occurrence, for example Kagyu (bka’ brgyud). A glossary is provided at the end of the volume.

docs.title: 1.6.1 Respectful Engagement
docs.text:
For millions of people these traditions are not merely objects of study but living paths of practice. The historical and philosophical analysis offered here is intended to complement, not to replace, the devotional and experiential dimensions of these traditions. Where the traditions’ own accounts differ from the conclusions of historical scholarship — on dates, authorship or the origin of texts — both are reported, and the difference is made explicit.

Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā tesaṃ hetuṃ tathāgato āha, tesañ ca yo nirodho evaṃvādī mahāsamaṇo.

Of those things that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told the cause, and also what their cessation is: such is the teaching of the Great Ascetic.

— Vinaya, Mahāvagga I.23.5

According to the Vinaya, these words were spoken by Assaji, one of the Buddha’s first five disciples, to the wandering ascetic Sāriputta, who on hearing them grasped the teaching and later became one of the Buddha’s chief disciples. The verse became one of the most widely inscribed formulas in the Buddhist world. It summarises the analytical core of the teaching: things arise from causes, and when the causes cease, the things cease. This is the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), discussed in Chapter 2.

docs.title: 1.7 The Chronological Framework
docs.text:
Absolute dates for early Indian history are uncertain, and the dates of the Buddha and Mahāvīra in particular have been debated for more than a century. The traditional Theravāda reckoning places the Buddha’s death in 544/543 BCE; the “corrected long chronology” long used in Western scholarship places his life at c. 563–483 BCE; most specialists now favour a “short chronology” that places his death around 400 BCE, give or take a few decades (Bechert 1991; Cousins 1996). This volume uses c. 480–400 BCE for the Buddha’s life (see the chronology in Table 1.3). Mahāvīra is traditionally dated 599–527 BCE (Śvetāmbara reckoning); since the early texts make him an older contemporary of the Buddha, most historians place him in the fifth century BCE as well (Dundas 2002).

Table 1.3. Chronological framework (academic dates first; traditional dates labelled) Period Buddhist tradition Jain tradition before 5th c. BCE Pārśva, 23rd Tīrthaṅkara, probably a historical teacher (traditional dates 877–777 BCE) 5th c. BCE The Buddha, c. 480–400 BCE (Theravāda traditional dates 624–544 BCE; older scholarly “corrected long chronology” c. 563–483 BCE); First Council at Rājagṛha after his death (tradition) Mahāvīra (traditional dates 599–527 BCE) c. 4th c. BCE Second Council at Vaiśālī, about a century after the Buddha’s death; later split between Sthaviras and Mahāsāṅghikas Tradition places a council at Pāṭaliputra and a migration south under Bhadrabāhu during a famine c. 268–232 BCE Aśoka’s reign and edicts; Third Council at Pāṭaliputra (Theravāda tradition); mission to Sri Lanka Ājīvikas and Nigaṇṭhas (Jains) named in Aśoka’s Pillar Edict VII 1st c. BCE Pāli canon written down in Sri Lanka (c. 29 BCE, tradition) Khāravela of Kaliṅga, a Jain king (Hāthīgumphā inscription) 1st c. BCE– 2nd c. CE Early Mahāyāna sūtras; Kuṣāṇa patronage; Gandhāra and Mathurā art Jain community at Mathurā (inscriptions); gradual Digambara–Śvetāmbara division c. 2nd–3rd c. CE Nāgārjuna Umāsvāti, Tattvārthasūtra (date disputed, between 2nd and 5th c.) 4th–5th c. CE Asaṅga, Vasubandhu; Buddhaghosa in Sri Lanka; Nālandā founded under the Guptas; Vinayas translated into Chinese; Sri Lankan nuns give ordination to Chinese women at Nanjing (433 or 434) Śvetāmbara canon redacted at Valabhī (c. 453 or 466 CE); Lokavibhāga (458 CE) 6th–7th c. CE Dignāga (c. 480–540), Dharmakīrti (6th–7th c.); Xuanzang in India (c. 630–643) Siddhasena Divākara, Samantabhadra (dates disputed) 8th–12th c. CE Vajrayāna; Pāla patronage; Vikramaśīla; transmission to Tibet; the Sri Lankan order of nuns lapses (11th c.) Akalaṅka, Haribhadra (8th c.); Jinasena (9th c.); Kharatara Gaccha’s founding debate (1024, tradition); Hemacandra (1088/89–1172); Vimala Vasahī at Mount Abu (1031) c. 1200 CE Sack of Odantapurī, Vikramaśīla and Nālandā during Turkish campaigns in Bihar and Bengal; Śākyaśrībhadra of Kashmir in Tibet (from 1204) Jain communities continue under new regimes in western India; Tapā Gaccha (1228, tradition); Lūṇa Vasahī at Mount Abu (1230) 13th–14th c. CE Buddhism fades in Kashmir; survives in Odisha, on the Tamil coast and in the Himalayan regions Prabhāvakacarita (1277/78) and Merutuṅga’s Prabandhacintāmaṇi (1305); Jinaprabha Sūri at the court of Muḥammad bin Tughluq; Mahendra Sūri’s Yantrarāja (1370) 15th c. CE Buddhism survives in Himalayan regions and pockets elsewhere Raṇakpur temple (15th c.); Loṅkā Śāh’s reform (origin of later non-image-worshipping orders) 19th–20th c. Mahābodhi Society (1891); Ambedkar’s conversion (1956); Tibetan exile in India (1959); ordination of Sri Lankan nuns at Sarnath (1996) Saṃvegī revival of wandering Śvetāmbara mendicants; Śrīmad Rājacandra and Gandhi; Kānjī Svāmī’s movement (from the 1930s); Aṇuvrat (1949)

docs.title: 1.8 Śramaṇa and Brāhmaṇa
docs.text:
The relationship between the Śramaṇa traditions and the Brahmanical or Vedic tradition was a long exchange of critique, borrowing and reinterpretation that lasted for many centuries.

A Continuum, Not Two Camps

Modern scholarship increasingly treats Śramaṇa and Brāhmaṇa as overlapping rather than sharply opposed milieus. Ideas of karma, rebirth and liberation appear in the early Upaniṣads as well as in the Buddhist and Jain canons, and scholars still debate which way the influences ran. Johannes Bronkhorst has argued that the region of “Greater Magadha” where both teachers lived was not yet Brahmanised in their time, and that Buddhism had later to adapt to a Brahmanism that became dominant only under and after the Mauryas (Bronkhorst 2007, 2011). Buddhist and Jain texts use Brahmanical vocabulary (often redefining it), and later Brahmanical thought absorbed Śramaṇa ideas of renunciation and non-violence. Jain authors such as Haribhadra (8th century) wrote surveys of the major philosophical systems, Buddhist and Brahmanical alike.

Brahmanical religion emphasised sacrifice (yajña), the authority of the Veda (śruti) and the order of social classes and life-stages (varṇāśrama). The Śramaṇa traditions challenged each of these: they criticised animal sacrifice in the name of non-harming, they grounded religious authority in the insight of their teachers rather than in the Veda, and in principle they opened the path to liberation to people of every class.

Na jaccā vasalo hoti, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo; kammanā vasalo hoti, kammanā hoti brāhmaṇo.

Not by birth is one an outcaste, not by birth is one a brāhmaṇa; by action one is an outcaste, by action one is a brāhmaṇa.

— Sutta Nipāta 136, Vasala Sutta

Such verses redefine the word “brāhmaṇa” in ethical terms; they did not abolish social hierarchy in Buddhist societies, a point discussed in Chapter 14. Influence also ran in the other direction and across many centuries, from the Nyāya replies to the Buddhist logicians to the debated Buddhist element in Advaita Vedānta; these exchanges are traced in Chapter 14 (Section 14.4).

docs.title: 1.9 Epistemological Foundations
docs.text:
Both traditions developed theories of knowledge (pramāṇa-śāstra) that shaped Indian philosophy as a whole (Table 1.4).

Table 1.4. Comparative epistemology: Buddhist, Jain and Nyāya positions (simplified) Feature Buddhist (Dignāga, Dharmakīrti) Jain (Umāsvāti, Akalaṅka) Nyāya Number of pramāṇas Two: perception and inference Two: direct (pratyakṣa) and indirect (parokṣa), covering five kinds of knowledge (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala) Four: perception, inference, comparison, testimony Perception Free of conceptual construction; grasps the momentary particular For Umāsvāti only supersensory cognition is direct; Akalaṅka adds sense-perception as “empirically direct” Arises from contact of sense and object; may be conceptual Testimony Treated as a form of inference A source of knowledge (śruta) An independent pramāṇa (śabda) Highest knowledge Insight that ends ignorance; the Buddha’s authority Omniscience (kevala-jñāna) Knowledge of the categories leading to liberation Self-awareness Cognition is self-aware (svasaṃvedana) for Dignāga; rejected by Candrakīrti Knowledge illuminates both itself and its object Not self-aware; a cognition is known by a further, introspective cognition (anuvyavasāya)

The table simplifies positions that each school argued over for centuries. The Buddhist column follows Dignāga (c. 480–540) and Dharmakīrti (6th–7th century), whose system, and the long line of later Buddhist epistemologists who answered its critics, is described in Chapter 5 (Section 5.8); the Jain column is explained in Chapter 9 (Section 9.6).

docs.title: 1.10 The Role of Language and Translation
docs.text:
The choice of language for sacred texts was itself significant. The Theravāda canon is preserved in Pāli, a Middle Indo-Aryan language, which the Pali Text Society (founded 1881) has published in roman script. Most Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna literature, and the works of the Buddhist logicians, are in Sanskrit or in the Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit of the sūtras. The Śvetāmbara Jain canon is in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit and the early Digambara scriptures in Jaina Śaurasenī; Jain authors from Umāsvāti onwards also wrote in Sanskrit, and Jain poets made Apabhraṃśa, the literary form of the late Middle Indo-Aryan vernaculars, one of their main languages (Chapter 12). Outside India the Buddhist canon was translated into classical Chinese by generations of translators and into classical Tibetan, whose canon, the Kangyur (bka’ ’gyur) and Tengyur (bstan ’gyur), preserves many works whose Sanskrit originals are lost.

The Vinaya (Cullavagga V.33) records that the Buddha refused a proposal to put his teaching into Vedic metre and allowed monks to learn it “in their own dialect” (sakāya niruttiyā). The phrase is ambiguous — it may mean the monks’ own languages or the Buddha’s own idiom — but the tradition generally took it as permitting translation, which greatly helped Buddhism to spread across language boundaries (Norman 1983). The Jains likewise used Prakrit for their canon, though Jain scholars later became masters of Sanskrit grammar: Hemacandra’s Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana covers both Sanskrit and the Prakrits (Chapter 12, Section 12.2).

docs.title: 1.11 The Śramaṇa Legacy in Indian Civilisation
docs.text:
The contributions of the two traditions to Indian civilisation reach beyond religion, and they differ in kind (Table 1.5). Buddhism left its largest mark through institutions: the great monasteries, which trained scholars from across Asia, and the transmission of Indian learning to Tibet, China and Southeast Asia. Jainism, which never spread far beyond India, left its mark through a continuous community: manuscript libraries, merchant patronage of temples and literature, and a share in the early literatures of Kannada, Tamil and Gujarati. Both contributed to logic and to the ethics of non-harming. The table is a guide to later chapters rather than a balance sheet; several of its entries are discussed critically where they arise.

Table 1.5. Some contributions of Buddhism and Jainism to Indian civilisation Domain Buddhist Jain Learning Great monasteries such as Nālandā, Valabhī and Vikramaśīla Manuscript libraries (bhaṇḍāras) and monastic scholarship Literature, grammar Pāli canon; Jātaka tales; Sanskrit poetry and drama (Aśvaghoṣa); Candragomin’s grammar Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa narrative; Kannada and Tamil classics; Hemacandra’s grammars and lexicons Art and architecture Sanchi, Ajanta, Ellora; Borobudur abroad Udayagiri–Khandagiri, Ellora, Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Dilwara, Raṇakpur Logic Dignāga, Dharmakīrti Anekāntavāda, syādvāda, nayavāda Ethics Compassion (karuṇā), loving-kindness (mettā) Non-harming (ahiṃsā) as the supreme duty Mathematics, astronomy Number-names in the Lalitavistara; calendar and astronomy of the Kālacakra Tantra Grades of number; cosmological geometry; Mahāvīra’s Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha; Mahendra Sūri’s Yantrarāja Medicine Monastic medicine in the Vinaya; Aśoka’s provision of medical care (Rock Edict II) Medical works such as Ugrāditya’s Kalyāṇakāraka Social thought Critique of birth-based status; order of nuns; Ambedkar’s movement Animal shelters (pāñjarāpoḷ); lay philanthropy

docs.title: 1.12 The Living Relevance of These Traditions
docs.text: In the modern world, the Buddhist emphasis on mindfulness (sati) has been adapted in secular clinical programmes, and the Jain idea of many-sidedness (anekāntavāda) has been invoked as a resource for tolerance and dialogue. The commitment of both traditions to non-harming has been read as a resource for ecological and animal ethics. Such modern applications are interpretations, sometimes far removed from the original contexts, and later chapters distinguish them from what the classical texts actually say.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Life and Teachings of the Buddha
2.1 The Historical Context
docs.text:
Siddhārtha Gautama, who would become the Buddha (the “Awakened One”), was born into the Śākya clan at Lumbinī (in present-day Nepal), probably in the fifth century BCE. The story of his path from a sheltered youth through renunciation and ascetic striving to the Middle Way and awakening has been retold, painted and sculpted across Asia for more than two thousand years.

The Buddha’s dates are uncertain; this volume follows the “short chronology” and places his life at c. 480–400 BCE, for the reasons given in Chapter 1 (Section 1.7). Whatever the exact dates, there is no serious doubt that the Buddha was a historical teacher of the middle Ganges valley. Most details of his biography, however, come from texts compiled long after his death, and the full life-story — from birth to final passing — was assembled only gradually in later works such as the Lalitavistara, the Buddhacarita of Aśvaghoṣa and the Pāli Nidānakathā (Gethin 1998). What can be recovered of the teaching itself is best read against its setting: Richard Gombrich has argued that many of the Buddha’s central ideas, among them his redefinition of karma as intention, were deliberate responses to the Brahmanical thought of his day (Gombrich 2009).

docs.title: 2.1.1 Birth and Early Life
docs.text:
According to the Pāli sources, Siddhārtha was born to King Śuddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā of the Śākya republic, whose capital was at Kapilavastu. The traditional accounts describe his miraculous birth in the Lumbinī grove (Figure 2.1), the prophecy of the sage Asita that the child would become either a great emperor (Cakravartin) or a great spiritual teacher (Buddha), and the subsequent efforts of his father to shield him from all knowledge of human suffering. Tradition also attributes to the newborn child a “lion’s roar” proclaiming that this would be his last birth:

Aggo ’ham asmi lokassa, seṭṭho ’ham asmi lokassa, jeṭṭho ’ham asmi lokassa. Ayam antimā jāti, na ’tthi dāni punabbhavo ti.

I am the foremost in the world, I am the best in the world, I am the eldest in the world. This is the last birth; there is now no more renewed existence.

— Majjhima Nikāya 123, Acchariyabbhutadhamma Sutta

The early discourses also contain verses in praise of the arising of Buddhas, such as the following:

Sukho buddhānaṃ uppādo, sukhā saddhammadesanā; sukhā saṅghassa sāmaggī, samaggānaṃ tapo sukho.

Happy is the birth of Buddhas, happy is the teaching of the True Dhamma; happy is the harmony of the Saṅgha, happy is the austerity of those in harmony.

— Dhammapada 194

Figure 2.1. The birth of the Buddha: Queen Māyā holding the branch of a tree in the Lumbinī grove, in a Gandhāra relief (c. 2nd–3rd century CE). The sculptors of Gandhāra (in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan) were among the first to represent the Buddha in human form. Photo: Ismoon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Four Sights and the Great Departure
docs.text:
In the later biographies the prince, despite his father’s precautions, meets on successive excursions beyond the palace an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic (samaṇa). The first three reveal the inevitability of ageing (jarā), disease (vyādhi) and death (maraṇa); the fourth shows that a life devoted to overcoming them is possible. The encounters shatter the illusion of a life insulated from suffering, and at the age of twenty-nine Siddhārtha leaves his palace, his wife Yaśodharā and his newborn son Rāhula in the Great Departure (Mahābhiniṣkramaṇa). The earliest accounts are much simpler. The canon mentions the young Gotama’s three palaces (AN 3.38) and describes his going forth plainly (MN 26), but it tells the story of the four sights only of a Buddha of the distant past, Vipassī (DN 14); its application to Siddhārtha, and the scene of the sleeping wife and son, belong to the later biographies.

According to tradition the quest lasted six years. Siddhārtha studied under two renowned teachers, Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta, mastered their meditative attainments and found them insufficient. He then practised extreme austerities (duṣkaracaryā) that nearly destroyed his body, before concluding that neither indulgence nor self-mortification led to liberation. The “Middle Way” (majjhimā paṭipadā) between them became a name for the whole path he went on to teach.

docs.title: 2.2 The Enlightenment
docs.text:
According to tradition, on the full-moon night of Vaiśākha (April–May), seated beneath the Bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa) at Bodhgaya, Siddhārtha attained Samyaksambodhi — perfect, complete enlightenment. The Pāli texts describe three stages of his awakening during the three watches of the night (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1. The three watches of the night of Enlightenment Watch Knowledge Gained Description First Watch Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa Knowledge of his own previous births through countless aeons Second Watch Cutūpapāta-ñāṇa (Divine Eye) Knowledge of the arising and passing away of all beings according to their karma Third Watch Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa Knowledge of the destruction of the āsavas (mental defilements), culminating in liberation

With the dawn, Siddhārtha Gautama had become the Buddha. Traditions differ on his first words: the Vinaya and the Udāna give other verses, while the Pāli commentaries regard the following verses of the Dhammapada as his first utterance of triumph:

Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ, gahakārakaṃ gavesanto — dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ. Gahakāraka diṭṭho si! Puna gehaṃ na kāhasi. Sabbā ete phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhitaṃ; visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayam ajjhagā.

Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the house-builder. Sorrowful is repeated birth. O house-builder, you are seen! You shall build no house again. All your rafters are broken, your ridgepole is destroyed; my mind has attained the unconditioned, achieved is the end of craving.

— Dhammapada 153–154

docs.title: 2.3 The Four Noble Truths (Ariya-Sacca)
docs.text:
The Buddha’s first discourse, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Dhamma), delivered at the Deer Park in Sarnath to his five former ascetic companions, laid out the foundational framework of his teaching: the Cattāri Ariyasaccāni (Four Noble Truths; Figure 2.2) (Bodhi 2000; Gethin 1998).

Idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ: jāti pi dukkhā, jarā pi dukkhā, byādhi pi dukkho, maraṇam pi dukkhaṃ, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho, piyehi vippayogo dukkho, yam p’ icchaṃ na labhati tam pi dukkhaṃ — saṅkhittena pañc’ upādānakkhandhā dukkhā.

““Now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, ageing is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not getting what one wishes is suffering — in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.””

— Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.11, trans. after Bodhi (2000)

Figure 2.2. The Four Noble Truths (Cattāri Ariyasaccāni), forming the foundational structure of the Buddha’s teaching. The medical analogy, widely used in the Buddhist tradition, highlights the pragmatic, therapeutic orientation of the Dhamma.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Suffering, Its Origin, Its Cessation and the Path
docs.text:
The Pāli term dukkha is usually translated “suffering”, but its range is wider. The commentarial tradition distinguishes three levels: ordinary pain, physical and mental (dukkha-dukkha); the suffering inherent in change, since even pleasant experiences pass (vipariṇāma-dukkha); and the unsatisfactoriness of conditioned existence as such (saṅkhāra-dukkha), which is what the first sermon means when it says that “the five aggregates of clinging are suffering”. The claim is not that life contains no pleasure, but that nothing conditioned can be a lasting refuge.

The second truth names the origin of suffering as craving (taṇhā, literally “thirst”), which the sermon divides into three: craving for sense pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), for existence and becoming (bhava-taṇhā), and for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). The third category is philosophically significant: the wish for annihilation is treated as another form of grasping, not as a way out, which is one reason why the Buddhist goal cannot be identified with mere extinction. The third truth asserts that craving can be abandoned without remainder, and calls its cessation nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa) — described in the canon not as a place or a state of existence but as the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) and the deathless (amata). The fourth truth is the path that leads there.

docs.title: 2.4 The Noble Eightfold Path (Ariya Aṭṭhaṅgika Magga)
docs.text:
The Eightfold Path is traditionally represented as a wheel with eight spokes, the Dhamma-wheel that the Buddha set in motion at Sarnath. Its eight factors are not stages to be completed one after another but aspects of a single training, which the tradition groups under three heads (tividhā sikkhā): wisdom, morality and meditation (Figure 2.3 and Table 2.2). The order of the groups is instructive. Right view comes first because some understanding of the problem is needed to begin; morality supports the calm of meditation; and meditation in turn deepens the understanding with which the path began. The Dhammapada calls the eightfold path the best of paths (Dhp 273) and goes on:

Es’ eva maggo n’ atth’ añño dassanassa visuddhiyā; etaṃ hi tumhe paṭipajjatha, mārass’ etaṃ pamohanaṃ.

This is the path, there is no other, for the purification of vision. Follow this path; it is the bewilderment of Māra.

— Dhammapada 274

Figure 2.3. The Noble Eightfold Path, depicted as the Dhamma wheel (Dhammacakka). The eight factors are grouped into the three trainings: wisdom (paññā), morality (sīla) and meditation (samādhi). Table 2.2. The Noble Eightfold Path: detailed description Group No. Factor (Pāli) Description Paññā 1 Sammā Diṭṭhi Right Understanding: understanding the Four Noble Truths, the nature of karma and rebirth, and the three characteristics of existence 2 Sammā Saṅkappa Right Intention: the resolve towards renunciation, goodwill, and harmlessness Sīla 3 Sammā Vācā Right Speech: abstaining from lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter 4 Sammā Kammanta Right Action: abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct 5 Sammā Ājīva Right Livelihood: earning one’s living in ways that do not cause harm Samādhi 6 Sammā Vāyāma Right Effort: the fourfold effort to prevent and abandon unwholesome states, and to develop and maintain wholesome states 7 Sammā Sati Right Mindfulness: the fourfold establishment of mindfulness (body, feelings, mind, and dhammas) 8 Sammā Samādhi Right Concentration: the development of the four jhānas (meditative absorptions)

docs.title: 2.5 The Middle Way (Majjhimā Paṭipadā)
docs.text:
The first sermon opens not with the four truths but with the Middle Way. Having lived in luxury as a prince and in self-mortification as an ascetic, the Buddha rejects both, and the rest of his teaching repeatedly applies the same move to philosophical questions — between the view that a person is an eternal self and the view that he is annihilated at death, for example.

Dve ’me, bhikkhave, antā pabbajitena na sevitabbā. Katame dve? Yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo hīno gammo pothujjaniko anariyo anatthasaṃhito, yo cāyaṃ attakilamathānuyogo dukkho anariyo anatthasaṃhito. Ete kho, bhikkhave, ubho ante anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati.

““Monks, these two extremes should not be practised by one who has gone forth. What two? That which is devoted to sensual pleasure — which is low, vulgar, ignoble, and unprofitable; and that which is devoted to self-mortification — which is painful, ignoble, and unprofitable. Avoiding both these extremes, the Middle Way realised by the Tathāgata produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to calm, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.””

— Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, SN 56.11

docs.title: 2.6 Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda)
docs.text:
Dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda, Pāli paṭiccasamuppāda) is the Buddha’s account of how suffering arises and how it can end. In its general form it states only that things arise in dependence on conditions and cease when the conditions cease. In its best-known application it analyses the process of suffering and rebirth as a chain of twelve links (nidāna; Figure 2.4), though the canon also gives shorter chains, and the division of the twelve links over three lives is a later commentarial interpretation (Gethin 1998; Siderits 2007). The teaching does important work in the system: it explains continuity from life to life without a permanent self that passes from one to the next, since each state is conditioned by the one before.

Imasmiṃ sati, idaṃ hoti; imass’ uppādā, idaṃ uppajjati. Imasmiṃ asati, idaṃ na hoti; imassa nirodhā, idaṃ nirujjhati.

When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.

— Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.21; Majjhima Nikāya 115

Figure 2.4. The twelve links (nidānas) of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda), forming the cycle of conditioned existence (saṃsāra). The colours mark the division into three lives made by the later commentarial (Abhidhamma) interpretation. The cessation of ignorance (avijjā) at the first link leads to the cessation of the entire chain.

docs.title: 2.7 The Three Characteristics of Existence (Tilakkhaṇa)
docs.text:
The three “marks” (tilakkhaṇa) are linked by an argument. Whatever is conditioned is impermanent (anicca), arising and passing away; what is impermanent cannot give lasting satisfaction and so is dukkha; and what is impermanent and unsatisfactory, and not under one’s control, cannot be the permanent self (attā) that the Brahmanical thinkers of the time sought. Hence all phenomena are non-self (anattā). The Dhammapada states the three insights in parallel verses, with a significant shift in the third: not only conditioned things (saṅkhārā) but all phenomena (dhammā), including the unconditioned, are without self.

Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā ti, yadā paññāya passati, atha nibbindatī dukkhe — esa maggo visuddhiyā. Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā ti, yadā paññāya passati, atha nibbindatī dukkhe — esa maggo visuddhiyā. Sabbe dhammā anattā ti, yadā paññāya passati, atha nibbindatī dukkhe — esa maggo visuddhiyā.

““All conditioned things are impermanent” — when one sees this with wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path to purification. “All conditioned things are unsatisfactory” — when one sees this with wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path to purification. “All phenomena are non-self” — when one sees this with wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering. This is the path to purification.”

— Dhammapada 277–279

docs.title: 2.8 The Jātaka Tales and the Perfections
docs.text:
The Jātaka collection of the Pāli canon, comprising 547 stories of the Buddha’s previous births, is among the best-loved parts of the Pāli canon. These narratives trace the Bodhisatta’s (the future Buddha’s) cultivation of the perfections (pāramī) over countless lifetimes, in forms ranging from a king to a monkey, from an elephant to a quail. Strictly, only the verses are canonical; the prose stories are preserved in the later commentary (Jātakaṭṭhavaṇṇanā), and many draw on the common stock of Indian folk narrative (Norman 1983).

The stories served several purposes at once. They showed the perfections being built up over many lives, which made the Buddha’s final awakening the outcome of a long moral career rather than a sudden gift; they gave monks and lay people exemplars of conduct; and they supplied the narrative programme of much early Buddhist art, from the reliefs of Bharhut and Sanchi to the murals of Ajanta. The Theravāda tradition counts ten perfections, first listed in the late canonical Buddhavaṃsa and Cariyāpiṭaka: generosity (dāna), morality (sīla), renunciation (nekkhamma), wisdom (paññā), energy (viriya), patience (khanti), truthfulness (sacca), resolve (adhiṭṭhāna), loving-kindness (mettā) and equanimity (upekkhā). The commentaries associate each with one of the ten “great Jātakas” that close the collection (Table 2.3); the Mahāyāna counts six perfections, or ten in an expanded list (Chapter 5).

Table 2.3. The ten “great Jātakas” (Mahānipāta, nos. 538–547) and the perfections traditionally associated with them No. Name Perfection Summary 538 Mūgapakkha (Temiya) Nekkhamma (renunciation) A prince feigns dumbness and paralysis for years to avoid becoming king 539 Mahājanaka Viriya (energy) A prince shipwrecked at sea swims on for seven days without giving up 540 Sāma (Suvaṇṇasāma) Mettā (loving-kindness) A devoted son, shot by a king, bears no ill-will 541 Nimi Adhiṭṭhāna (resolve) A righteous king tours the heavens and hells and keeps his resolve 542 Khaṇḍahāla (Candakumāra) Khanti (patience) A prince endures being condemned to sacrifice 543 Bhūridatta Sīla (virtue) A nāga prince keeps his precepts though captured by a snake-charmer 544 Mahānāradakassapa Upekkhā (equanimity) A Brahmā frees a king from a false view 545 Vidhurapaṇḍita Sacca (truthfulness) A wise minister keeps his word at the risk of his life 546 Mahā-ummagga (Mahosadha) Paññā (wisdom) A brilliant counsellor defeats his rivals by wit 547 Vessantara Dāna (generosity) A prince gives away everything, even his wife and children

The last of these, the Vessantara Jātaka, has been the most influential. Its story of a prince who gives away even his wife and children raised hard moral questions for its audiences, and it is still recited and performed at festivals across mainland Southeast Asia.

docs.title: 2.9 The Five Aggregates (Pañca Khandha)
docs.text:
The analysis of the person into five aggregates (pañca khandha) is the instrument by which the doctrine of non-self is argued. What we conventionally call a “person” is examined into material form, feeling, perception, volitional formations and consciousness (Table 2.4), and each is shown to be impermanent and beyond one’s control; no permanent self (attā) is found in any of them, singly or together.

Table 2.4. The Five Aggregates (Pañca Khandha) No. Pāli English Description 1 Rūpa Form/Matter The physical body and material objects; the four great elements (earth, water, fire, air) and their derivatives 2 Vedanā Feeling The affective tone of experience: pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral 3 Saññā Perception Recognition, identification, and categorisation of objects 4 Saṅkhāra Volitional formations Mental dispositions, intentions, and karmic imprints; the aggregate that drives rebirth 5 Viññāṇa Consciousness Awareness of objects through the six sense doors (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind)

Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā. Rūpañ ca h’ idaṃ, bhikkhave, attā abhavissa, nayidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyya, labbhetha ca rūpe: “Evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī” ti.

““Form, monks, is not-self. For if form were self, monks, then form would not lead to affliction, and one could have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus.’ ””

— Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, SN 22.59

According to the Vinaya (Mahāvagga I.6), this discourse, the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (Discourse on the Characteristic of Non-Self), was the Buddha’s second sermon, delivered to the same five ascetics at the Deer Park, all of whom became arahants on hearing it. Its argument is simple and has remained central to Buddhist philosophy: if any aggregate were the self, one could command it, and since none can be commanded and all are impermanent, none is the self.

docs.title: 2.10 The Doctrine of Karma and Rebirth
docs.text:
The Buddhist understanding of karma (kamma) shares the general Indian idea that actions bear fruit in this and later lives, but it differs from both the Brahmanical and the Jain conceptions in where it locates the act.

Scholarly Note: Karma as Intention

The Buddhist doctrine of karma differs from the Jain doctrine in a crucial respect. For Jainism, karma is a subtle form of matter (pudgala) that physically adheres to the soul. For Buddhism, karma is fundamentally intentional action (cetanā). As the Buddha stated: “Cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi” — “It is intention, monks, that I call karma” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63). The consequence is that, for the Buddhist, the moral quality of an action resides in the intention behind it, not in the physical act alone; the Jains, as Chapter 8 shows, judged that unintended harm also binds karma.

The Buddhist theory of karma operates within the framework of Paṭiccasamuppāda (Dependent Origination). Karmic actions produce results (vipāka) not through any metaphysical substance but through the causal process of consciousness itself. Wholesome (kusala) actions — those rooted in non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion — produce pleasant results, while unwholesome (akusala) actions — those rooted in greed, hatred, and delusion — produce painful results.

Manasā ce paduṭṭhena bhāsatī vā karoti vā, tato naṃ dukkham anveti cakkaṃ va vahato padaṃ. Manasā ce pasannena bhāsatī vā karoti vā, tato naṃ sukham anveti chāyā va anapāyinī.

““If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, then suffering follows one, as the wheel of the cart follows the foot of the ox. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, then happiness follows one, like a shadow that never departs.””

— Dhammapada 1–2 (last four lines of each verse)

docs.title: 2.11 The Chief Disciples
docs.text:
The canon remembers the Buddha’s community through particular people. A chapter of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 1.188–267) names the monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen who were “foremost” (etadagga) in some quality (Bodhi 2012). The list is formulaic, but it is revealing. The two chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, were brāhmaṇas who had followed the sceptic Sañjaya; the authority on the Vinaya, Upāli, had been a barber; and the nuns and lay followers receive their own lists alongside the monks, so that the text presents the fourfold community as a whole (Table 2.5; the lay followers are discussed in Chapter 13, Section 13.4.1).

Table 2.5. Some of the foremost disciples of the Buddha (after AN 1) Disciple Eminence Notes Sāriputta Foremost in wisdom The Buddha’s right-hand disciple; regarded by Theravāda tradition as the first transmitter of the Abhidhamma Moggallāna Foremost in psychic powers The Buddha’s left-hand disciple; renowned for supernormal abilities Mahākassapa Foremost in ascetic practices Presided over the First Council at Rājagaha Ānanda Foremost as personal attendant The Buddha’s cousin and devoted attendant; recited the Sutta Piṭaka at the First Council Upāli Foremost in Vinaya Originally a barber; recited the Vinaya Piṭaka at the First Council Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Foremost among nuns in seniority The Buddha’s foster-mother; first woman ordained as a bhikkhunī Khemā Foremost in wisdom (nuns) Former queen; attained Arahantship through insight into impermanence Uppalavaṇṇā Foremost in psychic powers (nuns) Attained the highest supernormal powers among the nuns Rāhula Foremost in training The Buddha’s own son; exemplar of monastic discipline Subhūti Foremost in dwelling without conflict Later a key interlocutor in the Prajñāpāramitā literature of the Mahāyāna

docs.title: 2.12 The Buddhist Ethics of Compassion
docs.text:
The ethics of the early texts is not only a matter of precepts. They also teach the cultivation of four attitudes, the “divine abodes” (brahmavihāra) or “boundless states” (appamaññā): loving-kindness (mettā), the wish that beings be happy; compassion (karuṇā), the wish that they be free from suffering; sympathetic joy (muditā) in the happiness of others; and equanimity (upekkhā), an impartiality that is not indifference. The name is itself an appropriation: the Buddha calls these states the way to companionship with Brahmā, reinterpreting the goal of the Brahmanical seeker in ethical terms.

Sukhino vā khemino hontu, sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā.

““May all beings be happy and secure; may all beings be happy at heart.””

— Mettā Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 145 (= Khuddakapāṭha 9)

The divine abodes are developed in meditation, but the texts present them as an orientation for the whole of life. The Mettā Sutta asks the practitioner to extend loving-kindness to all beings “whether seen or unseen, dwelling far or near, born or seeking birth” (Sn 147).

docs.title: 2.13 The Parinirvāṇa
docs.text:
According to tradition the Buddha taught for forty-five years, travelling across the Gangetic plains, establishing the Saṅgha (monastic community), and teaching beings from all walks of life. At the age of eighty, at Kuśinagara (Pāli Kusinārā, modern Kushinagar), he entered Parinirvāṇa — the final passing beyond the cycle of rebirth. The scene, the Buddha lying on his right side between twin sāla trees, became one of the standard subjects of Buddhist art; the colossal reclining image in Ajanta Cave 26 (5th century CE) is the best-known early Indian example.

His last words, as recorded in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Walshe 1995), are:

Handa dāni, bhikkhave, āmantayāmi vo: vayadhammā saṅkhārā, appamādena sampādetha.

Now then, monks, I address you: conditioned things are of a nature to decay; strive on with diligence.

— Dīgha Nikāya 16.6.7, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta

docs.title: 2.14 The Saṅgha: Foundation of the Buddhist Community
docs.text: The establishment of the Saṅgha (monastic community) is one of the Buddha’s most consequential institutional innovations. The Saṅgha provided the organisational framework within which the Dhamma could be practised, preserved, and transmitted across generations. The Buddha established a fourfold community (catu-parisa): monks (bhikkhus), nuns (bhikkhunīs), male lay followers (upāsakas), and female lay followers (upāsikās).

docs.title: 2.14.1 The Vinaya and Communal Governance
docs.text:
The Vinaya Piṭaka records the rules and procedures governing monastic life. Formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) were carried out by the monks resident within a boundary (sīmā), using fixed formulas (kammavācā) with a motion followed by one or three announcements; silence signified consent. Most acts required the agreement of all qualified monks present, but some disputes could be settled by a majority vote taken with voting-sticks (yebhuyyasikā). Disputes were settled by seven prescribed procedures (adhikaraṇa-samatha), among them settlement in the presence of the parties, majority vote and the “covering over with grass” of mutual offences. Rank within the community was fixed by seniority of ordination rather than by birth, caste or wealth; monastic property belonged to the Saṅgha as a whole rather than to individuals; and each newly ordained monk was placed for training under a preceptor (upajjhāya). These arrangements have often been compared with the assemblies of the republican clans (gaṇa, saṅgha) of the Buddha’s time, from which the word saṅgha itself was borrowed (Dutt 1962; Gethin 1998). How they worked in the life of a monk is described in Chapter 13.

Nineteenth-century scholars such as T. W. Rhys Davids admired these procedures as an early example of self-government. The comparison should not be pressed too far: the Saṅgha was a community of renunciants bound by a fixed code, not a representative assembly, and authority also rested on seniority and the teacher–pupil relationship.

docs.title: 2.14.2 The Order of Nuns
docs.text:
The establishment of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha (order of nuns) is among the most significant social acts attributed to the Buddha. According to the Vinaya, the order was founded at the request of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the Buddha’s foster mother, who approached him together with five hundred Sākyan women seeking ordination.

The Therīgāthā: Verses of the Elder Nuns

The Therīgāthā, in the Khuddaka Nikāya of the Pāli canon, is a collection of some 73 poems attributed to early Buddhist nuns. It is among the earliest surviving collections of poetry attributed to women anywhere. The verses express joy at liberation and freedom from the burdens of domestic life. The nun Muttā, for example, rejoices at being freed from “three crooked things” — the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband (Thig 11) (Hallisey 2015). The collection affirms that women could attain the highest goal (arahatta), a point the Buddha himself is reported to have conceded when the order of nuns was founded.

The same Vinaya account, however, also states that the Buddha hesitated to admit women and imposed eight “weighty rules” (garudhamma) that subordinate nuns to monks — for example, that a nun of a hundred years’ standing must bow to a monk ordained that day. Many scholars regard these rules, and the prediction that the admission of women would shorten the life of the teaching, as later additions. The order of nuns died out in Sri Lanka around the eleventh century and later in the other Theravāda countries, and has been revived only recently and controversially (Gethin 1998; Harvey 2013).

docs.title: 2.14.3 The Buddha’s Pedagogical Methods
docs.text:
The suttas portray the Buddha as a teacher who adapted his method to his audience — what the Mahāyāna would later systematise as skill in means (upāya-kauśalya). He led interlocutors to a conclusion by questions rather than by assertion, and he taught laymen by a graduated discourse (anupubbī-kathā) that began with generosity, morality and the heavens, went on to the limitations of sensual pleasure, and ended with the four noble truths. His discourses are full of similes (Table 2.6), several of which make a philosophical point about the teaching itself: the raft is to be left behind once the river is crossed, and the man struck by a poisoned arrow should not ask who shot it before having it drawn out. The suttas also show him urging listeners to test his teaching in their own experience, as in the Kālāma Sutta (AN 3.65), although they stress faith (saddhā) in the teacher as well; that much-quoted discourse is read in context in Chapter 3.

Table 2.6. Key similes (upamā) in the early discourses Simile Source Teaching Illustrated The Raft MN 22 Teachings are means, not ends; let go even of the Dhamma The Poisoned Arrow MN 63 Avoid speculation; focus on the practical task of ending suffering The Elephant Footprint MN 28 Spoken by Sāriputta: the Four Noble Truths contain all wholesome teachings The Handful of Leaves SN 56.31 The Buddha teaches only what is useful for liberation The Blind Turtle SN 56.48 The extreme rarity and preciousness of human birth The Chariot SN 5.10 Spoken by the nun Vajirā: a “being” is a conventional designation for a collection of parts

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Tripiṭaka: Three Baskets of the Dhamma
3.1 The Canonical Literature of Buddhism
docs.text:
The Tipiṭaka (Sanskrit: Tripiṭaka), literally “Three Baskets,” is the name given to the canonical collections of the early Buddhist schools. The Pāli Tipiṭaka preserved by the Theravāda school is the only early Buddhist canon to survive complete in an Indian language. It is one recension among several: other early schools had their own canons, which survive in part in Sanskrit and Gāndhārī fragments and in Chinese and Tibetan translation. Much of its content goes back to the early centuries of Buddhism, but it also contains later layers (Norman 1983; Gethin 1998).

The term piṭaka means “basket”; it may refer to containers for manuscripts or, as some scholars suggest, to the baskets passed from hand to hand by workmen — an image of transmission from teacher to pupil. The three divisions reflect three dimensions of the Buddha’s dispensation (sāsana; Figure 3.1): the Vinaya Piṭaka, the “basket of discipline”, contains the monastic rules and the narratives of their origin; the Sutta Piṭaka (Sanskrit Sūtra), the “basket of discourses”, contains the teachings of the Buddha and his chief disciples; and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka (Sanskrit Abhidharma), the “basket of higher teaching”, recasts the teaching as a systematic analysis. The tradition’s own view of what the canon preserves is expressed in the recollection of the Dhamma, recited daily in Theravāda monasteries:

Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, sandiṭṭhiko akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī ti.

Well proclaimed by the Blessed One is the Dhamma, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.

— The recollection of the Dhamma (e.g. AN 3.70; DN 16)

Figure 3.1. The structure of the Tipiṭaka (Three Baskets), the canonical scripture of Theravāda Buddhism.

docs.title: 3.2 The Vinaya Piṭaka: The Basket of Discipline
docs.text: The Vinaya Piṭaka constitutes the legal and institutional foundation of the Buddhist monastic community (Saṅgha). It contains the rules of conduct for monks (bhikkhus) and nuns (bhikkhunīs), together with the narratives explaining the circumstances under which each rule was established by the Buddha (Norman 1983; Hirakawa 1990).

docs.title: 3.2.1 Structure of the Vinaya
docs.text:
The Vinaya Piṭaka consists of three major divisions:

Suttavibhaṅga The analysis and classification of the Pātimokkha rules — 227 rules for monks and 311 for nuns. Each rule is accompanied by a narrative of its origin (nidāna), a word-by-word commentary, and case studies illustrating its application. Khandhaka Subdivided into the Mahāvagga (Great Section) and Cullavagga (Minor Section). The Mahāvagga opens with the narrative of the Buddha’s enlightenment and first teachings, and contains regulations for ordination, the observance day (uposatha), the rainy season retreat (vassa), and other communal practices. The Cullavagga deals with disciplinary proceedings, schisms, and the establishment of the order of nuns. Parivāra A later appendix that provides summaries and catechetical analyses of the rules in the preceding sections.

docs.title: 3.2.2 The Pātimokkha
docs.text:
The Pātimokkha (Sanskrit: Prātimokṣa) is the core code of monastic discipline, recited fortnightly by the assembled Saṅgha. The 227 rules for monks are classified into eight categories of decreasing severity (Table 3.1).

Table 3.1. Categories of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha Category Pāli Term No. Consequence Defeat Pārājika 4 Permanent expulsion from the Saṅgha Formal Meeting Saṅghādisesa 13 Temporary suspension; formal proceedings required Indeterminate Aniyata 2 Determination depends on circumstances Forfeiture Nissaggiya Pācittiya 30 Forfeiture of item and confession Expiation Pācittiya 92 Confession to another monk Confession Pāṭidesanīya 4 Acknowledgement to a monk Training Rules Sekhiya 75 Rules of decorum and etiquette Settling Disputes Adhikaraṇa-samatha 7 Procedures for resolving disputes

The four pārājika (“defeats”) — sexual intercourse, theft, killing a human being, and false claims of spiritual attainment — are the most serious offences and end a monk’s membership of the order. Each rule is presented with the story of the incident that led the Buddha to lay it down, followed by definitions, exceptions and cases. The Vinaya is therefore a body of case law as much as a list of prohibitions, and it is still the working code of Theravāda monasteries; how it shaped monastic life in practice is described in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 3.3 The Sutta Piṭaka: The Basket of Discourses
docs.text: The Sutta Piṭaka is the largest and most widely read division of the Tipiṭaka. It contains the discourses (suttas) of the Buddha and, to a lesser extent, those of his chief disciples. These discourses cover the entire range of the Buddha’s teaching, from practical ethical guidance to the analysis of the person and of liberation (Norman 1983; Warder 1970).

docs.title: 3.3.1 The Five Nikāyas
docs.text:
The Sutta Piṭaka is organised into five collections (nikāya), arranged by the length of their discourses or by principles of grouping that served memorisation.

The Dīgha Nikāya, the collection of long discourses, contains thirty-four suttas. Among them are the Brahmajāla Sutta, a survey of sixty-two speculative views; the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, on the fruits of the contemplative life, which reports the six rival teachers (Chapter 1); the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, on the Buddha’s last days; and the Sigālovāda Sutta on lay ethics. The Majjhima Nikāya, the middle-length discourses, has 152 suttas covering doctrine, practice and narrative, including the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta on the foundations of mindfulness, the Ānāpānasati Sutta on mindfulness of breathing and the Cūḷamālukya Sutta with its parable of the poisoned arrow. The Saṃyutta Nikāya groups nearly three thousand short suttas (the count varies between editions) by topic into fifty-six “connected” collections (saṃyutta), among them the first sermon and the main discourses on dependent origination, the aggregates and the sense bases. The Aṅguttara Nikāya arranges its material by number, from ones to elevens, a mnemonic device for oral transmission.

The Khuddaka Nikāya, the “minor” collection, is the most heterogeneous and the least fixed: its contents differ between the Sri Lankan, Thai and Burmese traditions. It contains some of the most widely read texts of the canon — the 423 verses of the Dhammapada, the early verse discourses of the Sutta Nipāta, the Udāna and Itivuttaka, the 547 Jātaka stories, and the poems of the elder monks and nuns (Theragāthā, Therīgāthā), the latter among the earliest collections of poetry attributed to women anywhere.

Na paresaṃ vilomāni, na paresaṃ katākataṃ; attano va avekkheyya katāni akatāni ca.

One should not look at the faults of others, nor at what others have done or left undone; one should consider only what one has done and left undone oneself.

— Dhammapada 50

docs.title: 3.4 The Abhidhamma Piṭaka: The Basket of Higher Teaching
docs.text: The Abhidhamma Piṭaka represents the systematic, analytical dimension of Buddhist thought. While the Sutta Piṭaka presents the Buddha’s teaching in the form of discourses tailored to specific audiences and occasions, the Abhidhamma abstracts from these contextual presentations and offers a comprehensive, impersonal analysis of reality in terms of ultimate constituents (paramatthas).

docs.title: 3.4.1 The Seven Books of the Abhidhamma
docs.text:
The Pāli Abhidhamma Piṭaka consists of seven treatises:

Dhammasaṅgaṇī (Enumeration of Phenomena) The foundational text, which classifies all phenomena (dhammas) under the headings of consciousness (citta), mental factors (cetasika), matter (rūpa), and Nibbāna. Vibhaṅga (The Book of Analysis) A detailed analysis of key doctrinal categories such as the aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, and faculties. Dhātukathā (Discourse on Elements) A discussion of how the various categories of the Abhidhamma relate to the elements (dhātus). Puggalapaññatti (Designation of Persons) A typology of persons according to their spiritual development and psychological characteristics. Kathāvatthu (Points of Controversy) Attributed by Theravāda tradition to Moggaliputta Tissa at the Third Council under Aśoka, though it grew over a longer period, this work addresses over 200 points of doctrinal dispute among early Buddhist schools. Yamaka (The Book of Pairs) An extensive logical analysis using pairs of questions to clarify the precise application of doctrinal terms. Paṭṭhāna (The Book of Conditional Relations) The most voluminous and intellectually demanding text of the entire Tipiṭaka, analysing 24 types of conditional relations (paccaya) among phenomena.

docs.title: 3.4.2 The Abhidhamma Matrix of Reality
docs.text:
The later Theravāda Abhidhamma, as summarised in Anuruddha’s Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha (Bodhi 1993), analyses all of reality into four categories of ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma; Table 3.2).

Table 3.2. The four categories of ultimate reality in Abhidhamma Category Pāli Term Description Count Consciousness Citta The knowing function; classified by type and level 89 (or 121) Mental Factors Cetasika Concomitants of consciousness: feelings, perceptions, volitions 52 Matter Rūpa Physical phenomena: the four great elements and their derivatives 28 Nibbāna Nibbāna The unconditioned element; the cessation of suffering 1

docs.title: 3.4.3 The Twenty-Four Conditional Relations
docs.text:
The Paṭṭhāna, the seventh and final book of the Abhidhamma, is held in particular reverence in Theravāda countries. It analyses twenty-four types of conditional relation (paccaya) through which phenomena condition one another. Some are relations of cause in the ordinary sense: the “root” condition (hetu) by which greed, hatred and delusion or their opposites underlie a mental state, the “object” condition (ārammaṇa) by which an object conditions the consciousness of it, and the “karma” and “result” conditions (kamma, vipāka) linking an intention to its later fruit. Others are relations of time and dependence: proximity and contiguity (anantara, samanantara) between successive moments of mind, co-nascence and mutuality (sahajāta, aññamañña) between states that arise together, pre-nascence and post-nascence (purejāta, pacchājāta), and support and decisive support (nissaya, upanissaya). The remainder are predominance, repetition, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance and non-disappearance.

Applied in all their permutations to every class of phenomena, these relations make the Paṭṭhāna the most detailed treatment of conditionality in the Pāli canon.

docs.title: 3.5 Transmission and Preservation
docs.text:
The Tipiṭaka was originally transmitted orally through a system of communal recitation. According to tradition the first formal compilation took place at the First Council (saṅgīti, “communal recitation”) at Rājagṛha, shortly after the Buddha’s death, where Ānanda recited the discourses and Upāli the monastic discipline. Historians regard the council narratives as idealised, but they reflect the real practice of communal recitation by which the texts were transmitted (Norman 1983).

According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, the text was first committed to writing in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE, during the reign of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi Abhaya, after a period of famine and war had threatened the continuity of oral transmission. The councils are summarised in Table 3.3; the last of them, the Burmese council of 1871, had the whole canon inscribed on marble (Figure 3.2).

Table 3.3. The Buddhist Councils and their contributions to canonical preservation Council Date (approx.) Location Significance First soon after the Buddha’s death (tradition) Rājagṛha Compilation of Vinaya and Sutta Piṭakas Second about a century later Vaiśālī Dispute over ten points of Vinaya; beginning of sectarian divisions Third c. 250 BCE (Theravāda tradition) Pāṭaliputra Under Aśoka; Kathāvatthu; missions sent abroad Writing down c. 29 BCE (tradition) Aluvihāra, Sri Lanka Canon committed to writing (other traditions count a “fourth council” under Kaniṣka in Kashmir) Fifth 1871 CE Mandalay, Myanmar Entire Tipiṭaka inscribed on 729 marble slabs Sixth 1954–56 Rangoon, Myanmar Comprehensive recension of the Pāli canon Figure 3.2. Shrines at the Kuthodaw Pagoda in Mandalay, each housing one of the 729 marble slabs on which the Pāli Tipiṭaka was inscribed after the Burmese “Fifth Council” of 1871. Photo: Philip Nalangan, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.6 The Art of Oral Transmission
docs.text:
The Tipiṭaka was transmitted orally for some three to four centuries before it was written down, and recitation remained central to monastic life long afterwards. The methods by which the early Saṅgha preserved its texts can be partly reconstructed from the texts themselves.

The System of Communal Recitation

The early Buddhist Saṅgha preserved the canonical texts by communal recitation (saṅgīti). Monks specialised as “reciters” (bhāṇaka) of particular collections: the commentaries speak of Dīgha-bhāṇakas (reciters of the Long Discourses), Majjhima-bhāṇakas (reciters of the Middle-Length Discourses) and others, and early inscriptions at Sanchi and Bharhut already name donors described as bhāṇakas or as knowing the piṭakas. Each group maintained its portion through regular communal recitation, a division of labour that combined specialisation with mutual checking.

The texts themselves show how they were made to be remembered. Stock phrases and refrains recur constantly and served as mnemonic anchors; the Aṅguttara Nikāya arranges its teachings by number; many sections end with a short verse summary (uddāna) that acts as an index; and the question-and-answer form of many suttas gives a natural frame for recitation. Regular group recitation allowed errors to be detected and corrected by the community, which is why the canon, though transmitted orally for centuries, shows a high degree of agreement with the parallel texts preserved by other schools in Chinese and Sanskrit.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Comparison with the Jain Āgamic Tradition
docs.text:
The Jain canon (Āgama) was transmitted by similar methods, with one important difference in its history. Jain tradition holds that the fourteen Pūrvas (“former texts”), which contained the oldest teaching, were gradually lost through famine and the failure of memory, and that the surviving Śvetāmbara canon was redacted only in the fifth century CE, at Valabhī; the Digambaras regard the ancient canon as lost altogether. The structure of the Jain canon and the history of its redaction are described in Chapter 8 (Section 8.5); Table 3.4 sets out the main contrasts (Dundas 2002).

Table 3.4. Comparison of Buddhist and Jain canonical traditions Feature Buddhist Tipiṭaka Jain Āgamas Language Pāli (Theravāda); Sanskrit (Mahāyāna) Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit (Śvetāmbara canon) Compiler(s) Ānanda (Suttas), Upāli (Vinaya) at First Council (tradition) Mahāvīra’s chief disciples (gaṇadhara), above all Sudharman (Śvetāmbara tradition); final redaction at Valabhī Written down c. 1st century BCE (Sri Lanka) 5th century CE (Valabhī, tradition) Divisions Three Piṭakas: Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma 45 texts in six groups for Mūrtipūjakas, 32 for other Śvetāmbaras (Table 8.3) Disputed portions Abhidhamma: some scholars regard as later Digambaras hold the ancient canon lost and rely on later scriptures such as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama Lost texts Canons of other early schools (mostly lost) The fourteen Pūrvas (entirely lost)

docs.title: 3.7 Detailed Analysis of Key Suttas
docs.text: Three discourses show the range of the Sutta Piṭaka: one on meditation, one often misread as a charter of free inquiry, and one on the duties of a householder.

docs.title: 3.7.1 The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta: Foundation of Mindfulness Practice
docs.text:
The Mahā-Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (DN 22) and its shorter counterpart in the Majjhima Nikāya (MN 10) constitute the most comprehensive meditation instruction in the Pāli Canon. It opens with a strong claim:

Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā, sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya, dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya, ñāyassa adhigamāya, nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya — yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.

““This is the direct path, monks, for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, for the realisation of Nibbāna — namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.””

— Dīgha Nikāya 22

The word ekāyano (“direct” or “one-way”) has been interpreted in various ways: as the “only way,” the “direct way,” or the way that leads to one destination (Nibbāna). Regardless of interpretation, the discourse establishes mindfulness (sati) as the central practice of the Buddhist path.

docs.title: 3.7.2 The Kālāma Sutta: Testing a Teaching
docs.text:
The Kālāma Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.65) is often cited as the Buddha’s “charter of free inquiry” — a statement of intellectual independence that has appealed strongly to modern readers (Bodhi 2012):
