Mā anussavena, mā paramparāya, mā iti-kirāya, mā piṭaka-sampadānena, mā takkahetu, mā nayahetu, mā ākāra-parivitakkena, mā diṭṭhi-nijjhānakkhantiyā, mā bhabbarūpatāya, mā “samaṇo no garū” ti.

““Do not go by oral tradition, by lineage of teaching, by hearsay, by a collection of scriptures, by logical reasoning, by inferential reasoning, by reflection on reasons, by the acceptance of a view after pondering it, by the seeming competence of a speaker, or because you think: ‘This ascetic is our teacher.’ ” The passage continues: when you know for yourselves that certain things are unwholesome and lead to harm, abandon them.”

— Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.65

The criteria the sutta offers are practical and ethical: whether a teaching, when adopted, leads to greed, hatred and delusion or to their absence, and whether it is blamed or praised by the wise. Read in context, it is advice to a bewildered audience on how to judge rival teachers, not a general licence to accept only what one finds reasonable; the same discourse goes on to describe the practice of the divine abodes and ends with the Kālāmas going for refuge to the Buddha (Bodhi 2012).

docs.title: 3.7.3 The Sigālovāda Sutta: The Layperson’s Code of Ethics
docs.text:
The Sigālovāda Sutta (DN 31), sometimes called “the layperson’s Vinaya,” provides a comprehensive ethical framework for householder life, covering duties towards parents, teachers, spouse, friends, servants, and religious practitioners (Table 3.5). Its systematic treatment of social ethics has been compared to the comprehensive ethical codes found in Jain lay practice (śrāvakācāra).

Table 3.5. The six directions of social duties in the Sigālovāda Sutta Direction Relationship Key Duties East Parents Support, honour, maintain the family traditions, be worthy of inheritance South Teachers Rise to greet, attend upon, listen eagerly, serve, learn the arts West Wife (and children) Courtesy, faithfulness, handing over authority in the home, provision of adornments North Friends Generosity, kind speech, acting for welfare, equality, honesty Nadir Servants/Workers Assign work according to ability, provide food and wages, care during illness Zenith Ascetics/Brahmins Acts of love in body, speech, and mind; keep one’s home open; supply needs

docs.title: 3.8 The Abhidhamma Analysis of Mind
docs.text:
The canonical Abhidhamma books and the later manuals do not add new doctrines so much as restate the teaching of the suttas in impersonal terms. Where a sutta speaks of “a person” who feels or decides, the Abhidhamma speaks of momentary events of consciousness (citta) accompanied by mental factors (cetasika), in the categories summarised in Table 3.2. The result is a detailed phenomenology of experience, which modern scholars have compared, with due caution, to topics in the philosophy of mind (Gethin 1998; Bodhi 1993). Two features illustrate its character: its theory of momentariness and its analysis of the process of perception.

Scholarly Note: Momentariness

The Abhidhamma’s analysis of a single moment of consciousness (citta-kkhaṇa) as consisting of three sub-moments — arising (uppāda), standing (ṭhiti), and dissolving (bhaṅga) — each of inconceivably brief duration, is an early and systematic analysis of the moment-to-moment structure of experience. The commentaries say that many billions of such moments pass in the time of a lightning-flash or the blink of an eye — a way of expressing their extreme brevity rather than a measurement. This radical impermanence at the finest temporal scale provides the experiential basis for the doctrine of anicca (impermanence) and anattā (non-self).

docs.title: 3.8.1 The Process of Consciousness (Citta-vīthi)
docs.text: The commentarial Abhidhamma describes a sense-cognition as a sequence of seventeen consciousness-moments (citta-kkhaṇa). The resting stream of consciousness (bhavaṅga) is disturbed by an object and cut off; the mind adverts to the sense door (pañcadvāra-āvajjana); a moment of sense consciousness, such as seeing, arises; it is received (sampaṭicchana), investigated (santīraṇa) and determined (voṭṭhapana); seven moments of “impulsion” (javana) follow; and two moments of registration (tadārammaṇa) close the process before the mind sinks back into the life-continuum. The scheme is ethical as well as descriptive. The javana moments are the karmically active phase, in which the mind responds to what it has perceived with greed or generosity, hatred or friendliness; everything before them is the result of past karma, and everything that matters for the future is decided in them.

docs.title: 3.9 The Early Schools and the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma
docs.text:
The Pāli canon is the canon of one school among many. Indian Buddhist sources speak conventionally of “eighteen schools” (nikāya), although the lists differ and more than eighteen names are known (Lamotte 1988; Hirakawa 1990). After the first division between the Sthaviras and the Mahāsāṅghikas, the Sthavira branch gave rise, among others, to the Sarvāstivāda, the Dharmaguptaka, the Mahīśāsaka, the “personalist” Vātsīputrīya–Sāṃmitīya group and the Theravāda of Sri Lanka. The schools were defined above all by their monastic codes, and several of their Vinayas survive: the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, in Chinese translation, became the standard code of East Asian Buddhism, and the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, preserved in Tibetan and in part in Sanskrit, became that of Tibet.

The most influential Abhidharma outside the Theravāda was that of the Sarvāstivāda, strong in Kashmir and the north-west. Its name (“the doctrine that everything exists”) refers to its distinctive thesis that dharmas exist in the past and the future as well as in the present, which it used to explain memory, knowledge of the past and the delayed ripening of karma. Its doctrine was codified in the great commentary Mahāvibhāṣā, compiled in Kashmir in the early centuries CE; tradition connects it with a council held under the Kuṣāṇa king Kaniṣka. The “Vaibhāṣikas”, who followed this commentary, analysed experience into seventy-five dharmas in five groups: eleven material dharmas, mind, forty-six mental factors, fourteen factors “dissociated from mind” and three unconditioned dharmas, namely space and two kinds of cessation (Williams and Tribe 2000; Gethin 1998).

Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa (“Treasury of Abhidharma”), some six hundred verses in eight chapters with the author’s own prose commentary and an appendix refuting the “person” of the personalists, set out the Vaibhāṣika system while criticising many of its positions from the standpoint of the Sautrāntikas, who denied the existence of past and future dharmas and held that every conditioned thing lasts only a moment. (Whether this Vasubandhu is the same person as the Yogācāra author of that name is debated.) The Kashmiri master Saṅghabhadra wrote a long rebuttal defending Vaibhāṣika orthodoxy, but the Abhidharmakośa became the standard textbook of Abhidharma in India, Tibet and East Asia, and its categories and arguments formed the background against which Madhyamaka, Yogācāra and the Buddhist logicians worked. The Abhidharma schools are placed among the other Indian philosophical systems in Volume 3 of this series (Darśana Darpaṇa).

docs.title: 3.10 Other Canonical Traditions
docs.text: The Pāli Tipiṭaka is the most complete surviving canon of an early school, but it is not the only witness to early Buddhism. The Chinese Buddhist canon (Dazangjing) contains translations of the discourse collections (Āgamas), Vinayas and Abhidharma treatises of several other early schools, together with Mahāyāna and tantric texts and Chinese works. The Tibetan canon, the Kangyur and Tengyur, preserves the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya and a large body of later Indian literature. Fragments of the Sanskrit canons of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda and other schools have been recovered from Central Asia, Gilgit and Gandhāra, and the Gāndhārī birch-bark scrolls (1st century BCE–2nd century CE) are the oldest Buddhist manuscripts known. Comparison of these parallel versions with the Pāli is the main method by which scholars now identify the early core of the tradition.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Theravāda: The Teaching of the Elders
4.1 Origins and Identity of Theravāda
docs.text:
The Theravāda (“Teaching of the Elders”) is the only one of the early Indian schools of Buddhism to survive to the present day as a living school with its own canon. (The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, by contrast, survives in East Asia only as the monastic code of Mahāyāna monks and nuns.) Theravādins understand themselves as preserving the authentic Dhamma-Vinaya (Doctrine and Discipline) as taught by the Buddha and compiled at the First Council, and they often point to his instruction, near the end of his life, that his followers should rely on the teaching rather than on any successor:

Attadīpā viharatha attasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā, dhammadīpā dhammasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā.

Dwell with yourselves as your island, with yourselves as your refuge, with no other refuge; dwell with the Dhamma as your island, with the Dhamma as your refuge, with no other refuge.

— Dīgha Nikāya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Walshe 1995)

The term Theravāda (Sanskrit: Sthaviravāda) refers to the “Doctrine of the Elders” (theras), signifying the senior monks who, according to tradition, maintained the orthodox teachings in the face of various innovations and reinterpretations proposed by other groups. Some time after the Second Council at Vaiśālī, about a century after the Buddha’s death, the Saṅgha divided into the Sthaviras (“Elders”) and the Mahāsāṅghikas (“Great Community”), and further schools developed from each. Historically, the Theravāda is the branch of the Sthavira lineage that became established in Sri Lanka, centred on the Mahāvihāra monastery of Anurādhapura; from there it spread to mainland Southeast Asia, where it became dominant from the eleventh to the fourteenth centuries (Gombrich 2006; Gethin 1998).

docs.title: 4.1.1 The Vibhajjavāda Heritage
docs.text: The Theravāda school is closely associated with the Vibhajjavāda (“Doctrine of Analysis”) — a tradition that emphasised careful, analytical investigation of the Dhamma. The Third Council at Pāṭaliputra, convened under Emperor Aśoka (c. 250 BCE), is regarded in the Sri Lankan chronicles as the council at which the Vibhajjavādin position was vindicated, and from which the Theravāda mission to Sri Lanka was dispatched under the leadership of Aśoka’s son, the Venerable Mahinda.

docs.title: 4.2 The Pāli Commentarial Tradition
docs.text: While the Tipiṭaka provides the canonical foundation, the Theravāda intellectual tradition is equally characterised by a rich commentarial literature (Aṭṭhakathā) and sub-commentarial literature (Ṭīkā) that systematise, explain, and extend the canonical teachings.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Buddhaghosa and the Visuddhimagga
docs.text:
The central figure of the Theravāda commentarial tradition is Bhadantācariya Buddhaghosa (5th century CE), described in the later chronicles as a brāhmaṇa from India (the region is disputed) who travelled to Sri Lanka and, working from the older Sinhala commentaries of the Mahāvihāra, produced the standard Pāli commentaries on the major divisions of the Tipiṭaka.

His principal independent work, the Visuddhimagga (“Path of Purification”), became the standard exposition of Theravāda doctrine and practice (Buddhaghosa 1956). It is a commentary on a single verse of the Saṃyutta Nikāya (quoted below), arranged under the three trainings of morality, concentration and wisdom (Table 4.1), and its authority is such that later Theravāda has largely read the canon through it.

Table 4.1. Structure of the Visuddhimagga Division Training Chapters Content Part I Sīla (Morality) 1–2 The foundation of moral discipline; the Pātimokkha rules; ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) Part II Samādhi (Concentration) 3–13 Forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna); development of jhāna (meditative absorption); divine abodes (brahmavihāra) Part III Paññā (Wisdom) 14–23 Abhidhamma analysis; dependent origination; the five aggregates; insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa); the path and its fruit

Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño cittaṃ paññañ ca bhāvayaṃ, ātāpī nipako bhikkhu so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ.

A wise man, established in virtue, developing mind and wisdom, a monk ardent and discerning — he can disentangle this tangle.

— Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23, the verse on which the Visuddhimagga is a commentary

docs.title: 4.3 Vipassanā Meditation
docs.text: Vipassanā (“insight”) meditation constitutes the distinctive meditative practice of the Theravāda tradition. While samatha (tranquillity) meditation aims at the development of deep concentration (jhāna), Vipassanā aims at the direct, experiential insight into the three characteristics of existence: anicca (impermanence), dukkha (unsatisfactoriness), and anattā (non-self) (Gethin 1998; Gombrich 2006).

docs.title: 4.3.1 The Satipaṭṭhāna Method
docs.text:
The foundational text for Vipassanā practice is the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (“Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness,” DN 22), which lays out four domains of mindful observation (Figure 4.1).

Figure 4.1. The Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna), the core framework of Vipassanā meditation in the Theravāda tradition.

docs.title: 4.3.2 The Stages of Insight
docs.text: The Theravāda tradition, drawing on the canonical Paṭisambhidāmagga and the Visuddhimagga, describes in its later manuals a progressive sequence of sixteen insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa). The meditator first learns to distinguish mental from material events (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) and to see their conditions (paccaya-pariggaha); then comprehends them as impermanent, unsatisfactory and non-self (sammasana) and sees their arising and passing away (udayabbaya). As attention settles on their passing, the series continues through knowledges of dissolution (bhaṅga), of fearfulness, misery and disenchantment, of the desire for deliverance, of re-observation, and of equanimity towards all formations (saṅkhārupekkhā). The last four — conformity, “change of lineage” (gotrabhū), path and fruition — occupy only a few moments at the point of awakening, and the sequence ends with a reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa) in which the meditator surveys what has been attained. The scheme is a map drawn by teachers for teachers; modern meditation masters disagree about how literally it describes experience.

docs.title: 4.4 The Four Stages of Awakening
docs.text:
The Theravāda tradition recognises four distinct stages of awakening, each marked by the eradication of specific mental fetters (saṃyojana; Table 4.2).

Table 4.2. The four stages of awakening in Theravāda Buddhism Stage Fetters Abandoned Result Sotāpanna (Stream-Enterer) Identity view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals At most 7 more rebirths; never reborn in lower realms Sakadāgāmī (Once-Returner) Weakening of sensual desire and ill-will At most one more return to the human realm Anāgāmī (Non-Returner) Complete abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will Reborn in the Pure Abodes; attains Nibbāna there Arahant (Worthy One) Desire for material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance Complete liberation; no further rebirth

docs.title: 4.5 The Theravāda Worldview: Buddhist Cosmology
docs.text:
The Theravāda tradition preserves a detailed cosmological framework describing thirty-one planes of existence (bhūmi) through which beings cycle in accordance with their karma (Figure 4.2).

Figure 4.2. The thirty-one planes of existence in Buddhist cosmology, arranged from the lowest hell realms to the highest formless realm. Beings cycle through these planes driven by karma and craving.

docs.title: 4.6 The Forty Meditation Subjects (Kammaṭṭhāna)
docs.text:
The Visuddhimagga systematises the meditative tradition of Theravāda Buddhism into forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), each suited to different temperaments and spiritual needs (Table 4.3).

Table 4.3. The forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) classified by category Category Number Subjects Ten Kasiṇas 10 Earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, light, space Ten Asubhas (Corpse meditations) 10 Bloated, livid, festering, cut-up, gnawed, scattered, hacked & scattered, bleeding, worm-infested, skeleton Ten Anussatis (Recollections) 10 Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, morality, generosity, devas, death, body, breathing, peace Four Brahma-vihāras 4 Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity Four Formless spheres 4 Infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, neither-perception-nor-non-perception One Perception 1 Perception of the repulsiveness of food One Analysis 1 Analysis of the four elements

The selection of the appropriate meditation subject is guided by the practitioner’s temperament (carita). The Visuddhimagga identifies six temperament types: greedy (rāga-carita), hateful (dosa-carita), deluded (moha-carita), faithful (saddhā-carita), intelligent (buddhi-carita), and speculative (vitakka-carita). For example, the corpse meditations are prescribed for those with a greedy temperament, while the brahma-vihāras are prescribed for those with a hateful temperament.

docs.title: 4.7 The Jhānas: Meditative Absorptions
docs.text:
The development of concentration (samādhi) through the practice of samatha (tranquillity) meditation leads to the attainment of the jhānas — states of deep meditative absorption characterised by stillness, clarity and happiness. The Theravāda tradition describes four form-sphere jhānas (rūpa-jhāna) and four formless jhānas (arūpa-jhāna; Table 4.4).

Table 4.4. The eight jhānas (meditative absorptions) Jhāna Name Characteristics 1st Rūpa First Jhāna Vitakka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), pīti (rapture), sukha (happiness), ekaggatā (one-pointedness) 2nd Rūpa Second Jhāna Pīti, sukha, ekaggatā — thought factors have ceased 3rd Rūpa Third Jhāna Sukha, ekaggatā — rapture has faded; mindfulness and clear comprehension 4th Rūpa Fourth Jhāna Upekkhā (equanimity), ekaggatā — neither pleasure nor pain; purified mindfulness 1st Arūpa Sphere of Infinite Space Transcending form; attention on boundless space 2nd Arūpa Sphere of Infinite Consciousness Attention on boundless consciousness 3rd Arūpa Sphere of Nothingness Attention on the absence of anything 4th Arūpa Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception The subtlest state of consciousness

Vivicc’ eva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati.

““Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, one enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.””

— Stock formula for the first jhāna, e.g. Dīgha Nikāya 2 (Sāmaññaphala Sutta)

The jhānas serve as the foundation for the development of vipassanā (insight). While the jhānas themselves do not constitute enlightenment, they provide the mental stability and clarity necessary for the penetrating insight into the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) that leads to liberation.

docs.title: 4.8 The Commentarial and Sub-Commentarial Literature
docs.text:
The Theravāda intellectual tradition extends far beyond the canonical texts. A vast literature of commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), sub-commentaries (ṭīkā), and independent treatises (pakaraṇa) elaborates, systematises, and extends the canonical teachings (Table 4.5).

Table 4.5. Major works of the Theravāda commentarial tradition Work Author Significance Visuddhimagga Buddhaghosa (5th cent.) The definitive compendium of Theravāda path and practice Aṭṭhasālinī Buddhaghosa Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Sammohavinodanī Buddhaghosa Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha Anuruddha (c. 10th–12th cent.; date disputed) Concise manual of Abhidhamma; the most widely studied Abhidhamma text today Milindapañha Anonymous (composite; core perhaps 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE) Dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the monk Nāgasena Vimuttimagga Upatissa (early centuries CE; survives in Chinese) An earlier “Path of Freedom” closely related to the Visuddhimagga Paṭisambhidāmagga Canonical (Khuddaka Nikāya) Analytical treatise on insight knowledge Nettipakaraṇa Attributed to Mahākaccāna Hermeneutical method for interpreting the Buddha’s discourses

Scholarly Note: The Milindapañha

The Milindapañha (“Questions of King Milinda”) is a lively philosophical dialogue, though it is a non-canonical work in most Theravāda countries (it is included in the Burmese canon). It records a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander I (Milinda, who ruled in northwestern India c. 155–130 BCE) and the Buddhist monk Nāgasena. The text’s famous “chariot simile” — in which Nāgasena demonstrates that a chariot is nothing over and above its parts, just as a person is nothing over and above the five aggregates — is one of the classic arguments for the doctrine of anattā (non-self). Whether or not it records an actual conversation, the text reflects the encounter between Buddhism and the Greek rulers of the north-west.

docs.title: 4.9 Theravāda Buddhism in Southeast Asia
docs.text:
Theravāda Buddhism became the dominant religious and cultural force in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, shaping the civilisations of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Laos for many centuries (Table 4.6).

Table 4.6. Theravāda Buddhism in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia Country Period of Establishment Distinctive Features Sri Lanka c. 250 BCE (Mission of Mahinda) Custodian of the Pāli Canon; Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa kingdoms; Great Chronicle (Mahāvaṃsa); monastic forest tradition Myanmar c. 5th cent. CE; reformed 11th cent. Bagan temple complex; the Shwedagon Pagoda; strong Abhidhamma tradition; lay meditation movement Thailand c. 13th cent. (Sukhothai) Royal patronage; Dhammayut and Mahā Nikāya fraternities; Thai Forest Tradition (Ajahn Mun lineage) Cambodia c. 13th–14th cent. Replaced the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Mahāyāna cults of the Angkorian kings; survived the Khmer Rouge period Laos c. 14th cent. Pha That Luang stūpa; integration with indigenous spirit traditions; That Luang Festival

In each of these countries, Theravāda Buddhism became deeply interwoven with national identity, royal authority, artistic expression, and social organisation. The Saṅgha served not only as a spiritual institution but as a centre of education, literacy, and social welfare, and monastery schools long provided basic education for boys in Myanmar, Thailand and elsewhere.

docs.title: 4.9.1 Chronicles, Reforms and Ordination Lineages
docs.text:
The Sri Lankan chronicles, the Dīpavaṃsa (4th–5th century) and the Mahāvaṃsa (attributed to Mahānāma, 5th–6th century), are the main source for the Theravāda account of the councils and of Mahinda’s mission. They are monastic histories written from the standpoint of the Mahāvihāra and must be used critically (Gombrich 2006). For centuries the Mahāvihāra competed with the Abhayagiri and Jetavana monasteries of Anurādhapura, which were more open to Mahāyāna and tantric ideas; in the twelfth century King Parākramabāhu I (r. 1153–1186) unified the Saṅgha under Mahāvihāra orthodoxy.

Because valid ordination requires an unbroken succession of properly ordained monks, the Theravāda countries repeatedly renewed their lineages from one another. Burmese tradition credits King Anawrahta of Pagan (r. 1044–1077) with establishing Theravāda after his conquest of Thaton, and the Kalyāṇī inscriptions of King Dhammazedi (1479) record a reform in which Burmese monks were reordained in the Sri Lankan lineage. In 1753, when the Sri Lankan order had declined, monks from Ayutthaya in Siam re-established higher ordination at Kandy, founding the Siyam Nikāya; because it admitted only men of the Goyigama caste, the Amarapura (early nineteenth century) and Rāmañña (1864) Nikāyas were later founded with ordination lineages brought from Burma. In Siam the future King Mongkut (Rama IV), while still a monk, founded the reformist Dhammayuttika order in the 1830s (Gombrich 2006; Harvey 2013).

docs.title: 4.10 Modern Theravāda and the Vipassanā Movement
docs.text:
In the twentieth century meditation, long regarded in most Theravāda countries as a specialist pursuit of a few monks, became a mass practice for lay people. The movement began in Burma. Ledi Sayadaw (1846–1923), a monk and scholar, taught meditation and Abhidhamma to laymen, partly as a defence of Buddhism under colonial rule, and some of his lay pupils became teachers in their turn; through one of them, Saya Thetgyi, and his pupil Sayagyi U Ba Khin, the method reached S. N. Goenka (1924–2013), a Burmese-Indian businessman whose free ten-day residential courses are now held in many countries and have brought a Burmese form of Theravāda practice to a wide Indian public. Mahasi Sayadaw (1904–1982) developed the “noting” technique, the continuous mental labelling of present experience, and spread it through a network of centres in Burma and abroad. Among those trained in his method was Dipa Ma (Nani Bala Barua, 1911–1989), a Bengali Barua Buddhist widow from Chittagong who became a renowned teacher in Kolkata and later taught in the United States. In Thailand the forest tradition of Ajahn Mun produced teachers such as Ajahn Chah (1918–1992), whose Western disciples founded monasteries in Europe, North America and Australasia.

These movements changed Theravāda. They made meditation, rather than merit-making alone, the mark of a serious lay Buddhist; they produced teachers, many of them women, outside the monastic hierarchy; and they presented the Buddha’s teaching as a practical method of mental training, an emphasis that has made it attractive abroad and has also been criticised as a modern simplification of the tradition (Gombrich 2006; Harvey 2013).

docs.title: 4.11 The Theravāda Saṅgha Today
docs.text: Theravāda remains the majority religion of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos, and it has established a presence in the West through migration, monastic foundations and the spread of meditation. Its monks continue to treat the Pāli canon, read through Buddhaghosa’s commentaries, as the authoritative record of the Buddha’s teaching. The tradition’s claim to be the conservative heir of the earliest Saṅgha has a real basis in the age of its canon and the continuity of its Vinaya; but it is also, as the chronicles and the repeated reforms of its ordination lineages show, the product of a long and contested history in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

docs.title: 5.1 The Emergence of the Mahāyāna
docs.text:
The Mahāyāna (“Great Vehicle”) was one of the most far-reaching developments in Indian Buddhism. Emerging gradually within the early Buddhist schools between roughly the first century BCE and the second century CE — and remaining for several centuries a minority movement within Indian monasteries — the Mahāyāna introduced transformative new ideas about the nature of Buddhahood, the path to enlightenment, and the ultimate nature of reality.

The term Mahāyāna signifies the “Great Vehicle” — great in the sense that it aspires to carry all sentient beings to liberation, not merely the individual practitioner. This universal soteriological vision is embodied in the ideal of the Bodhisattva — the being who aspires to attain complete Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings.

docs.title: 5.1.1 Historical Development
docs.text: The origins of the Mahāyāna remain a subject of scholarly debate. The earliest Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines), appear to have taken shape from about the first century BCE; the earliest dated Mahāyāna texts are Chinese translations made by Lokakṣema in the late second century CE (Williams 2009; Harvey 2013). Older theories that the movement was essentially led by lay people, centred on the worship of stūpas, are now widely doubted. Jan Nattier’s study of an early sūtra, the Inquiry of Ugra (Ugraparipṛcchā), shows a bodhisattva path conceived as a demanding vocation for a few, with the forest-dwelling monk as its model and the householder bodhisattva only a lesser case (Nattier 2003). Scholars now emphasise instead the aspiration of some monks to follow the Buddha’s own path to full Buddhahood rather than to arhatship; the development of the idea of the Buddha from historical teacher to a figure present in many worlds; visionary practices that were believed to bring the practitioner into the presence of Buddhas and so to authorise new scriptures; and the philosophical pressure of the earlier Abhidharma analyses, which the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras criticised. For several centuries Mahāyāna monks lived in the same monasteries, under the same Vinayas, as their non-Mahāyāna brethren (Chapter 13), and Joseph Walser has argued that early Mahāyāna authors such as Nāgārjuna had to write in ways acceptable to such mixed communities (Walser 2005).

docs.title: 5.2 The Bodhisattva Ideal
docs.text:
The Bodhisattva (literally “enlightenment-being” or “being [destined for] awakening”) is the central figure of the Mahāyāna path. The early schools also knew the bodhisattva path, but as the exceptional career of a future Buddha, and they held up the arhat — one who has attained liberation by following a Buddha’s teaching — as the goal for most practitioners; Theravāda still does so, while honouring the bodhisatta ideal. The Mahāyāna sūtras, which polemically called the arhat’s path a “lesser vehicle” (hīnayāna), urge every practitioner to aim for full Buddhahood: the bodhisattva, motivated by mahākaruṇā (great compassion), vows to attain awakening for the sake of all beings and to go on working in the world until they are liberated.

ākāśasya sthitir yāvad yāvac ca jagataḥ sthitiḥ, tāvan mama sthitir bhūyāj jagadduḥkhāni nighnataḥ.

As long as space endures and as long as the world endures, so long may I endure, destroying the sufferings of the world.

— Śāntideva (8th century), Bodhicaryāvatāra 10.55

docs.title: 5.2.1 The Bodhisattva Vow (Praṇidhāna)
docs.text:
The Bodhisattva path begins with the generation of Bodhicitta — the “mind of enlightenment” or the aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. This aspiration is formalised in vows (praṇidhāna). In East Asian Buddhism the best-known formulation is the “Four Great Vows”, composed in Chinese (it is traditionally associated with the Tiantai master Zhiyi, 6th century) and recited daily in many monasteries:

Sentient beings are numberless — I vow to save them all. Delusions are inexhaustible — I vow to end them all. The Dharma gates are boundless — I vow to enter them all. The Buddha way is unsurpassed — I vow to attain it.

docs.title: 5.2.2 The Six Pāramitās (Perfections)
docs.text: The bodhisattva practises six perfections (pāramitā): generosity (dāna), morality (śīla), patience (kṣānti), effort (vīrya), meditation (dhyāna) and wisdom (prajñā). Expanded lists add four more — skill in means (upāya), vow (praṇidhāna), power (bala) and knowledge (jñāna) — to make ten, which correspond to the ten stages. The list overlaps with the Theravāda perfections (Chapter 2), but its emphasis differs: the sixth perfection, wisdom, is understood as insight into emptiness (śūnyatā), and the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras insist that the other five are perfections only when they are practised with that insight, without fixing on giver, gift or recipient as real entities.

docs.title: 5.2.3 The Ten Bhūmis (Stages)
docs.text: The Daśabhūmika Sūtra and related texts map the bodhisattva’s career onto ten stages (bhūmi), each associated with the perfection of one of the ten perfections. The first, the “joyous” (pramuditā), begins with the arising of the mind of awakening and the practice of generosity; the stages then rise through the “stainless” (vimalā), “luminous” (prabhākarī), “radiant” (arciṣmatī), “difficult to conquer” (sudurjayā) and “facing” (abhimukhī) stages, in which morality, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom are perfected in turn. The seventh, “far-going” (dūraṅgamā), perfects skill in means; with the eighth, “immovable” (acalā), the bodhisattva can no longer fall back; and the ninth (sādhumatī, “good intelligence”) and tenth (dharmameghā, “cloud of Dharma”) lead to consecration as a Buddha. The scheme turned an aspiration that the earlier schools had reserved for a few future Buddhas into a path that any committed practitioner could, in principle, enter.

docs.title: 5.3 Prajñāpāramitā: The Perfection of Wisdom
docs.text:
The Prajñāpāramitā (“Perfection of Wisdom”) literature is the earliest body of Mahāyāna scripture and the source of its central philosophical idea. Ranging from the vast Śatasāhasrikā (100,000 lines) to the concentrated essence of the Hṛdaya Sūtra (Heart Sūtra), this literature expounds the central Mahāyāna insight into Śūnyatā (emptiness) (Conze 1973; Williams 2009).

Iha Śāriputra rūpaṃ śūnyatā, śūnyataiva rūpam; rūpān na pṛthak śūnyatā, śūnyatāyā na pṛthag rūpam. Yad rūpaṃ sā śūnyatā, yā śūnyatā tad rūpam.

Here, O Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and the very emptiness is form; emptiness does not differ from form, form does not differ from emptiness; whatever is form, that is emptiness, whatever is emptiness, that is form.

— Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra (Heart Sūtra)

The Heart Sūtra, a short text whose Indian origin some scholars have questioned, is chanted daily in monasteries from Japan to Tibet and Vietnam. Its paradoxical formulations state the central claim of the Perfection of Wisdom: that the ultimate nature of all phenomena is emptiness of inherent existence (śūnyatā), and that this emptiness is not a void apart from things but the way in which things themselves exist.

docs.title: 5.4 Śūnyatā: The Doctrine of Emptiness
docs.text:
Śūnyatā (“emptiness,” “voidness”) is the key philosophical concept of the Mahāyāna, and its proper understanding is essential for comprehending the Madhyamaka and, to a significant extent, the Yogācāra philosophies (Williams 2009; Siderits 2007).

Śūnyatā does not mean “nothingness” or “non-existence.” Rather, it signifies the absence of svabhāva (inherent existence, self-nature, own-being) in all phenomena. All things arise in dependence upon causes and conditions (Pratītyasamutpāda), and therefore no thing possesses independent, self-sufficient existence. This is what it means for something to be “empty” — empty of self-existence, but not empty of conventional existence and functional efficacy.

docs.title: 5.5 Madhyamaka: The Middle Way Philosophy of Nāgārjuna
docs.text: The philosophical school that most rigorously developed the doctrine of Śūnyatā is the Madhyamaka (“Middle Way”), founded by Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE). Almost nothing certain is known of his life. Later legend made him the recoverer of the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras from the realm of the serpents (nāga), an alchemist and an abbot of Nālandā (Chapter 7); his letter of advice to a king, the Ratnāvalī, suggests that he worked under the Sātavāhanas of the Deccan, and Walser places him in a monastery of the Krishna valley (Walser 2005). His arguments set the terms of Mahāyāna philosophy for a millennium and drew sustained replies from the Nyāya and other schools.

docs.title: 5.5.1 Nāgārjuna and the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā
docs.text:
Nāgārjuna’s magnum opus, the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (“Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way”), consists of 448 verses organised in 27 chapters. In this work, Nāgārjuna subjects every fundamental philosophical category — causation, motion, the self, time, the Buddha, and Nirvāṇa itself — to a rigorous dialectical analysis and demonstrates that none of them possesses svabhāva (inherent existence).

Na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyāṃ nāpy ahetutaḥ utpannā jātu vidyante bhāvāḥ kva cana ke cana.

Neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without cause do things ever arise anywhere.

— Mūlamadhyamakakārikā I.1

This verse, which opens the first chapter after the dedicatory verses, encapsulates the Madhyamaka method (Garfield 1995; Westerhoff 2009): a systematic examination and refutation of all possible theories of origination, demonstrating that no account of inherent causation can withstand philosophical scrutiny.

docs.title: 5.5.2 The Two Truths
docs.text:
Nāgārjuna’s arguments might seem to deny that anything exists at all. He answers the charge with the distinction between two truths. Conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is the level of everyday practice, at which things exist, function and interact under the names and categories of ordinary life; ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is the recognition that none of them exists by its own nature. The two are not two worlds. Emptiness is the ultimate nature of the very things that are conventionally real, and the ultimate can be taught only by relying on the conventional:

Dve satye samupāśritya buddhānāṃ dharmadeśanā; loka-saṃvṛti-satyaṃ ca satyaṃ ca paramārthataḥ.

The Dharma taught by the Buddhas is based on two truths: the conventional truth of the world and the ultimate truth.

— Mūlamadhyamakakārikā XXIV.8

The same reasoning leads to the claim that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not ultimately distinct, since neither has a nature of its own that could separate it from the other:

Na saṃsārasya nirvāṇāt kiṃcid asti viśeṣaṇam; na nirvāṇasya saṃsārāt kiṃcid asti viśeṣaṇam.

There is no distinction whatsoever between Saṃsāra and Nirvāṇa; there is no distinction whatsoever between Nirvāṇa and Saṃsāra.

— Mūlamadhyamakakārikā XXV.19

docs.title: 5.5.3 Later Madhyamaka
docs.text:
The Madhyamaka school underwent significant development after Nāgārjuna, branching into two main sub-schools:

Prāsaṅgika Associated with Buddhapālita (c. 470–540 CE) and Candrakīrti (c. 600–650 CE), who held that a Mādhyamika should use only prasaṅga (reductio ad absurdum) arguments, drawing out the unwanted consequences of an opponent’s position without advancing an independent thesis. Svātantrika Associated with Bhāviveka (c. 500–570 CE), who criticised Buddhapālita and held that a Mādhyamika may also use independent (svatantra) inferences of the kind formalised by Dignāga.

These two labels were coined later by Tibetan scholars to classify Indian authors; the Indian thinkers themselves did not use them as names of schools (Williams and Tribe 2000). A later synthesis of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra was made by Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla in the eighth century (Section 5.8.3).

docs.title: 5.6 Yogācāra: The Mind-Only School
docs.text: The second great philosophical school of the Mahāyāna is the Yogācāra (“Practice of Yoga”), also known as Vijñānavāda (“Doctrine of Consciousness”) or Cittamātra (“Mind-Only”). Systematised by the brothers Asaṅga and Vasubandhu (4th–5th century CE; their exact dates are disputed), who drew on earlier texts such as the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra and teachings that tradition attributes to Maitreya, the Yogācāra school developed a detailed analysis of consciousness and its objects.

docs.title: 5.6.1 The Eight Consciousnesses
docs.text:
The Yogācāra school posits eight types of consciousness (vijñāna; Table 5.1).

Table 5.1. The eight consciousnesses of the Yogācāra school No. Consciousness Description 1–5 Five Sense Consciousnesses Visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness 6 Mano-vijñāna Mental consciousness: the discursive, conceptual mind 7 Manas (or Kliṣṭamanas) The “afflicted mind”: the deep, unconscious layer of self-grasping that underlies the sense of a permanent “I” 8 Ālaya-vijñāna The “storehouse consciousness”: the fundamental ground consciousness that stores the seeds (bīja) of all experiences and karmic imprints

The storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) answers a problem that the earlier Abhidharma had left open: if every mental event lasts only a moment, where are the traces of past actions kept until they ripen? It functions as a repository of karmic seeds (bīja) that ripen under appropriate conditions to produce the manifold appearances of the world. Modern scholars have compared the Yogācāra analysis of consciousness with themes in phenomenology, while debating whether the school should be read as an idealism (Williams 2009).

docs.title: 5.6.2 The Three Natures (Trisvabhāva)
docs.text: The doctrine of the three natures (trisvabhāva) is the Yogācāra counterpart of the two truths. The “imagined” nature (parikalpita) is the way things appear to the unawakened mind, as independent objects set over against an independent subject; it is a conceptual superimposition with no reality of its own. The “dependent” nature (paratantra) is the flow of experience itself, arising from causes and conditions. The “consummate” nature (pariniṣpanna) is the dependent nature seen free of the imagined one — experience without the duality of subject and object. The scheme allowed Yogācāra authors to say, against what they saw as a nihilistic reading of the Madhyamaka, that something is real (the dependent flow of consciousness) even though the world as we ordinarily construe it is not.

docs.title: 5.7 The Tathāgata-garbha Doctrine
docs.text:
A third major strand of Mahāyāna philosophical thought, alongside Madhyamaka and Yogācāra, is the Tathāgata-garbha (“Buddha-womb” or “Buddha-embryo”) doctrine. This teaching holds that all sentient beings possess within themselves the garbha (womb, seed, matrix) of Buddhahood — an inherent potential for enlightenment that is obscured by adventitious defilements but never destroyed.

The Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra illustrates this teaching with nine similes: the buddha-nature in beings is like honey surrounded by bees, a grain inside its husk, gold fallen into filth, or a treasure buried beneath a poor man’s house (Williams 2009). The sūtra’s formula “all beings are tathāgatagarbhas”, that is, contain the Tathāgata as an embryo (sarvasattvās tathāgatagarbhāḥ, quoted in Sanskrit as the Buddha’s words in the commentary on the Ratnagotravibhāga, since the sūtra itself survives only in Chinese and Tibetan), is taken up and systematised in the Ratnagotravibhāga.

The key texts of this tradition include the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the Śrīmālādevīsiṃhanāda Sūtra, and the Ratnagotravibhāga (attributed in Tibetan tradition to Maitreya and Asaṅga, in Chinese tradition to Sāramati). The doctrine had its greatest influence in East Asia, where, mediated especially by the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, it was an important influence on Chinese Huayan (whose scriptural basis was the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) and on the Japanese idea of “original enlightenment” (hongaku).

Tathāgatagarbha, Madhyamaka and Yogācāra

How the Tathāgatagarbha doctrine relates to Madhyamaka and Yogācāra was debated for centuries, above all in Tibet. Tsongkhapa (1357–1419) and the Gelug school identified the garbha with the emptiness of the mind: because the mind lacks inherent existence, its defilements can be removed and awakening is possible. On this reading, sūtra passages that speak of a permanent essence endowed with the qualities of a Buddha are of interpretable meaning (neyārtha), not to be taken literally. The Jonang school of Dolpopa (1292–1361) held the opposite. The ultimate, the luminous nature of mind (prabhāsvara-citta) endowed with the qualities of Buddhahood, is permanent and real; it is “empty of other” (gzhan stong) — of the adventitious, conventional phenomena that are extraneous to it — but not empty of its own nature, whereas conventional phenomena are “empty of self” (rang stong) (Williams 2009).

docs.title: 5.8 Buddhist Logic: Dignāga and Dharmakīrti
docs.text: The logicians Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, both Mahāyāna monks, created a system of epistemology and logic (pramāṇa) that became a common point of reference for Indian philosophers of every school. Their aim was not logic for its own sake: by showing what can be known by perception and inference alone, they sought to establish the Buddhist doctrines of momentariness and non-self, and the reliability of the Buddha’s teaching, on grounds that an opponent could not reject.

docs.title: 5.8.1 Dignāga’s Reforms
docs.text:
Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE), sometimes called the “father of Buddhist logic”, reshaped Indian epistemology with his Pramāṇasamuccaya (“Compendium of Valid Cognition”). He held that there are only two means of valid knowledge, perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna), because there are only two kinds of object: the unique particular, grasped by perception free of concepts, and the general characteristic, grasped by inference and conceptual thought. Testimony and comparison, which the Naiyāyikas counted separately, are reduced to inference. His theory of meaning by exclusion (apoha) explained how words can refer without real universals: the word “cow” does not name a positive “cowness” but excludes everything that is not a cow. He reformulated the inference-for-others from the five members of the Nyāya syllogism to three, and he set out precise conditions for a valid reason (hetu) in his “wheel of reasons” (hetucakra; Table 5.2). The wheel classifies the nine possible ways in which a reason can be present in, or absent from, the “similar cases” (sapakṣa, where the property to be proved is known to occur) and the “dissimilar cases” (vipakṣa, where it is known not to occur); only two of the nine give valid inferences, two give contradictory reasons, and the rest are inconclusive (Hattori 1968; Williams and Tribe 2000).

Table 5.2. Dignāga’s hetucakra (“wheel of reasons”): the occurrence of the reason in similar and dissimilar cases In all similar cases In some similar cases In no similar case In no dissimilar case Valid (no. 2) Valid (no. 8) Inconclusive, “uncommon” (no. 5) In some dissimilar cases Inconclusive (no. 3) Inconclusive (no. 9) Contradictory (no. 6) In all dissimilar cases Inconclusive (no. 1) Inconclusive (no. 7) Contradictory (no. 4)

docs.title: 5.8.2 Dharmakīrti’s Elaboration
docs.text:
Dharmakīrti (6th–7th century) further developed Dignāga’s system in his Pramāṇavārttika (“Commentary on Valid Cognition”), which became the standard textbook of logic and epistemology in Tibetan monasteries (Dunne 2004). (Frauwallner’s long-accepted dates of c. 600–660 have been revised by some recent scholars to the later sixth century; this volume uses the broader range.) Dharmakīrti made the distinction between the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) the basis of an ontology: only what is capable of causal efficacy is ultimately real, and that is the momentary particular. He gave a causal theory of perception, in which a valid perception must be produced by its object, and he grounded inference in a necessary connection (vyāpti) between reason and property, which can rest only on identity of nature (svabhāva) or on causality (kārya); the third kind of reason, non-perception (anupalabdhi), establishes absence. On these foundations he argued that whatever exists is momentary (kṣaṇikatva).

arthakriyāsamarthaṃ yat tad atra paramārthasat; anyat saṃvṛtisat proktaṃ, te svasāmānyalakṣaṇe.

Whatever is capable of causal efficacy is here ultimately real; anything else is said to be conventionally real. These are, respectively, the particular and the universal characteristic.

— Dharmakīrti, Pramāṇavārttika 3.3 (= 2.3 in Miyasaka’s chapter order)

The Buddhist logical tradition shaped all later Indian epistemology. Brahmanical philosophers — the Naiyāyikas Uddyotakara, Vācaspati Miśra and Udayana, and the Mīmāṃsaka Kumārila — wrote extensive refutations of Buddhist positions, and the sharpening of Nyāya technique in these debates prepared the way for the “new” Nyāya (Navya-Nyāya) of Gaṅgeśa in the fourteenth century. The Jain logicians Akalaṅka and Vidyānanda similarly engaged with Buddhist logic while developing their own system (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 5.8.3 After Dharmakīrti
docs.text:
Dharmakīrti’s work was the starting point of a school that lasted five centuries, and it was this later tradition, more than Dignāga and Dharmakīrti themselves, that the Brahmanical and Jain philosophers of the late first millennium were answering. Commentators such as Devendrabuddhi and Śākyabuddhi expounded the Pramāṇavārttika; Dharmottara (8th century), whose commentary on Dharmakīrti’s Nyāyabindu was widely read in Kashmir, refined the theory of perception; and Prajñākaragupta’s Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra read Dharmakīrti as a defender of the Buddha’s authority as well as of logic (Dunne 2004; Williams and Tribe 2000).

In the eighth century Śāntarakṣita, a Nālandā scholar who helped to found the first Tibetan monastery (Chapter 6), wrote the Tattvasaṅgraha, a verse compendium that examines and rejects, one by one, the doctrines of the rival schools — a creator God, Sāṃkhya’s primordial nature, the permanent self of the Naiyāyikas and Jains, the eternal Veda of the Mīmāṃsakas, real universals — and ends with a defence of the Buddha’s omniscience against Kumārila. His pupil Kamalaśīla’s commentary (Pañjikā) quotes many of the opponents’ works, some of them otherwise lost. Śāntarakṣita also joined Dharmakīrti’s epistemology to Madhyamaka, treating the Yogācāra analysis as a stage on the way to the recognition that nothing has intrinsic nature (McClintock 2010).

The last great phase of the school belongs to Vikramaśīla in the late tenth and eleventh centuries. Jñānaśrīmitra and his pupil Ratnakīrti wrote treatises proving momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), restating the theory of exclusion and refuting proofs of God and of other minds; Mokṣākaragupta’s Tarkabhāṣā later summarised the system as a handbook. The Naiyāyika Udayana’s Ātmatattvaviveka and Nyāyakusumāñjali, the classic Brahmanical defences of the self and of God, were written largely against these authors. When the eastern monasteries were destroyed around 1200 (Chapter 7), the school ended in India, but its texts were translated into Tibetan, and its arguments survived in the works of its Nyāya and Jain opponents.

docs.title: 5.9 The Concept of Upāya (Skilful Means)
docs.text:
One of the most distinctive and practically significant doctrines of the Mahāyāna is upāya-kauśalya (“skill in means”) — the principle that the Buddha and advanced Bodhisattvas adapt their teachings and methods to the capacities, temperaments, and circumstances of the beings they are guiding. The doctrine allowed Mahāyāna authors to explain the diversity of Buddhist teachings, including the older teachings they claimed to surpass, as adaptations to different audiences; critics, ancient and modern, have noted that it also made almost any innovation defensible.

The Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra (Lotus Sūtra) articulates this principle through its famous parables, including the Parable of the Burning House: a father, seeing his children playing inside a burning house, lures them out by promising them different types of carriages (goat-carts, deer-carts, ox-carts), only to give them all the finest carriage (the Great White Ox-Cart). The different vehicles represent the diverse Buddhist paths, while the great carriage represents the one supreme vehicle (ekayāna) of the Mahāyāna.

docs.title: 5.10 Key Mahāyāna Sūtras
docs.text: The Mahāyāna produced a vast body of sūtra literature, much of it surviving only in Chinese and Tibetan translation. Besides the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, which supplied the Madhyamaka with its themes, the most influential were the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka (Lotus Sūtra), with its teaching of the one vehicle (ekayāna) and of the Buddha’s immeasurable life; the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa, whose hero is a lay bodhisattva who answers the question of non-duality with silence; the Avataṃsaka, with its vision of the interpenetration of all phenomena; the Laṅkāvatāra, important for Yogācāra and for Chan and Zen; and the Sukhāvatīvyūha sūtras, the basis of devotion to the Buddha Amitābha and his “Pure Land”. Several of these became the founding scriptures of East Asian schools, so that the Mahāyāna known in China and Japan was in large part built on Indian texts that had little institutional weight in India itself. The Buddhist schools are placed among the other Indian philosophical systems in Volume 3 of this series (Darśana Darpaṇa).

docs.title: 6.1 The Tantric Transformation
docs.text:
The Vajrayāna (“Diamond Vehicle” or “Thunderbolt Vehicle”) represents the third major stream of Buddhist development, emerging within the Mahāyāna. Ritual use of mantras and protective spells is old in Buddhism, but the tantras proper appear from about the seventh century CE, and the most radical “yoginī” tantras from the ninth and tenth centuries (Davidson 2002; Williams and Tribe 2000). Sometimes also called Tantrayāna (“Vehicle of Tantra”) or Mantrayāna (“Vehicle of Sacred Syllables”), the Vajrayāna introduced a radical new approach to the Buddhist path: the transformation of ordinary experience — including sensory desire, emotional energy, and the body itself — into the means of enlightenment.

The term vajra carries a double meaning: “diamond” (signifying indestructibility and clarity) and “thunderbolt” (signifying irresistible power). The Vajrayāna understands the enlightened mind as having the nature of a vajra — adamantine, luminous, and unbreakable.

docs.title: 6.1.1 Philosophical Foundations
docs.text: The Vajrayāna accepts the philosophy of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra and adds to it a distinctive theory of practice (Snellgrove 1987). If all beings possess the nature of a Buddha (the Tathāgatagarbha doctrine of Chapter 5), awakening is not produced from outside but uncovered; if saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not ultimately distinct, as Nāgārjuna had argued, the passions (kleśa) need not be suppressed but can be transformed into the material of awakening. The tantras locate that transformation in the body, which they describe as a network of channels (nāḍī), winds (prāṇa) and drops (bindu) to be worked on in yoga, and they make it depend on the teacher, who confers the consecrations that alone give access to the practice and who is to be regarded as the Buddha in person.

docs.title: 6.2 The Tantric Literature
docs.text:
The Vajrayāna produced a vast body of tantric literature, classified by later Tibetan scholars into four (or in some schemes, six) classes of tantra (Table 6.1).

Table 6.1. Classification of Buddhist Tantras Class Sanskrit Characteristics Kriyā Tantra Kriyā-tantra Emphasis on external ritual, purification, and recitation of mantras Caryā Tantra Caryā-tantra Balance of external ritual and internal yoga Yoga Tantra Yoga-tantra Emphasis on internal meditative yoga; deity visualisation Highest Yoga Tantra Anuttarayoga-tantra The most advanced practices involving the subtle body, the transformation of passions, and the direct realisation of luminous emptiness

docs.title: 6.2.1 Indian Scriptures and Their Interpreters
docs.text:
The four-class scheme is a later systematisation. The Indian texts themselves appeared over some four centuries, and modern scholars can date them only approximately (Davidson 2002; Williams and Tribe 2000). The Mahāvairocana Sūtra (Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi), probably composed in the mid-seventh century, and the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha, of the late seventh century, set out the maṇḍala of the five Buddhas, consecration (abhiṣeka) and the practitioner’s meditative identification with a deity; both were translated into Chinese in the eighth century. The Guhyasamāja Tantra (eighth century) became the basis of two Indian exegetical schools, the “Ārya” school, whose authors took the names of Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva (they are not the Madhyamaka philosophers), and the school of Buddhajñānapāda. The “yoginī” tantras of the ninth and tenth centuries, such as the Hevajra and the Cakrasaṃvara, added cremation-ground imagery, circles of female deities and sexual yoga. The Kālacakra of the early eleventh century was the last major Indian tantra.

In the great monasteries of the Pāla period tantra became a subject of scholastic study alongside Madhyamaka and logic. Ratnākaraśānti (c. 1000) and Abhayākaragupta (fl. c. 1100), both associated with Vikramaśīla, wrote commentaries and ritual manuals as well as philosophical treatises; Abhayākaragupta’s Vajrāvalī, on the rituals of the maṇḍala, and his Niṣpannayogāvalī, which describes twenty-six maṇḍalas and their deities, became standard references in Nepal and Tibet.

Scholars have long noted close parallels between the Buddhist yoginī tantras and Śaiva tantric literature in deities, ritual and even wording. Alexis Sanderson has argued that passages of the Buddhist yoginī tantras were adapted from Śaiva texts (Sanderson 2009), and Davidson places the whole movement in the political culture of the early medieval courts (Davidson 2002); the direction and extent of borrowing remain under discussion. Buddhist tantra, its transmission to China and Japan and its relationship with Śaiva tantra are treated more fully in Volume 6 of this series (Tantra–Āgama).

docs.title: 6.3 The Eighty-Four Mahāsiddhas
docs.text:
Among the most colourful and significant figures in the Vajrayāna tradition are the Caturaśīti Mahāsiddha — the Eighty-Four Great Accomplished Ones. These were tantric adepts (Figure 6.1), mostly from eastern India, who lived between approximately the eighth and twelfth centuries CE. The standard list of eighty-four, with their legends, comes from a collection of biographies attributed to Abhayadatta, preserved in Tibetan (Dowman 1985). A selection is given in Table 6.2.

Table 6.2. Selected Mahāsiddhas and their distinguishing features Name Occupation/Background Teaching/Significance Tilopa Sesame grinder Said by tradition to have received teachings directly from Vajradhara; source of the Kagyu lineage Nāropa Nālandā scholar Six Yogas of Nāropa; guru of Marpa the Translator Saraha Brahmin / arrow-maker Doha songs of spontaneous realisation; foundational Mahāmudrā Lūipa Prince / fish-gut eater Overcame royal pride through extreme asceticism Virūpa Monk (of Nālandā in Tibetan tradition) Master of the Lamdre (Path with the Result) tradition Ghaṇṭāpa Scholar Transformed passion into realisation through tantric union Kukkuripa Dog lover Attained realisation through compassion for a stray dog Jālandhara Brahmin Master of the Cakrasaṃvara tantra Kāṇhapa (Kṛṣṇācārya) Yogin “The dark one”; author of songs in the Caryāgīti; Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara practice Śabaripa (Śavari) Hunter Transformed the act of hunting into dharma practice

In the legends, the Mahāsiddhas come from all walks of life — kings and beggars, scholars and illiterates, brāhmaṇas and outcastes, men and women; the list of eighty-four includes several women, such as Lakṣmīṅkarā and the sisters Mekhalā and Kanakhalā. Their songs (dohā, caryāgīti) and stories express the Vajrayāna principle that enlightenment is accessible to all, regardless of social station, and that the most ordinary activities can become vehicles for awakening.

The Caryāgīti or Caryāpada, a collection of tantric songs attributed to siddhas such as Kāṇhapa, Lūipa and Śabaripa, composed perhaps between the tenth and twelfth centuries, preserves some of the earliest literature in the early forms of Bengali, Assamese and Odia.

Figure 6.1. A Tibetan painting of four mahāsiddhas, three of them with consorts, in a landscape: Saraha, Ḍombi Heruka, Nāropa and Virūpa (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 18th century). The unconventional appearance of the siddhas expresses the Vajrayāna claim that awakening transcends ordinary social categories. Painting: Tibetan, unknown artist, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.4 The Kālacakra Tantra
docs.text: The Kālacakra Tantra (“Wheel of Time”) is the last of the major Indian Buddhist tantras. Tradition holds that the Buddha taught it at Dhānyakaṭaka (in present-day Andhra Pradesh) and that it was preserved in the hidden kingdom of Śambhala; historians date its composition to the early eleventh century, and its calendar is reckoned from 1027 CE. (The Sanskrit word kālacakra is also used by Jain authors, in a different sense, for the cycle of cosmic time described in Chapter 11.) The tantra is organised around a correspondence between three “wheels of time”: an outer Kālacakra, the cosmos with its planets, seasons and ages, for which the text sets out an elaborate astronomical and calendrical system; an inner Kālacakra, the body with its channels, winds and drops; and an “other” (alternative) Kālacakra, the path of practice by which the outer and inner cycles are mastered and transcended (Wallace 2001). Its astronomy, which combines Indian methods with features of its own, made it one of the few Buddhist texts with a substantial mathematical content, and it became the basis of the Tibetan calendar. It is also unusual in referring explicitly to Islam and in foreseeing a final war against the “barbarians” (mleccha), a sign of the conditions in north-western India at the time of its composition.

docs.title: 6.5 Mantra, Maṇḍala and the Teacher
docs.text:
A mantra (traditionally glossed “instrument of the mind”) is a sacred syllable or phrase recited as a vehicle of concentration and of identification with a deity. The best-known Buddhist mantra is the six-syllable formula of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion:

Oṃ Maṇi Padme Hūṃ

The popular rendering “the jewel in the lotus” is grammatically doubtful; maṇipadme is probably a vocative addressed to a female deity, “O jewel-lotus one” (Lopez 1998).

The maṇḍala (“circle”) is a diagram of the palace of a deity and its retinue, drawn in coloured powders, painted or visualised. In tantric ritual the practitioner visualises himself or herself at its centre, identified with the presiding deity, while hand gestures (mudrā) engage the body in the same act. None of this is open to the uninitiated. Access to a tantra requires consecration (abhiṣeka) by a qualified teacher (guru; Tibetan lama, bla ma), and the texts demand that the pupil see the teacher as inseparable from the Buddha. The secrecy and the authority of the teacher distinguish tantric practice from the public teaching of the sūtras.

docs.title: 6.6 Goddesses and Women in Tantric Buddhism
docs.text:
Female deities have a larger place in the Vajrayāna than in any earlier form of Buddhism (Shaw 2006). The most widely worshipped is Tārā, the “saviour”, whose images appear in the cave monasteries of western India by the sixth or seventh century; she is invoked as a protector from the “eight great perils” — lions, elephants, fire, snakes, robbers, fetters, floods and demons — and became, in Pāla Bengal and later in Tibet, a figure of devotion in her own right, in green and white forms and in a set of twenty-one manifestations. The Perfection of Wisdom itself was personified as the goddess Prajñāpāramitā, “mother of all Buddhas”, whose images were made in the Pāla monasteries and in Java. The yoginī tantras added fierce female deities such as Vajrayoginī and Vajravārāhī and the ḍākinīs, female figures of the cremation ground who initiate and guide the practitioner. Older goddesses also continued to be worshipped: Hārītī, an ogress converted by the Buddha into a protector of children, appears with her consort Pāñcika in the monasteries of Ajanta and Gandhāra, and Vasudhārā, a goddess of abundance, became especially popular among the Newar Buddhists of Nepal.

The prominence of female deities does not by itself show that women held high status in tantric communities. The texts are written mostly from the standpoint of a male practitioner, for whom women appear as consorts in sexual yoga. Miranda Shaw has argued that women were active and sometimes leading participants, citing the female siddhas and the songs and treatises attributed to women; other scholars read the same evidence more cautiously (Shaw 2006; Davidson 2002).

docs.title: 6.7 Vajrayāna in India: Sites and Patrons
docs.text:
The Vajrayāna was an Indian development, and its main centres were the monasteries of Bihar, Bengal and Odisha under the Pāla and Bhauma-Kara kings (8th–12th centuries; Table 6.3). In these institutions tantra was studied alongside Madhyamaka and logic: Vikramaśīla was founded by the Pāla king Dharmapāla and became the principal centre of tantric scholarship in its last two centuries, and Somapura (Paharpur) and Jagaddala in Bengal were large monasteries of the same network. The Odishan monasteries of Ratnagiri, Udayagiri and Lalitgiri have yielded the richest body of tantric Buddhist sculpture in India, including images of Tārā, of the five Buddhas of the maṇḍala and of fierce deities (Chapter 7, Section 7.11.4). The mahāsiddhas’ songs in the Caryāpada show the same tradition expressed in the early vernaculars of the east. At the other end of the subcontinent, the Himalayan valleys of Kashmir, Ladakh and Spiti linked Indian tantric Buddhism with western Tibet; the monastery of Tabo (996) still preserves murals in a style derived from Kashmir.

Table 6.3. Key Vajrayāna sites in India Site Location Significance Vikramaśīla Bihar Premier centre of Vajrayāna learning; ordination centre for Tibetan monks Odantapurī Bihar Model for the first Tibetan monastery (Samye) Jagaddala Bengal (now Bangladesh) Late Pāla foundation (Rāmapāla); centre of tantric learning and of translation for Tibet Somapura Mahāvihāra Bangladesh One of the largest Buddhist monasteries; UNESCO World Heritage Site Ratnagiri, Udayagiri, Lalitgiri Odisha “Diamond Triangle” of tantric Buddhist sites; major sculptural remains Tabo Monastery Himachal Pradesh Founded 996 CE; preserves some of the finest Buddhist murals in India

docs.title: 6.8 The Transmission to Tibet
docs.text:
Tibetan Buddhism took its texts, its monastic discipline and most of its tantric lineages from India, in two main periods (Snellgrove 1987; Samuel 1993). In the first, under the Tibetan kings of the seventh to ninth centuries, the Nālandā scholar Śāntarakṣita and the tantric master Padmasambhava were invited to Tibet, and the first monastery was founded at Samye on the model, Tibetan tradition says, of Odantapurī. Kamalaśīla’s three Bhāvanākramas (“Stages of Meditation”), written in the late eighth century, set out a gradual path combining calm (śamatha) and analytical insight (vipaśyanā); according to Tibetan histories they were connected with a debate at Samye (c. 792–794) in which Kamalaśīla’s gradualism prevailed over the “sudden” approach of the Chinese Chan master Moheyan. Modern scholars regard the accounts of the debate as partly legendary, but the Indian gradual path did become the norm in Tibet (Williams 2009; Samuel 1993).

The second period, from the late tenth century, began after the collapse of the Tibetan monarchy and drew on the Pāla monasteries and on Kashmir. Atiśa of Vikramaśīla (Chapter 7) taught in Tibet from 1042; Tibetan translators studied in Bihar, Bengal, Kashmir and Nepal; and the lineages from which the later Tibetan schools descend were brought from India in these decades. The Kagyu (bka’ brgyud) school traces its teaching through Marpa to the Indian siddhas Tilopa and Nāropa, whose “six yogas” of inner heat, illusory body, clear light, dream, intermediate state and transference of consciousness are Indian tantric practices, and its doctrine of the “great seal” (mahāmudrā) to the songs of Saraha; the Sakya (sa skya) school took its “path and result” (lam ’bras) teachings from the siddha Virūpa; and the Kadam school of Atiśa’s followers was later absorbed into the Gelug (dge lugs) of Tsongkhapa (1357–1419). The Nyingma (rnying ma) school, which looks back to Padmasambhava, also preserves a “great perfection” (rdzogs chen) teaching whose developed form historians regard as largely Tibetan (Samuel 1993). Many Indian works, tantric and philosophical, survive only in their Tibetan translations. The Tibetan schools themselves, and Buddhist tantra in China and Japan, are treated in Volume 6 (Tantra–Āgama).

docs.title: 6.9 Vajrayāna Art and Iconography
docs.text:
The Vajrayāna produced a visual art in which images are supports for ritual and visualisation rather than objects of contemplation in their own right. Pāla bronzes and stone sculpture, illustrated palm-leaf manuscripts, and later the painted scrolls (thang ka) and sand maṇḍalas of the Himalayan monasteries (Figure 6.2) depict a pantheon of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, protectors and ḍākinīs whose forms, colours and attributes are fixed by the ritual texts, such as Abhayākaragupta’s manuals.

Figure 6.2. Monks at work on a sand maṇḍala, hidden from view under a canopy, on the stage of a modern Kālacakra initiation. Behind them hang painted scrolls, among them the Kālacakra deity with his consort and a painted maṇḍala. Photo: Wonderlane, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Vajrayāna is often presented, especially in popular writing, as a Tibetan religion. Its history points the other way. Its scriptures, its exegetical schools and its ritual manuals were composed in the monasteries and courts of eastern and north-western India between the seventh and twelfth centuries, in close and sometimes competitive contact with Śaiva tantra; and it was the destruction of those monasteries around 1200, not any lack of vitality, that ended its Indian history. What survives in the Himalayan regions, in Tibet, Mongolia and the Newar community of Nepal is, to a large extent, the last phase of Indian Buddhism preserved outside India.

docs.title: 7.1 The Saṅgha: Foundation of Buddhist Institutional Life
docs.text: The Saṅgha (“community”) is the third of the Three Jewels (triratna) of Buddhism, alongside the Buddha and the Dhamma. The Buddha established the Saṅgha as the institutional vehicle for preserving, practising and transmitting his teaching. Over the centuries the larger monasteries also became centres of learning, where monks studied not only the scriptures but grammar, logic, medicine and the arts (Dutt 1962).

docs.title: 7.1.1 Organisation of the Early Saṅgha
docs.text: The Vinaya’s rules for collective decision, seniority by ordination and the fortnightly recitation of the Pātimokkha are described in Chapter 2 (Section 2.14). Two further institutions made the monastery a place of study: the three-month rains retreat (vassa), when wandering monks settled in one place and the residences that sheltered them gradually became permanent; and the bond between pupil and preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya), through which texts and practice were passed on (Dutt 1962).

docs.title: 7.2 Nālandā Mahāvihāra
docs.text: Nālandā, in the old kingdom of Magadha (present-day Bihar), was the most celebrated Buddhist monastery of India. It flourished as a centre of learning from the fifth century CE to about 1200, attracting students from across the Buddhist world (Dutt 1962; Scharfe 2002).

docs.title: 7.2.1 History and Patronage
docs.text: The Buddha is said in the Pāli texts to have stayed at Nālandā village, but the great monastery was a later foundation. Xuanzang records that it was begun by a king called Śakrāditya, usually identified with the Gupta emperor Kumāragupta I (c. 415–455 CE), and enlarged by his successors. Seals and inscriptions found at the site confirm royal and private patronage over many centuries (Xuanzang 1884; Dutt 1962). After the Guptas, Harṣa of Kanauj (r. 606–647) is said by Xuanzang’s biographer Huili to have supported the monastery with the revenues of about a hundred villages (Huili (Hwui Li) 1888); an inscription found at the site records a gift in the time of Yaśovarman of Kanauj (8th century); and the Pāla kings of Bengal and Bihar (8th–12th centuries), notably Dharmapāla and Devapāla, were its patrons in its last centuries. A copper plate of Devapāla records endowments at Nālandā made at the request of the Śailendra king Bālaputradeva of Sumatra and Java, who had built a monastery there — a sign of how far the monastery’s reputation reached.

docs.title: 7.2.2 The Curriculum
docs.text:
The accounts of the Chinese visitors Xuanzang (in India c. 630–643) and Yijing (in India 673–685) are our main sources for teaching at Nālandā in its prime (Table 7.1) (Xuanzang 1884; Yijing (I-tsing) 1896).

Table 7.1. Subjects studied at Nālandā according to the Chinese pilgrims Category Subjects Buddhist doctrine Scriptures and Abhidharma of several schools; Mahāyāna texts; Madhyamaka and Yogācāra; Vinaya Logic and epistemology Hetu-vidyā, especially the works of Dignāga and (later) Dharmakīrti Grammar Śabda-vidyā: Sanskrit grammar, including Pāṇini’s system Other systems The Vedas and Brahmanical philosophy such as Sāṃkhya, studied for debate Medicine Cikitsā-vidyā Arts and crafts Śilpasthāna-vidyā Tantra From about the 8th century, Vajrayāna texts and ritual

docs.title: 7.2.3 The Site
docs.text: Excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India from 1915 onwards exposed a row of large brick monasteries (vihāras) built around open courtyards, facing a row of temples and stūpas across an open space. The largest monument, known as “Temple 3”, is a stūpa enlarged in at least seven building phases and is traditionally associated with the disciple Sāriputta. Seals bearing the legend of the “community of venerable monks of the great monastery of Nālandā” were found in quantity. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Numbers, Libraries and Myths
docs.text:
The Chinese accounts give an impression of size and seriousness. Xuanzang describes keen debate and says that strangers who wished to enter were put hard questions by the keeper of the gate; in Beal’s translation, “those who fail compared with those who succeed are as seven or eight to ten”. His biographer Huili gives the number of resident monks as about ten thousand and that of learned teachers as 1,510 (Huili (Hwui Li) 1888); Yijing, a generation later, speaks of more than three thousand monks (Yijing (I-tsing) 1896). These figures are approximate and may include monks from the surrounding establishments (Scharfe 2002).

Historical Note: The “nine million manuscripts”

Popular writing often claims that Nālandā’s library held “nine million manuscripts” and burned for months. Neither claim is found in Xuanzang, Yijing or any other contemporary source. The names of a library complex called Dharmagañja, with three buildings (Ratnasāgara, Ratnodadhi and Ratnarañjaka), come from much later Tibetan tradition, notably Tāranātha (1608) (Tāranātha 1970). Nālandā certainly possessed large collections of manuscripts — Yijing copied hundreds of texts there — but their size is unknown.

docs.title: 7.2.5 Scholars Associated with Nālandā
docs.text:
Later tradition, especially Tibetan tradition, associates many famous Buddhist thinkers with Nālandā. Some associations are historical; others are anachronistic, since the monastery was founded in the fifth century.

Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE) Tibetan tradition makes him an abbot of Nālandā, but he lived centuries before its foundation. Asaṅga and Vasubandhu (4th–5th c.) Also linked with Nālandā by later tradition; the historical connection is uncertain. Dignāga (c. 480–540) and Dharmakīrti (6th–7th c.) The logicians are associated with Nālandā in Tibetan sources; their works were certainly studied there. Śīlabhadra (7th c.) The Yogācāra master who was head of Nālandā when Xuanzang studied there. Śāntideva (8th c.) According to tradition, composed the Bodhicaryāvatāra at Nālandā. Śāntarakṣita (8th c.) A Nālandā scholar who synthesised Madhyamaka and Yogācāra and helped to found the first Tibetan monastery at Samye. Nāropa (11th c.) Said to have served as a gatekeeper-scholar of Nālandā before becoming a tantric adept.

docs.title: 7.3 Vikramaśīla Mahāvihāra
docs.text:
Vikramaśīla, founded by the Pāla king Dharmapāla (r. c. 775–812) in eastern Bihar (the excavated site at Antichak, Bhagalpur district), became the leading centre of tantric Buddhist learning in the later Pāla period (Dutt 1962). Tibetan sources describe a hierarchy of learned “gatekeeper scholars” (dvārapaṇḍita) and a strong link with Tibet.

The most famous scholar associated with Vikramaśīla is Atiśa Dīpaṅkara Śrījñāna (982–1054). Born in Bengal, he studied with many teachers, travelled to Suvarṇadvīpa (in present-day Indonesia) to study with the master Dharmakīrti of Suvarṇadvīpa, and became a senior teacher at Vikramaśīla. In 1040 he left for western Tibet at the invitation of its rulers, reaching Tibet in 1042; there he wrote the Bodhipathapradīpa (“Lamp for the Path to Awakening”) and spent the rest of his life. His work shaped the Kadam school and, through it, the later Gelug tradition (Chattopadhyaya 1967). Atiśa is thus a Vikramaśīla figure, not, as is sometimes said, one of the last scholars of Nālandā.

docs.title: 7.4 Other Major Monasteries
docs.text: Odantapurī (Bihar) A Pāla foundation (attributed in Tibetan sources to Gopāla or Dharmapāla) near modern Bihar Sharif; Tibetan tradition holds that it served as a model for Samye. Somapura Mahāvihāra (Paharpur, Bangladesh) Founded by Dharmapāla, as its seals record; one of the largest single monasteries in South Asia, with 177 cells around a vast cruciform shrine. A UNESCO World Heritage Site. Jagaddala (northern Bengal) Founded by Rāmapāla (late 11th century); an important centre in the last decades of Pāla rule. Valabhī (Gujarat) A great monastic centre of the 6th–8th centuries under the Maitraka kings, which Yijing compared with Nālandā; Xuanzang reports that most of its monks followed the Sāṃmitīya school. Takṣaśilā (Taxila, in present-day Pakistan) An ancient city famous as a place of learning (see below), but not a university.

docs.title: 7.5 Takṣaśilā: Teachers, Not a University
docs.text:
Takṣaśilā (Taxila), in the north-west of the subcontinent, has a reputation in Indian tradition as a city of learning. The Jātaka stories often send young men there to study with a famous teacher, and later tradition links the grammarian Pāṇini and the statesman Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya) with the region. It is often described as “the world’s first university”. The evidence does not support that description. The Jātakas describe individual teachers taking private pupils in their homes; there is no evidence of a corporate institution with a campus, curriculum or degrees (Scharfe 2002). Excavations by John Marshall revealed three successive cities (Bhir Mound, Sirkap and Sirsukh) and many Buddhist monasteries and stūpas of the Kuṣāṇa period, such as the Dharmarājikā stūpa and the Jauliāṅ monastery, which were damaged in the troubled fifth and sixth centuries.

Takṣaśilā lay at the meeting point of Indian, Iranian, Greek and Central Asian cultures. The art of the wider Gandhāra region, which produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form, reflects this mixture.

docs.title: 7.6 The Pāla Dynasty and Buddhist Patronage
docs.text:
The Pāla dynasty of Bengal and Bihar (c. 750–1160) was the last great royal patron of Buddhist institutions in India. Its kings — notably Dharmapāla (c. 775–812), Devapāla (c. 812–850) and Mahīpāla I (c. 988–1038) — founded or endowed several great monasteries (Table 7.2), while also supporting Brahmanical temples and brāhmaṇa grantees.

Table 7.2. Major Buddhist monasteries of the Pāla period Monastery Founder/patron Period Notes Nālandā Gupta kings; later Pāla support c. 5th–12th c.
