The oldest and most famous centre Vikramaśīla Dharmapāla late 8th c.–c. 1200 Tantric studies; strong links with Tibet Odantapurī Pāla kings (Tibetan tradition) 8th c.–c. 1200 Model for Samye (Tibetan tradition) Somapura Dharmapāla late 8th c.–12th c. Vast monastery with cruciform shrine Jagaddala Rāmapāla late 11th–early 13th c. One of the last Pāla foundations

The Pāla period also produced a distinctive style of Buddhist art — bronze and stone sculpture and illustrated palm-leaf manuscripts — that influenced the art of Nepal, Tibet, Myanmar and Java (Huntington 1985).

docs.title: 7.7 The Curriculum and Methods of Instruction
docs.text:
Mahāyāna sources such as the Bodhisattvabhūmi name five fields of knowledge (pañca vidyāsthāna) in which a bodhisattva should be trained: the “inner science” (adhyātma-vidyā) of Buddhist doctrine and practice, the science of reasons (hetu-vidyā), that is, logic, epistemology and debate, the science of language (śabda-vidyā) or grammar, the science of healing (cikitsā-vidyā), and the arts and crafts (śilpasthāna-vidyā). The list justified the study of subjects that were not Buddhist in themselves, on the ground that a bodhisattva needs them to help others and to defeat opponents in debate; Xuanzang and Yijing describe the same range of studies at Nālandā (Table 7.1).

Teaching combined the oral exposition of texts by senior scholars, memorisation, private study, tutorial guidance from a preceptor, and debate. Yijing’s account describes the daily life of monks in some detail, including ritual, study and the rules of monastic discipline (Yijing (I-tsing) 1896). Indian educational institutions more generally, Brahmanical as well as Buddhist and Jain, are discussed in Volume 22 of this series (Manas and Śikṣā).

docs.title: 7.8 Medicine in the Monasteries
docs.text:
Medicine (cikitsā-vidyā) was one of the five sciences of the Mahāyāna curriculum, and care of the sick was a duty of the monastic community from the beginning. The Vinaya’s section on medicines (Mahāvagga VI) allows sick monks five “medicines” — ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey and molasses — and regulates the use of roots, fruits, salts and other remedies. Another section (Mahāvagga VIII) tells the stories of Jīvaka Komārabhacca, physician to King Bimbisāra and to the Buddha, and records the Buddha’s rebuke to monks who had neglected a sick companion: whoever would attend on him, he said, should attend on the sick. Aśoka’s Rock Edict II speaks of medical provision for people and for animals and of the planting of medicinal herbs, roots and fruits. Kenneth Zysk has argued that the wandering ascetics and then the Buddhist monasteries played a significant part in forming the empirical, rational medicine later codified as Āyurveda (Zysk 1991).

Yijing devoted several chapters of his record to Indian medicine, describing its eight branches and the practice of fasting during illness (Yijing (I-tsing) 1896). Indian medical learning also travelled with Buddhism to Tibet, where the root text of Tibetan medicine, the Four Tantras (rgyud bzhi), draws heavily on Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, itself translated into Tibetan; whether Vāgbhaṭa was a Buddhist is debated. Jain authors wrote medical works too: the Digambara Ugrāditya’s Kalyāṇakāraka (9th century) presents Āyurveda in a Jain frame and rejects remedies that require the killing of animals. These texts record what their authors taught; they are not evidence that the remedies work. Classical Indian medicine is the subject of Volume 13 of this series (Āyurveda).

docs.title: 7.9 The Buddhist Art of Debate
docs.text:
Debate was a central activity in Indian intellectual life, and the monasteries were among its arenas. The Nyāya tradition classified debate into three kinds, a scheme widely shared (Table 7.3).

Table 7.3. Kinds of debate in the Nyāya classification Type Sanskrit Description Honest debate Vāda Both parties seek the truth by valid means of knowledge Disputation Jalpa Aimed at victory; quibbles and other illegitimate tactics used Destructive debate Vitaṇḍā Refuting the opponent without defending any thesis of one’s own

Xuanzang describes vigorous public debate at Nālandā and at royal courts, where a defeated debater might lose his reputation and his patrons. Later Buddhist and Jain hagiographies are full of debates in which the loser and his followers convert — stories that tell us more about the prestige of debate than about particular historical events. Philosophical exchanges between schools were mostly conducted in writing: the Naiyāyika Uddyotakara, for example, criticised Dignāga in his commentary on the Nyāyasūtra, and Dharmakīrti in turn answered his critics.

Scholarly Note: Debate in Tibet

The Tibetan monastic debate practice — in which a standing challenger questions a seated defender, punctuating each point with a clap — is a Tibetan development, but it rests on the Indian Buddhist logical curriculum transmitted to Tibet, above all the works of Dharmakīrti (Samuel 1993).

docs.title: 7.10 The Spread of Buddhism Across Asia
docs.text:
From its Indian heartland Buddhism spread across much of Asia, carried by monks, merchants and royal envoys (Table 7.4).

Table 7.4. The spread of Buddhism across Asia (approximate dates) Region Period Notes Sri Lanka 3rd c. BCE Mission of Mahinda (tradition); Pāli canon preserved Gandhāra and Central Asia 2nd c. BCE–10th c. CE Kuṣāṇa patronage; Silk Road oasis kingdoms; route to China China 1st c. CE onwards Translation of sūtras; Chan, Pure Land, Tiantai and Huayan schools Korea 4th c. CE Via China; Seon (Chan) and other schools Japan 6th c. CE Via Korea and China; Zen, Pure Land, Shingon, Nichiren Southeast Asia early centuries CE onwards Mahāyāna and Brahmanical (Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava) cults first (Borobudur, 9th c.); Theravāda dominant on the mainland from the 13th–14th c. Tibet 7th–8th c. CE Royal patronage; Indian Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Mongolia 13th c.; revived 16th c. Via Tibet

docs.title: 7.11 The Decline of Buddhism in India
docs.text: By the fourteenth century Buddhism had almost disappeared from most of the Indian plains, surviving mainly in the Himalayan regions and in a few scattered communities, while it flourished in Sri Lanka, Tibet, East and Southeast Asia. How a religion so deeply rooted in India came to vanish from its homeland is one of the major questions of Indian religious history. Historians agree that there was no single cause; they differ on the weight to give to each factor (Harvey 2013; Jaini 1980; Elverskog 2010; Verardi 2011).

docs.title: 7.11.1 A Long Contraction
docs.text: The decline was gradual and uneven. Already in the seventh century Xuanzang described many monasteries in ruins or deserted, especially in the north-west, even as others flourished (Xuanzang 1884). In much of India, Buddhist presence came to be concentrated in large, royally endowed monasteries rather than spread among village communities. In the south, Buddhism weakened from the seventh century onwards, while Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional movements (the Nāyaṉmārs and Āḻvārs) won popular and royal support; Buddhist communities nonetheless survived at Nāgapaṭṭinam and elsewhere for several more centuries. By the eleventh and twelfth centuries the main strongholds of Indian Buddhism were the great monasteries of Bihar and Bengal under the Pālas, along with Kashmir and pockets in Odisha and the south.

docs.title: 7.11.2 Factors Within Indian Society
docs.text:
Several long-term factors weakened Buddhism’s position:

  • Dependence on patronage. Large monasteries depended on land grants and royal favour. When dynasties changed or patrons turned to Brahmanical temples and grantees — as most Indian rulers did in the early medieval period — monasteries lost their resources.

  • A thin lay base. Buddhism had no distinctive lay life-cycle rituals to compare with the Brahmanical saṃskāras performed by household priests, and its lay followers were not organised as a separate community. Lay people could honour Buddhist monks while relying on brāhmaṇas for birth, marriage and death rites, and when the monasteries fell they were readily absorbed into Hindu society. Jaini contrasts this with Jainism, whose monks cultivated a disciplined lay community with its own rites, codes of conduct and caste-like social identity — one reason, he argues, why Jainism survived when Buddhism did not (Jaini 1980).

  • Competition and assimilation. Revived Brahmanical traditions, especially devotional Vaiṣṇavism and Śaivism, competed successfully for royal and popular support. Bronkhorst argues that brāhmaṇas had already, from the last centuries BCE, secured a place at royal courts as advisers and ritual specialists that Buddhist monks did not seek to fill (Bronkhorst 2016). The Buddha was absorbed into the Vaiṣṇava scheme as an incarnation (avatāra) of Viṣṇu, and at the level of ritual and iconography, late Indian Buddhist tantra and Śaiva tantra came to resemble each other closely (Davidson 2002).

  • Hostility and polemic. Brahmanical texts contain polemics against Buddhists, and there are episodes of hostility, such as the persecution attributed to the Śuṅga king Puṣyamitra by later Buddhist sources and the attacks on monasteries recorded for the Hūṇa ruler Mihirakula. Verardi argues that Brahmanical opposition was a major and underrated factor; other historians regard these episodes as local and see competition for patronage as more important (Verardi 2011; Harvey 2013).

docs.title: 7.11.3 The Turkish Conquest of Bihar and Bengal
docs.text:
The final blow to the great monasteries of the east came with the campaigns of the Ghurid general Muḥammad Bakhtiyār Khaljī in Bihar and Bengal at the end of the twelfth century (c. 1193–1205). The Ṭabaqāt-i Nāṣirī of Minhāj al-Sirāj Jūzjānī, written about 1260, describes the capture of a fortified place in Bihar which turned out to be a “college” full of books and shaven-headed brāhmaṇas, who were killed; most historians identify this with the monastery of Odantapurī (Minhāj-ud-dīn 1881; Wink 1997). Vikramaśīla was destroyed around the same time, and Nālandā was sacked. These were not acts against Buddhism alone — the campaigns also struck Brahmanical temples and the states that had protected the monasteries — but because Buddhist learning was concentrated in a few great institutions, their loss was decisive.

Nālandā did not vanish overnight. The Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin, who visited Bihar in 1234–1236, found the site largely ruined but met the aged master Rāhula Śrībhadra still teaching some seventy students there, under threat of further raids (Roerich 1959). Some monks fled to Nepal and Tibet, carrying manuscripts with them; many Sanskrit Buddhist texts survive today only because they were preserved there.

docs.title: 7.11.4 Regional Histories: Kashmir, Odisha and the Tamil Country
docs.text:
The story of decline is usually told from Bihar and Bengal, but the chronology differed from region to region. Three regions outside the Pāla heartland show how varied the end of Indian Buddhism was.

Kashmir and the north-west. Kashmir was one of the oldest and most learned centres of Indian Buddhism. Sri Lankan tradition credits Aśoka’s missionary Majjhantika with bringing Buddhism to Kashmir and Gandhāra; northern tradition, recorded by Xuanzang, places in Kashmir the council held under the Kuṣāṇa king Kaniṣka, at which the great Sarvāstivāda commentaries (vibhāṣā) were compiled. The orthodox Sarvāstivādins of Kashmir — the “Kashmiri Vaibhāṣikas” whose views Vasubandhu summarised and criticised in the Abhidharmakośa (Chapter 3), and whom the Kashmiri master Saṅghabhadra defended against him — set the standard of Abhidharma learning across northern India and Central Asia. Kashmir was also a training-ground for translators who carried Buddhism to China: Kumārajīva studied there as a boy, and Kashmiri monks such as Buddhayaśas and Guṇavarman worked in China in the early fifth century. Xuanzang, who spent two years in Kashmir in the 630s, found about a hundred monasteries and some five thousand monks (Xuanzang 1884; Naudou 1980).

Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148–49), the chronicle of the Kashmiri kings, records many Buddhist foundations by kings, queens and ministers — among them the monastery and stūpa built by Caṅkuṇa, a Central Asian minister of King Lalitāditya in the eighth century — and shows Buddhist and Brahmanical institutions flourishing side by side under the same patrons. It also records the despoiling of temple images, Buddhist and Hindu alike, by the Kashmiri king Harṣa (r. 1089–1101) to obtain their metal (Kalhaṇa 1900). In the late tenth and eleventh centuries Kashmir became a principal source of Buddhism for western Tibet: the translator Rinchen Zangpo (958–1055) studied there and brought Kashmiri artists back with him, and the monastic paintings of western Tibet and Ladakh preserve much of the Kashmiri style. The Kashmiri master Śākyaśrībhadra (1127–1225), who had taught in the monasteries of Bihar and Bengal, reached Tibet in 1204 after their destruction and gave monastic ordination to the young Sakya Paṇḍita, founding a Vinaya lineage still remembered in Tibet. Buddhism in Kashmir itself faded in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; the Ladakhi prince Rinchana, a Buddhist who seized the Kashmiri throne in 1320, became a Muslim soon afterwards, and the valley’s later religious history belongs to Śaivism and Islam (Naudou 1980).

Odisha. Xuanzang found Buddhism strong in Oḍra (central and northern Odisha), with about a hundred monasteries and some ten thousand monks of the Mahāyāna (Xuanzang 1884). Under the Bhauma-Kara kings (8th–10th centuries), several of whom styled themselves devout Buddhists, the monasteries of the Assia hills flourished. Ratnagiri, excavated by Debala Mitra in 1958–61, revealed a large monastery with a main stūpa surrounded by hundreds of votive stūpas, seals bearing the name of the “community of venerable monks of the great monastery of Śrī-Ratnagiri”, and a wealth of Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna sculpture; nearby Lalitgiri, where relic caskets were recovered in later excavations, and Udayagiri belong to the same network (Mitra 1971). Odisha was linked by sea with China: the Chinese record that a king of the region sent a Sanskrit manuscript of the Gaṇḍavyūha to the Tang court in 795 (Sen 2003). Buddhist activity at Ratnagiri continued into the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, later than at most sites in the Ganges valley. Some modern writers have seen Buddhist ideas surviving under a Vaiṣṇava surface in the devotional poetry of the sixteenth-century Odia “five companions” (pañcasakhā), with its language of the void (śūnya); the argument is suggestive but contested. The tantric dimension of these sites is discussed in Volume 6 (Tantra–Āgama).

The Tamil country. The Tamil country was for several centuries a centre of Pāli scholarship as well as of Sanskrit Buddhism. Buddhadatta, an older contemporary of Buddhaghosa, wrote his Vinaya and Abhidhamma manuals at a monastery on the Kāverī, and the commentator Dhammapāla, author of many of the later Pāli commentaries, is associated by tradition with a monastery near Kāñcī; Dharmapāla of Kāñcī, the Yogācāra master, headed Nālandā in the sixth century. The Tamil Buddhist epic Maṇimēkalai is discussed in Chapter 14. Buddhism lost ground in the south from the seventh century to the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional movements (Section 7.11.1), but it survived on the coast, sustained by maritime trade. At Nāgapaṭṭinam a monastery was built around 1006 by the Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya in Sumatra, with revenues granted by the Chola kings Rājarāja I and Rājendra I, and hundreds of Buddhist bronzes of the eleventh to sixteenth centuries have been found there (see Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra). A brick tower at Nāgapaṭṭinam, known to European sailors as the “Chinese pagoda” and probably the last standing Buddhist structure of the port, was demolished in 1867 (Sen 2003).

These regional histories confirm the general picture: Buddhism in India ended not at one moment but over several centuries, at different times in different places, and its last centres were often those connected with Tibet, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia by routes of pilgrimage and trade.

docs.title: 7.11.5 Survival and Revival
docs.text: Buddhism did not entirely disappear. It survived in Ladakh, Lahaul and Spiti, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and the Darjeeling hills; in the Newar community of the Kathmandu valley; among the Barua and other communities of Chittagong; and for a time in pockets of Bengal and Odisha. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries a revival began: archaeologists such as Alexander Cunningham identified and excavated the great Buddhist sites; the Sri Lankan reformer Anagārika Dharmapāla founded the Mahābodhi Society in 1891 and campaigned for Buddhist access to Bodhgaya; and in 1956 B. R. Ambedkar led a mass conversion to Buddhism at Nagpur, the beginning of the largest Buddhist community in modern India (Chapter 14, Section 14.8.1). Tibetan refugees, who followed the Dalai Lama into exile in 1959, re-established their monastic universities in India.

docs.title: 7.12 Nālandā in Memory and History
docs.text:
Figure 7.1. The excavated ruins of Nālandā Mahāvihāra, with the great stūpa known as Temple 3 at the left. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. Photo: Indianvagabond, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The memory of Nālandā has acquired great symbolic importance in modern India. The Nalanda University Act of 2010 established a new international university near the ancient site (Figure 7.1). It is important, however, to remember the historical Nālandā as it was — a Buddhist monastery whose members studied Buddhist doctrine and the sciences useful to it — rather than as a modern secular university projected into the past.

The history of the monasteries cuts both ways. They were among the most important centres of learning in pre-modern Asia: they trained scholars from India, China, Tibet and Southeast Asia, produced and preserved a vast literature, and carried Indian Buddhism to Tibet. But the same concentration of learning, wealth and personnel in a few great institutions, dependent on royal patronage and only loosely tied to a lay community, made Indian Buddhism vulnerable. The decline described in this chapter was the result of a long contraction, the loss of patronage, competition and assimilation, and finally the destruction of the eastern monasteries around 1200. Chapter 13 returns to the question from the side of lay practice and compares the very different Jain pattern.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Mahāvīra and the Tīrthaṅkara Tradition
8.1 The Antiquity of the Jain Tradition
docs.text:
The Jain tradition (Jaina Dharma) traces its origins far beyond the historical figure of Mahāvīra to a lineage of twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras (“Ford-Makers”) who, in successive ages, have established the path of liberation. The Tīrthaṅkaras are called “ford-makers” because they establish a ford (tīrtha) — the fourfold community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen — across the river of suffering and rebirth, enabling others to cross.

Jainism, like Buddhism, recognises a series of teachers in past ages; it regards its teaching as eternal (śāśvata), periodically revealed anew by twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras in each half-cycle of time (Table 8.1) (Dundas 2002; Jaini 1979). Historians accept Mahāvīra and, in all probability, Pārśva as historical; the earlier Tīrthaṅkaras belong to sacred history.

docs.title: 8.1.1 The Twenty-Four Tīrthaṅkaras
docs.text:
The Tīrthaṅkaras of the present descending half-cycle form a sacred history that runs from Ṛṣabha, who in Jain tradition taught humanity agriculture, crafts and writing at the end of an age of plenty, to Mahāvīra. The intervals between them, and their life-spans and statures, diminish as the age declines: the earlier Tīrthaṅkaras are given lives of immense length, while Pārśva is said to have lived a hundred years and Mahāvīra seventy-two. The twenty-second, Neminātha, is made a cousin of Kṛṣṇa, which links Jain sacred history to the epic world of the Mahābhārata. Because the images of all the Jinas show the same serene figure, seated or standing in meditation, each is identified in sculpture by an emblem (lāñchana) carved on the pedestal and, in painting, by a conventional colour (Table 8.1); several emblems differ between the two sects.

Table 8.1. The twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras of the present half-cycle, with their emblems (lāñchana) and colours. Some emblems differ between the sects: Digambaras give a red goose for Sumati, a wish-granting tree for Śītala, a porcupine (sometimes rendered “bear”) for Ananta and a fish for Ara, where Śvetāmbaras give a curlew, the śrīvatsa, a hawk and the nandyāvarta diagram. No. Name Symbol Colour Notes 1 Ṛṣabhadeva (Ādinātha) Bull Golden First Tīrthaṅkara; taught agriculture, crafts, and writing 2 Ajitanātha Elephant Golden 3 Sambhavanātha Horse Golden 4 Abhinandananātha Monkey Golden 5 Sumatinātha Curlew Golden 6 Padmaprabha Lotus Red 7 Supārśvanātha Swastika Green 8 Candraprabha Moon White 9 Puṣpadanta Crocodile (makara) White 10 Śītalanātha Śrīvatsa Golden 11 Śreyāṃsanātha Rhinoceros Golden 12 Vāsupūjya Buffalo Red 13 Vimalanātha Boar Golden 14 Anantanātha Hawk Golden 15 Dharmanātha Vajra Golden 16 Śāntinātha Deer Golden 17 Kunthunātha Goat Golden 18 Aranātha Nandyāvarta Golden 19 Mallinātha Water jar Blue Female Tīrthaṅkara (Śvetāmbara tradition) 20 Munisuvrata Tortoise Black 21 Naminātha Blue lotus Golden 22 Neminātha (Ariṣṭanemi) Conch Black Cousin of Kṛṣṇa (traditional) 23 Pārśvanātha Serpent Blue Probably historical (traditional dates 877–777 BCE) 24 Mahāvīra (Vardhamāna) Lion Golden Historical; 5th c. BCE (traditional dates 599–527 BCE)

docs.title: 8.1.2 Pārśvanātha: The Penultimate Tīrthaṅkara
docs.text: Pārśvanātha (traditionally dated c. 877–777 BCE) is the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara and the earliest whom most historians accept as historical. The Uttarādhyayana (ch. 23) describes a meeting between Keśin, a follower of Pārśva, and Gautama, a disciple of Mahāvīra, which suggests that an older community of Pārśva’s followers merged with Mahāvīra’s. Pārśva’s followers observed a fourfold restraint (cāturyāma dharma): non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness. According to Jain tradition, Mahāvīra made explicit the fifth vow of celibacy (brahmacarya), expanding the code to the Pañca Mahāvrata.

docs.title: 8.2 The Life of Mahāvīra
docs.text: Vardhamāna Mahāvīra (traditional Śvetāmbara dates 599–527 BCE; a calculation based on the twelfth-century author Hemacandra, followed by Jacobi, gives c. 468 BCE for his death; most historians, following the Buddhist evidence that he was a contemporary of the Buddha, place him in the fifth century BCE) is the 24th and last Tīrthaṅkara of the current time cycle. He was born at Kuṇḍagrāma near Vaiśālī (in present-day Bihar) into the Kṣatriya clan of the Jñātṛkas, and his life-story shares certain structural parallels with that of the Buddha while differing in significant details. Like the Buddha’s, it is known mainly from texts compiled long after his death, notably the Ācārāṅga and the Kalpasūtra (Jacobi 1884).

docs.title: 8.2.1 Birth and Early Life
docs.text: According to Śvetāmbara tradition, the soul of the future Mahāvīra descended from the divine realm of Puṣpottara into the womb of Devānandā, a Brahmin woman, and was subsequently transferred (by Indra’s command) to the womb of Triśalā, a Kṣatriya queen. Digambaras reject the story of the transferred embryo. His father was Siddhārtha, a chieftain of the Jñātṛka clan. From the time of his conception, prosperity increased in the family — hence the name Vardhamāna (“the Increasing One”). The two sects differ again on his household life: Śvetāmbaras relate that he married Yaśodā and had a daughter, Priyadarśanā, whereas Digambaras hold that he never married.

docs.title: 8.2.2 Renunciation and Asceticism
docs.text: At the age of thirty Vardhamāna renounced the household life. The Ācārāṅga’s account of the following twelve and a half years, among the oldest passages of the canon, describes an asceticism far more severe than anything the Buddha accepted. According to this text he discarded his single robe after about thirteen months and thereafter went naked (Digambaras hold that he was naked from the start); he fasted for long periods, kept silence (mauna), endured heat, cold, insects and the hostility of villagers without complaint, and walked and ate with constant care not to harm small creatures. The narrative is the model for the Jain mendicant’s discipline described in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Attainment of Kevala-jñāna
docs.text: After twelve and a half years of ascetic practice, Vardhamāna attained Kevala-jñāna — omniscience, the infinite, unbounded knowledge that encompasses all substances, all modes, all times. In Jain doctrine this follows the destruction of the four “destructive” (ghātin) karmas that obscure the soul’s knowledge, perception and energy and delude it (Table 8.5); the remaining, non-destructive karmas sustain the body until death. He was now Jina (“Conqueror”) — conqueror of the inner enemies of desire, hatred, and delusion — and Mahāvīra (“Great Hero”).

docs.title: 8.2.4 Teaching and Nirvāṇa
docs.text: For some thirty years Mahāvīra taught in Magadha, Videha and the neighbouring regions, spending the rainy seasons at towns such as Rājagṛha and Vaiśālī. According to tradition, his first followers were eleven learned brāhmaṇas, led by Indrabhūti Gautama, who became his chief disciples (gaṇadhara) and organised the community; Śvetāmbaras hold that the canon as it now exists descends from the gaṇadhara Sudharman. The Kalpasūtra numbers his community as 14,000 monks, 36,000 nuns and a much larger number of lay men and women (Jacobi 1884). Mahāvīra died at the age of seventy-two at Pāvā (identified by tradition with Pāvāpurī in Bihar), attaining final liberation (nirvāṇa). Jains celebrate the event at Dīvālī, and the Jain era (Vīra Nirvāṇa Saṃvat) is reckoned from it.

docs.title: 8.3 The Five Mahāvratas (Great Vows)
docs.text: The ethical core of Jain teaching is expressed in five great vows (mahāvrata) taken by mendicants: non-violence (ahiṃsā), abstention from harming any living being in thought, word or deed; truthfulness (satya), speaking only what is true and not hurtful; non-stealing (asteya), taking nothing that has not been given; celibacy (brahmacarya); and non-possession (aparigraha), the renunciation of property and of attachment to it. Lay people take the same five vows in a limited form as “lesser vows” (aṇuvrata), described in Chapter 11. The great vows are total: a mendicant renounces harm to all beings, a layman only intentional harm to beings that can move, and the difference between the two is the difference between the two ways of life.

docs.title: 8.3.1 Ahiṃsā: The Supreme Dharma
docs.text:
Of the five vows non-violence comes first, and the others are often explained as its applications. Jain analysis of violence (hiṃsā) is notably fine-grained. Harm can be done by body, speech or mind — by a blow, by a lie or harsh word, or by ill-will — and in each case it may be done oneself (kṛta), caused to be done by others (kārita) or approved when others do it (anumodita). The mendicant renounces all nine combinations. Because karma binds through activity and passion rather than through intention alone, even unintended harm, if it results from carelessness, is a fault; hence the stress on vigilance in every action.

The Ācārāṅga, the oldest Jain canonical text, grounds this ethic in a simple observation: all beings are fond of life, like pleasure and hate pain, shun destruction and long to live; to all, life is dear (Ācārāṅga 1.2.3) (Jacobi 1884). Modern Jains and others have drawn on the passage in discussions of animal welfare and ecological ethics.

docs.title: 8.4 The Jain Classification of Living Beings
docs.text:
Jain biology classifies living beings (jīvas) according to the number of sense-faculties they possess (Table 8.2).

Table 8.2. Jain classification of living beings by sense faculties Senses Category Examples 1 (touch) Ekendriya Earth-bodies, water-bodies, fire-bodies, air-bodies, plants 2 (touch + taste) Dvīndriya Worms, leeches, shellfish 3 (touch + taste + smell) Trīndriya Ants, lice, some insects 4 (+ sight) Caturindriya Flies, bees, butterflies 5 (+ hearing) Pañcendriya Fish, birds, mammals, humans 5 + mind Samanaska (saṃjñin) Five-sensed beings with mind: humans, gods, hell-beings and higher animals

The inclusion of earth, water, fire, and air-bodies (pṛthvīkāya, apkāya, tejaskāya, vāyukāya) as living beings with souls is a distinctive feature of Jain thought. In the classical texts it underlies the mendicant’s rules of restraint — not digging, not using unboiled water, not lighting or extinguishing fires; modern Jain writers have also read it as an ecological ethic (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 8.5 The Jain Āgamic Literature
docs.text:
The canonical literature of Jainism, known as the Āgamas or Siddhānta, was transmitted orally for many centuries. Jain tradition holds that the fourteen Pūrvas (“former texts”), which contained the oldest teaching, were gradually lost through famine and the failure of memory, and that the surviving Śvetāmbara canon was redacted and written down at a council at Valabhī in Gujarat under Devarddhigaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa, 980 or 993 years after Mahāvīra’s death (c. 453 or 466 CE). The Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjakas recognise 45 canonical texts, while the Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī Śvetāmbaras accept 32. The Digambaras hold that the ancient canon was lost; they treat as scripture the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyaprābhṛta and the works of later teachers such as Kundakunda, arranged in four “expositions” (anuyoga) (Dundas 2002). Table 8.3 sets out the structure of the 45-text Śvetāmbara canon.

Table 8.3. Structure of the 45-text Śvetāmbara (Mūrtipūjaka) canon Category Number Principal Texts Aṅgas (Limbs) 11 + 1 lost Ācārāṅga, Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Sthānāṅga, Samavāyāṅga, Vyākhyāprajñapti, Jñātādharma-kathā, Upāsaka-daśā, Antakṛddaśā, Anuttaraupapātikadaśā, Praśnavyākaraṇa, Vipāka-śruta, Dṛṣṭivāda (lost) Upaṅgas (Sub-limbs) 12 Aupapātika, Rājapraśnīya, Jīvābhigama, Prajñāpana, etc. Cheda-sūtras 6 Texts on monastic discipline and procedure Mūla-sūtras 4 Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Āvaśyaka, Piṇḍaniryukti Prakirṇakas (Miscellaneous) 10 Various supplementary texts Nandī and Anuyogadvāra 2 Hermeneutical and encyclopaedic texts

Dhammo maṃgalam ukkiṭṭhaṃ, ahiṃsā saṃjamo tavo; devā vi taṃ namaṃsanti jassa dhamme sayā maṇo.

Dharma is the highest good fortune: non-violence, self-restraint and austerity. Even the gods bow to one whose mind is always set on dharma.

— Daśavaikālika 1.1

docs.title: 8.5.1 The Ācārāṅga Sūtra: The Oldest Jain Text
docs.text:
The Ācārāṅga Sūtra (“Discipline of Conduct”) is the first of the Aṅgas, and its first book (śrutaskandha) is widely regarded as the oldest stratum of the Jain canon, though it cannot be dated precisely (Dundas 2002). It is the main source for Mahāvīra’s ascetic practice and for the early Jain reflection on violence and non-violence, and it states the principles of mendicant life in a form that later texts elaborate.

The first book contains the famous declaration (Ācārāṅga 1.4.1) that the Arhats of past, present and future all teach the same: no breathing, existing, living, sentient creature should be slain, ill-treated, abused, tormented or driven away. Another passage (1.5.5) tells the reader that the one whom he intends to kill, to tyrannise or to torment is “none other than yourself” — an identification of oneself with the victim that forms an ethical foundation of Jain ahiṃsā (Jacobi 1884; Dundas 2002).

docs.title: 8.5.2 Commentaries and Manuscript Libraries
docs.text:
The Śvetāmbara canon is read through several layers of commentary (Dundas 2002). The earliest are the niryuktis, concise Prakrit verse glosses traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu. They were expanded in Prakrit verse bhāṣyas, of which Jinabhadra’s Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya (6th–7th century) is the best known, and in Prakrit prose cūrṇis, such as those of Jinadāsa (7th century). From the eighth century the commentaries were written in Sanskrit: Haribhadra commented on several canonical texts, Śīlāṅka (9th century) on the first two Aṅgas, Abhayadeva (11th century) on nine of the Aṅgas, and Malayagiri (12th century) on many others. The Digambara counterparts are the great commentaries on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Kaṣāyaprābhṛta: Vīrasena’s Dhavalā (completed 816 CE) and the Jayadhavalā, completed by his pupil Jinasena. For centuries the only known manuscripts of these works were palm-leaf copies kept at Mūḍabidri in Karnataka, and they were published only in the twentieth century.

Copying manuscripts and presenting them to monks was regarded as a meritorious “gift of knowledge” (jñānadāna), and lay donors and monastic lineages built up collections known as bhaṇḍāras (“storehouses”), kept in temples and monastic lodgings, above all in western India. The fifteenth-century Kharatara Gaccha teacher Jinabhadrasūri founded or reorganised several of them, including the great collection at Jaisalmer; others survive at Patan, Khambhat and elsewhere (Dundas 2002). These libraries hold many of the oldest surviving Indian manuscripts on palm leaf and paper. They preserved not only Jain works but also Brahmanical and Buddhist texts on grammar, poetics and logic, some of which are known from no other source — Arcaṭa’s commentary on Dharmakīrti’s Hetubindu, for example, was recovered from a manuscript at Patan. Knowledge itself is venerated in an annual rite: Śvetāmbaras worship books on Jñāna Pañcamī in the month of Kārttika, and Digambaras celebrate Śruta Pañcamī, which commemorates the writing down of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama.

docs.title: 8.6 Fourteen Stages of Spiritual Development (Guṇasthāna)
docs.text:
The Jain tradition describes fourteen stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna) through which the soul progresses from complete bondage to complete liberation (Table 8.4).

Table 8.4. The fourteen Guṇasthānas (stages of spiritual development) Stage Name Description 1 Mithyātva Wrong belief; complete spiritual ignorance 2 Sāsvādana Downfall from right belief; taste of truth quickly lost 3 Samyagmithyātva Mixed state; oscillation between right and wrong belief 4 Avirata-samyaktva Right belief without vows; faith established but conduct not yet disciplined 5 Deśavirata Partial self-discipline; layperson observing the aṇuvratas 6 Pramattavirata Complete vows but with lapses of attention; minor transgressions 7 Apramattavirata Complete vows without lapses; vigilant self-discipline 8 Apūrvakaraṇa Unprecedented spiritual exertion; suppression of passions begins 9 Anivṛttibādara Continued suppression; gross passions eliminated 10 Sūkṣmasāmparāya Only the subtlest greed remains 11 Upaśāntakaṣāya Passions fully suppressed (but not yet destroyed) 12 Kṣīṇakaṣāya Passions completely destroyed; the ghātin karmas annihilated 13 Sayogakevalin Omniscience with bodily activity; the state of every omniscient being, Tīrthaṅkara or not, while alive 14 Ayogakevalin Omniscience without any bodily, verbal, or mental activity; immediately precedes liberation

The scheme is a theory of karma as much as a map of the path: each stage is defined by which kinds of karma have been suppressed or destroyed, so that progress is described in the same terms as bondage. Two features are distinctive. The path can be lost as well as gained — a soul in which the passions have only been suppressed (stage 11) falls back — and the stage of right faith without vows (stage 4) is placed well below the lay discipline (stage 5), which in turn is below the mendicant’s. Liberation is thus presented as the end of a long, graded purification rather than as a sudden insight.

docs.title: 8.7 Jain Meditation (Dhyāna)
docs.text:
The Jain tradition has its own contemplative theory, parallel to but distinct from the Buddhist. The Tattvārthasūtra and the canon classify “meditation” (dhyāna) in a way that surprises a modern reader, since two of its four types are bad. “Sorrowful” meditation (ārta-dhyāna) is the mind fixed on pain, loss, illness or unfulfilled desire, and “wrathful” meditation (raudra-dhyāna) the mind fixed on violence, deceit or possessions. Both bind karma. The wholesome types are “virtuous” meditation (dharmya-dhyāna), which contemplates the teaching of the Jinas, the causes of suffering and the means of removing them, the fruits of karma and the structure of the universe, and “pure” meditation (śukla-dhyāna), possible only in the highest stages, which leads directly to the destruction of karma and to omniscience. Meditation, in other words, is any sustained concentration of the mind; what matters is its object.

Later Jain authors drew on the wider Indian yoga tradition. Haribhadra’s Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya (8th century) describes eight “views” (dṛṣṭi) of spiritual progress and correlates them explicitly with the eight limbs of Patañjali’s yoga; Śubhacandra’s Jñānārṇava (11th–12th century) and Hemacandra’s Yogaśāstra (12th century), written for the Caulukya king Kumārapāla, present Jain ethics and meditation in the vocabulary of yoga (Dundas 2002). In the twentieth century Ācārya Mahāprajña of the Terāpanthī order developed prekṣā dhyāna (“perception meditation”), a modern system intended also for lay practitioners. The wider history of yoga is the subject of Volume 5 of this series (Yoga Taraṅgiṇī).

docs.title: 8.8 The Two Sects: Digambara and Śvetāmbara
docs.text:
The Jain community gradually divided into two major traditions. Each tells its own story of the split: Digambaras link it to a famine in Magadha in the time of Bhadrabāhu and Candragupta Maurya (c. 300 BCE), when part of the community migrated south (Figure 8.1 shows a later Jain monument in the south) and preserved the old discipline of nudity. Both sects place the decisive break in the late first century CE (c. 80 CE), each presenting it as the other side’s departure from the original community. Historians see a gradual divergence that crystallised by about the fifth century CE (Dundas 2002; Jaini 1991):

Digambara (“Sky-Clad”) Fully initiated monks of this tradition practise complete nudity as a mark of total renunciation; nuns wear white robes. The Digambaras hold that women cannot attain liberation in a female body (they must first be reborn as men), since they cannot practise nudity (Jaini 1991), that the Tīrthaṅkaras do not eat after attaining omniscience, and that the original canon — the Aṅgas as well as the Pūrvas — has been lost. Śvetāmbara (“White-Clad”) Monks and nuns of this tradition wear simple white garments. The Śvetāmbaras hold that women can attain liberation (the 19th Tīrthaṅkara, Mallinātha, was a woman according to their tradition), that the Tīrthaṅkaras do eat, and that the canonical Āgamas preserve the authentic teaching.

Inscriptions offer an independent check on these traditions. Numerous inscriptions from the Jain site of Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā at Mathurā, most of them from the Kuṣāṇa period (1st–3rd centuries CE), record gifts of images and shrines by monks, nuns and lay people, many of them women, and name monastic groups (gaṇa, kula, śākhā) that correspond to those in the list of elders in the Kalpasūtra. They show an organised Jain community in north India at that date, before the sectarian division had hardened (Dundas 2002).

Despite these differences, both sects share the fundamental doctrines of Jainism: the reality of the soul (jīva), karma as a material substance, the possibility of liberation through the three jewels, and the centrality of ahiṃsā.

docs.title: 8.8.1 Later Sub-Traditions
docs.text:
Each of the two traditions later divided further, usually over questions of discipline and worship rather than doctrine (Dundas 2002; Cort 2001; Babb 1996).

Among the Śvetāmbaras, the majority, known as Mūrtipūjakas (“image-worshippers”), venerate images of the Tīrthaṅkaras in temples and are organised in monastic lineages (gaccha), of which the Tapā and Kharatara Gacchas are the largest today. In the fifteenth century the Gujarati layman Loṅkā Śāh argued that image worship had no warrant in the canonical texts. Movements that grew out of his critique led, in the seventeenth century, to the Sthānakavāsīs, who reject temple worship and whose mendicants wear a mouth-cloth (muhpattī) at all times to protect tiny beings in the air. In 1760 Ācārya Bhikṣu founded the Terāpanthī order, which also rejects image worship and is organised under a single ācārya; in the twentieth century its leader Ācārya Tulsī launched the Aṇuvrat movement (1949), which promotes a simplified set of ethical vows for people of any religion. These two non-image-worshipping orders accept a canon of 32 texts.

Among the Digambaras, a long-standing distinction developed between the bhaṭṭārakas — clothed clerics who administered temples, libraries and community affairs during the many centuries when naked monks were rare — and lay reform movements. In the seventeenth century the Digambara Terāpanthīs, a lay-led reform movement in north India, rejected the authority of the bhaṭṭārakas and certain temple rituals, while the Bīsapanthīs continued older practices. The tradition of fully naked Digambara monks, which had become very rare, was revived in the early twentieth century by Ācārya Śāntisāgara (1872–1955).

These divisions coexist with a strong sense of shared identity. In modern India, all Jain groups jointly celebrate occasions such as Mahāvīra Jayantī, and in 1974 they agreed on a common flag and emblem for the 2,500th anniversary of Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa, bearing the motto parasparopagraho jīvānām.

docs.title: 8.9 Jainism in the South
docs.text:
For more than a thousand years the Digambara tradition was strongest not in the Ganges valley but in the Deccan and the Tamil country, and much of its literature, art and organisation took shape there (Desai 1957; Dundas 2002).

Origins. Digambara tradition holds that Bhadrabāhu led part of the community south during a twelve-year famine in Magadha, accompanied by the Maurya emperor Candragupta, who ended his life by sallekhanā on the hill at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa still called Candragiri. The inscriptions there that record this story are several centuries later than the events, and historians treat the royal connection with caution. Older evidence comes from the Tamil country: natural caverns in the hills around Madurai, fitted with rock-cut stone beds, carry Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions from about the second century BCE onwards recording gifts to ascetics. Many scholars connect these shelters with Jain monks, though not every one can be assigned to a particular sect.

Royal patronage. In Karnataka the Gaṅga kings of Talakāḍ, the Kadambas, the Cālukyas of Bādāmi and the Rāṣṭrakūṭas all supported Jain monks and temples. Pulakeśin II’s Aihoḷe inscription of 634 CE, one of the finest Sanskrit poems in stone, was composed by the Jain poet Ravikīrti for his temple on Meguti hill. Amoghavarṣa I (r. c. 814–878) was a patron of the Digambara teachers Jinasena and Guṇabhadra, and the Gaṅga minister Cāmuṇḍarāya commissioned the Bāhubali colossus (Figure 8.1). Under the Hoysaḷas, Jain generals and ministers such as Gaṅgarāja, and Queen Śāntaladevī, wife of Viṣṇuvardhana, endowed temples at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa and elsewhere. The southern Digambara mendicants were organised in lineages (saṅgha, gaṇa) such as the Mūla Saṅgha and the Drāviḍa Saṅgha, which the tenth-century Darśanasāra says was founded at Madurai in 470 CE.

Figure 8.1. The feet of the colossal statue of Bāhubali (Gommaṭeśvara) at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Karnataka, with a worshipper. The statue, about 17.4 metres (57 feet) high, was commissioned in the late tenth century (c. 981–983) by Cāmuṇḍarāya, minister of the Gaṅga kings; Kannada inscriptions are visible at its base. Photo: Dey.sandip, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Contraction and survival. From the seventh century the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional movements won royal support in the Tamil country. The Śaiva hagiographies tell of Jain monks defeated in debate at the Pāṇḍya court and put to death; these are partisan accounts written centuries later, but they reflect a real loss of patronage. Jain art nevertheless continued for some time: the carved shelters of Kalugumalai and the paintings of Sittannavasal date from the eighth and ninth centuries, and a small Tamil Jain community survives today. In Karnataka, Jain patronage weakened from the twelfth century with the rise of the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) movement and of Vaiṣṇava devotion, but the tradition never disappeared. Bhaṭṭāraka seats at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa and Mūḍabidri still function, the colossal Bāhubali images at Kārkaḷa (1432) and Veṇūr (1604) were set up long after the Gaṅga age, and Karnataka remains, with Maharashtra, a centre of Digambara life. Jain contributions to Kannada and Tamil literature are discussed in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 8.10 The Three Jewels (Ratnatraya)
docs.text:
The Jain path to liberation is summed up in the “three jewels” (ratnatraya): right faith or insight (samyak darśana), the conviction that the categories of reality taught by the Tīrthaṅkaras are true; right knowledge (samyak jñāna) of those categories — of the soul, of what is not soul and of their relation; and right conduct (samyak cāritra), the practice of the vows, austerities and meditation. The three are a single path, not three alternatives, and the order matters: conduct without faith and knowledge does not lead to liberation. The formula opens the Tattvārthasūtra:

Samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritrāṇi mokṣamārgaḥ.

Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct together constitute the path to liberation.

— Tattvārthasūtra I.1, Umāsvāti

This is the opening aphorism of Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra (Umāsvāti 1994) (also called Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra), the most authoritative and universally accepted philosophical text in the Jain tradition, revered by both Digambaras and Śvetāmbaras.

docs.title: 8.11 Jain Karma Theory
docs.text:
The Jain theory of karma is distinctive in treating karma not merely as a moral law but as a material substance — an extremely fine, invisible form of matter (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul and obscures its inherent qualities of infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy (Jaini 1979; Schubring 1962).

Activity of body, speech and mind draws karmic matter into the soul (āsrava); the passions (kaṣāya) — anger, pride, deceit and greed — make it stick (bandha); discipline stops the inflow (saṃvara); austerity and meditation wear away what has already been bound (nirjarā); and when all karma is gone the soul is liberated (mokṣa). These processes form five of the seven categories of reality (tattva) set out in Chapter 9 (Table 9.3).

The Jain tradition identifies eight types of karma, classified into “destructive” (ghātin) and “non-destructive” (aghātin) categories (Table 8.5).

Table 8.5. The eight types of karma in Jain philosophy Type Sanskrit Effect Destructive (ghātin) karmas Knowledge-obscuring Jñānāvaraṇīya Obscures the soul’s infinite knowledge Perception-obscuring Darśanāvaraṇīya Obscures the soul’s infinite perception Deluding Mohanīya Produces delusion regarding faith and conduct Obstructive Antarāya Obstructs the soul’s infinite energy Non-destructive (aghātin) karmas Feeling-producing Vedanīya Produces pleasant and unpleasant experiences Lifespan-determining Āyuṣya Determines the duration of life in a particular form Name-determining Nāma Determines the body, its qualities, and condition Status-determining Gotra Determines the family, status, and social standing

docs.title: Chapter 9: Jain Philosophy: Anekāntavāda, Syādvāda, and Nayavāda
9.1 The Distinctive Tools of Jain Philosophy
docs.text:
Jain philosophy is one of the most original of the classical Indian systems (Matilal 1981; Dundas 2002). While the Jain tradition shares with the Buddhist and Brahmanical schools a concern with liberation (mokṣa), it developed three distinctive philosophical tools — anekāntavāda (the doctrine of non-one-sidedness), syādvāda (the doctrine of conditional predication) and nayavāda (the theory of standpoints) — with which it claimed to do justice to a reality that has many aspects at once.

These three doctrines are not separate theories but interconnected aspects of a single philosophical vision. Anekāntavāda is the ontological thesis: reality is many-sided. Nayavāda is the epistemological method: reality can be apprehended from multiple standpoints. Syādvāda is the logical expression: any proposition about reality must be qualified by the conditional particle syāt (“in some respect,” “from a certain standpoint”) (Long 2009; Matilal 1981).

docs.title: 9.2 Anekāntavāda: The Doctrine of Non-Absolutism
docs.text: Anekāntavāda (literally “the doctrine of non-one-sidedness” or “many-sidedness”) is the Jain ontological principle that reality is complex, multi-dimensional, and not reducible to any single characterisation. Every entity (vastu) possesses infinite attributes (dharma), and any single description captures only one aspect of the whole.

docs.title: 9.2.1 The Parable of the Blind Men and the Elephant
docs.text:
A popular illustration of Anekāntavāda is the parable of the blind men and the elephant. Its earliest known version is Buddhist (Udāna 6.4), where it illustrates the quarrels of sectarian teachers; Jain authors later adopted it to illustrate the partial truth of one-sided views.

A group of blind men each touch a different part of an elephant: one touches the trunk and declares the elephant to be like a snake; another touches the leg and declares it to be like a pillar; another touches the tail and declares it to be like a rope; and so on. Each is partially right, but none possesses the complete truth. Only by integrating all perspectives can the full reality of the elephant be apprehended.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Philosophical Implications
docs.text: The classical formulation is Siddhasena Divākara’s: every view is true in its own sphere and false when it denies the others. Rival philosophies are therefore not simply wrong but one-sided (ekānta); each grasps a real aspect of things and errs only in taking that aspect for the whole. The Buddhist who says that everything is momentary is right about modes, and the Vedāntin who says that reality is permanent is right about substance; the Jain view, which affirms both, claims to include what is true in each. Modern Jain writers have drawn from this a lesson of intellectual humility and tolerance, but in its classical setting the doctrine was also a strategy of argument, which allowed Jain logicians to absorb and subordinate their opponents’ positions (Chapter 11, Section 11.6).

docs.title: 9.3 Syādvāda: The Doctrine of Conditional Predication
docs.text: Syādvāda (the doctrine of “perhaps” or “in some respect”) is the logical method by which Anekāntavāda is expressed in propositions. According to Syādvāda, any proposition about reality can be stated in seven modes (saptabhaṅgī), each qualified by the particle syāt (“in some respect,” “from a certain standpoint”).

docs.title: 9.3.1 The Seven-Fold Predication (Saptabhaṅgī)
docs.text:
Taking as an example the proposition “the pot exists” (ghaṭa asti), the seven modes are set out in Table 9.1 and Figure 9.1.

Table 9.1. The seven modes of Syādvāda (Saptabhaṅgī) No. Mode (Sanskrit) Meaning 1 Syād asti In some respect, it exists (e.g., as a clay object, in a certain place and time) 2 Syād nāsti In some respect, it does not exist (e.g., it is not a cloth, not in another place) 3 Syād asti nāsti In some respect, it both exists and does not exist (considering different aspects successively) 4 Syād avaktavya In some respect, it is inexpressible (both properties simultaneously cannot be verbally expressed at once) 5 Syād asti avaktavya In some respect, it exists and is inexpressible 6 Syād nāsti avaktavya In some respect, it does not exist and is inexpressible 7 Syād asti nāsti avaktavya In some respect, it exists, does not exist, and is inexpressible Figure 9.1. The Saptabhaṅgī (seven-fold predication) of Syādvāda, arranged to show how the seven modes are built from three basic predications.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Logical Sophistication
docs.text: The Saptabhaṅgī is not a violation of the law of non-contradiction, as critics have sometimes alleged. Each of the seven modes applies from a different standpoint (naya) and in a different respect. The Jain logicians were careful to specify that “exists” and “does not exist” are predicated of the same entity but with respect to different attributes, times, places, or natures. In the standard example, a clay pot “exists” with respect to its own substance (clay), place, time and state, and “does not exist” with respect to another substance (such as metal), another place, time or state; there is no contradiction because the respects differ. Modern scholars have discussed whether the scheme is best understood as a many-valued logic, a logic of context-relative assertion or a theory of perspectives (Matilal 1981; Ganeri 2001).

docs.title: 9.4 Nayavāda: The Theory of Standpoints
docs.text: Nayavāda (the theory of nayas, or “standpoints”) is the epistemological complement to Anekāntavāda and Syādvāda. A naya is a particular standpoint or perspective from which reality is viewed. Each naya captures a partial truth; error arises when a partial perspective is mistaken for the whole truth (nayābhāsa).

docs.title: 9.4.1 The Seven Nayas
docs.text:
The standard list, given in the Tattvārthasūtra and its commentaries, has seven nayas in two groups (Table 9.2). The first three look at things as substances (dravyārthika): the “common-sense” standpoint (naigama) that takes the general and the particular together, as when one says “I am cooking” while still lighting the fire; the “collective” standpoint (saṅgraha) that attends only to what things have in common, such as being; and the “practical” standpoint (vyavahāra) that divides the collective into the kinds that ordinary usage needs. The last four look at modes (paryāyārthika): the “straight-thread” standpoint (ṛjusūtra) that considers only the present moment, which the Jains regarded as the Buddhist error when taken by itself; and three linguistic standpoints, which attend to the grammatical form of a word (śabda), to its etymology, so that synonyms are not treated as identical (samabhirūḍha), and to the moment at which a word’s meaning is actually realised (evambhūta), so that Indra is “Indra” only while exercising lordship. The list runs from the widest to the narrowest view, and each is valid within its limits.

Table 9.2. The seven Nayas (standpoints) of Jain epistemology Group No. Naya Description Dravyārthika (Substance- oriented) 1 Naigama The common-sense standpoint that grasps both universal and particular without distinguishing them 2 Saṅgraha The synthetic standpoint that focuses on the universal, generic aspect 3 Vyavahāra The practical standpoint that focuses on the particular, empirical aspect Paryāyārthika (Mode- oriented) 4 Ṛjusūtra The straight-thread standpoint that focuses on the present moment 5 Śabda The verbal or linguistic standpoint; the analysis of words and their referents 6 Samabhirūḍha The etymological standpoint that derives meaning from word-roots 7 Evambhūta The “such-like” standpoint that restricts the meaning to what is presently actualised

docs.title: 9.5 The Six Dravyas (Substances)
docs.text:
Jain metaphysics recognises six eternal, uncreated substances (dravya) (Schubring 1962; Long 2009). Souls (jīva) are conscious, infinite in number and each eternally individual. Matter (pudgala) has colour, taste, smell and touch, and makes up bodies, speech, mind and karma itself. Space (ākāśa) gives room to everything else and extends beyond the inhabited universe (loka) into an infinite empty space. Two further substances are peculiar to Jainism: dharma, the medium that makes motion possible, and adharma, the medium of rest; they fill the loka but not the space beyond it, which is why liberated souls, rising, stop at its summit. Time (kāla), counted as a substance by most authors, accounts for change and succession. The terms dharma and adharma here have nothing to do with their moral sense elsewhere in Indian thought.

Each substance (dravya) possesses qualities (guṇa) and modes (paryāya). The substance itself is permanent, while its modes change from moment to moment. This ontological framework allows the Jain philosopher to affirm both permanence and change, both identity and difference — an expression of Anekāntavāda at the metaphysical level.

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Jīva–Ajīva Distinction
docs.text:
The most fundamental ontological distinction in Jainism is between jīva (soul, consciousness) and ajīva (non-soul, unconscious matter). The five non-soul substances (pudgala, ākāśa, dharma, adharma, and kāla) are all ajīva.

The soul so understood is eternal and individual; its defining quality is consciousness (cetanā); it is an agent (kartā) and an experiencer (bhoktā) of the fruits of its acts; and, unusually among Indian theories of the self, it is of the same size as the body it occupies, expanding and contracting like the light of a lamp in a large or a small room. Its infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy are its own nature, obscured but not destroyed by karma, so that liberation is the recovery of what the soul always was.

This position stands in sharp contrast to the Buddhist doctrine of anātman (no-self), which denies the existence of a permanent, unchanging soul.

docs.title: 9.6 Jain Epistemology: The Pramāṇas
docs.text: The Jain tradition recognises five types of knowledge (jñāna), which from Umāsvāti onwards are organised under two pramāṇas, direct and indirect (Umāsvāti 1994). Sensory knowledge (mati), gained through the senses and the mind, and verbal or scriptural knowledge (śruta), gained through words and texts, are indirect (parokṣa), because they depend on instruments outside the soul. Clairvoyance (avadhi), limited in space and time, knowledge of the minds of others (manaḥparyāya), and omniscience (kevala), the unlimited knowledge of all substances and all their modes in all times, are direct (pratyakṣa), known by the soul without the senses. The classification inverts ordinary usage, in which sense-perception is the model of direct knowledge; later logicians, beginning with Akalaṅka, therefore also called ordinary perception “empirically direct” (sāṃvyavahārika pratyakṣa) to accommodate the usage of other schools. Omniscience, the knowledge of every kevalin, of whom the Tīrthaṅkaras are the teaching exemplars, is the goal of the path.

docs.title: 9.7 The Tattvas: Categories of Reality
docs.text:
Jain philosophy identifies seven (or, in expanded formulations, nine) fundamental categories of reality (tattvas) that provide the conceptual framework for understanding the soul’s bondage and liberation (Table 9.3).

Table 9.3. The seven (or nine) Tattvas of Jain philosophy No. Tattva English Description 1 Jīva Soul The conscious, eternal, individual entity 2 Ajīva Non-soul The five non-conscious substances: matter, space, dharma, adharma, time 3 Āsrava Influx The inflow of karmic matter into the soul through activities of body, speech, and mind 4 Bandha Bondage The binding of karmic matter to the soul through passions 5 Saṃvara Stoppage The prevention of new karmic influx through ethical discipline 6 Nirjarā Shedding The destruction of accumulated karma through austerity and meditation 7 Mokṣa Liberation Complete freedom from all karma; the soul’s attainment of infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy 8* Puṇya Merit Influx of auspicious karma through wholesome actions 9* Pāpa Demerit Influx of inauspicious karma through unwholesome actions

* Added in the nine-fold scheme (navatattva), common in Śvetāmbara teaching; the Tattvārthasūtra (I.4) lists seven.

Jīvājīvāsrava-bandha-saṃvara- nirjarā-mokṣās tattvam.

Soul, non-soul, influx, bondage, stoppage, shedding, and liberation — these are the categories of reality.

— Tattvārthasūtra I.4, Umāsvāti

The comprehension of these seven tattvas constitutes samyak-jñāna (right knowledge), which, together with samyak-darśana (right faith) and samyak-cāritra (right conduct), forms the path to liberation.

docs.title: 9.8 Major Jain Philosophers and Their Works
docs.text:
The principal Jain philosophers, listed in Table 9.4, wrote in constant exchange with Buddhist and Brahmanical opponents, and several of their works survive partly because they quote those opponents at length.

Table 9.4. Major Jain philosophers and their contributions Philosopher Period Key Works and Contributions Umāsvāti between 2nd and 5th c. CE (disputed) Tattvārthasūtra — the most authoritative compendium of Jain philosophy, accepted by both sects Kundakunda disputed: traditionally 1st c.; estimates range from 2nd to 8th c. CE Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra, Niyamasāra, Pañcāstikāya — foundational Digambara philosophy; distinction between niścaya-naya and vyavahāra-naya Siddhasena Divākara c. 5th c. CE Sanmatitarka; the Nyāyāvatāra attributed to him may be by a later Siddhasena — pioneering work in Jain logic Samantabhadra c. 6th c. CE (disputed) Āptamīmāṃsā — systematic defence of the Jain theory of knowledge Akalaṅka c. 8th cent. CE Tattvārtharājavārttika, Laghīyastraya, Aṣṭaśatī — refutation of Buddhist logic; development of Jain epistemology Haribhadra Sūri c. 8th cent. CE Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, Anekāntajayapatākā — comparative survey of the philosophical systems; critique of Buddhist positions Prabhācandra c. 11th cent. CE Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa — comprehensive epistemological treatise Hemacandra 1088/89–1172 CE Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, grammars of Sanskrit and Prakrit, histories; honoured as Kalikālasarvajña (“the omniscient of the Kali age”) Yaśovijaya 17th cent. CE Jainatarkabhāṣā — integration of Navya-Nyāya logic with Jain philosophy

docs.title: 9.8.1 Kundakunda and the Two-Standpoint Theory
docs.text:
Kundakunda, whose date is disputed (traditional accounts place him in the first century CE, while some modern scholars place him as late as the eighth), is the most revered author of the Digambara tradition (Dundas 2002). His distinction between the niścaya-naya (ultimate standpoint) and the vyavahāra-naya (conventional standpoint) shaped all later Digambara thought.

From the ultimate standpoint, the soul is pure consciousness, untouched by karma, eternally free. From the conventional standpoint, the soul is bound by karma, caught in the cycle of rebirth, and in need of liberation. Both standpoints are valid — a characteristic expression of Jain anekāntavāda applied to the self.

docs.title: 9.8.2 Haribhadra Sūri and Comparative Philosophy
docs.text: Haribhadra Sūri (c. 8th century CE) is notable as an early practitioner of comparative philosophy. His Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (“Compendium of the Six Philosophies”) gives an even-handed summary of six systems — Buddhist, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā — with a brief account of the materialist Lokāyata; it does not, as is sometimes said, treat Yoga and Vedānta as separate systems. His approach embodies the Jain principle of anekāntavāda — the recognition that different philosophical systems capture different aspects of a complex reality.

docs.title: 9.9 Jain Logic and the Challenge to Buddhist Epistemology
docs.text:
The Jain logicians engaged in extensive and sophisticated debates with their Buddhist counterparts, particularly regarding the nature of perception, the validity of omniscience, and the theory of universals.

Scholarly Note: Akalaṅka and Dharmakīrti

The Jain philosopher Akalaṅka (8th century CE) mounted a systematic critique of Dharmakīrti’s epistemology. He accepted that there are two pramāṇas but redefined them: the direct (pratyakṣa) includes both ordinary sense-perception and the supersensory knowledge of the Jain tradition, while the indirect (parokṣa) includes memory, recognition (pratyabhijñā), inductive reasoning (tarka), inference and scriptural testimony — several of which Dharmakīrti had refused to count as valid cognition. He also attacked the Buddhist doctrines of momentariness and of meaning by exclusion (apoha), arguing that they made stable knowledge and moral responsibility impossible (Dundas 2002; Ganeri 2001). Table 9.5 summarises the key points of disagreement.

Table 9.5. Key points of disagreement between Jain and Buddhist epistemology Issue Buddhist Position (Dharmakīrti) Jain Position (Akalaṅka) Nature of reality All phenomena are momentary (kṣaṇika) Substances are permanent; modes change Universals Unreal; apoha (exclusion) theory Real; every entity has both general and particular aspects (sāmānya-viśeṣātmaka) Self/Soul No-self (anātman); stream of moments Eternal, individual soul (jīva) Omniscience Dharmakīrti stresses the Buddha’s authority on what matters for liberation; later Buddhists defend full omniscience Affirmed as the highest form of knowledge (kevala) Number of pramāṇas Two: perception and inference Two: direct and indirect, the latter including memory, recognition, tarka, inference and testimony Nature of perception Non-conceptual; unique particular Both conceptual and non-conceptual forms

docs.title: 9.10 Comparison with Buddhist and Brahmanical Philosophies
docs.text:
The Jain position is easiest to see against its neighbours.

Versus Buddhist Anātman While Buddhism denies the existence of a permanent self (anātman), Jainism affirms the reality of an eternal, individual soul (jīva). For the Jain, the soul is the knower, the agent, and the experiencer; the Buddhist reduces these to a stream of momentary mental events. Versus Advaita Vedānta While Advaita Vedānta posits a single, universal Self (Brahman/Ātman), Jainism insists on the plurality and individuality of souls. Each soul is distinct even in liberation. Versus Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika The Jain system shares with Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika a realist metaphysics, but differs in its theory of substance (six dravyas versus the Vaiśeṣika’s seven padārthas) and in its distinctive logical method (Syādvāda versus the Nyāya syllogism).

Seen together, the doctrines of many-sidedness, conditional predication and standpoints give the Jain system its characteristic shape: a realism that affirms both permanence and change, and a logic designed to state that double affirmation without contradiction. Modern Jain writers have drawn on this framework as a resource for dialogue between traditions; in its classical setting it was also a weapon of debate, used to show that rival systems each grasped only part of the truth. The place of Jain philosophy among the Indian philosophical systems is discussed further in Volume 3 of this series (Darśana Darpaṇa).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Mathematics in the Jain Tradition
10.1 Mathematics and the Jain Worldview
docs.text:
Jain authors took a sustained interest in number, measure and calculation. The interest was not, for the most part, “pure” mathematics in the modern sense. It arose from the needs of a cosmology that describes a vast but measurable universe, from a theory of karma that counts and classifies the kinds and quantities of karmic matter bound to the soul, and from a monastic scholarship that prized exhaustive classification. The result is a body of material, scattered through canonical and post-canonical texts, that historians of mathematics have studied since the early twentieth century (Datta 1929; Plofker 2009).

The main themes of that material are:

  • a classification of quantities into the numerable (saṅkhyāta), the innumerable (asaṅkhyāta) and the infinite (ananta), each with internal grades;

  • very large numbers and time-units, defined by thought-experiments with pits filled with seeds or hairs;

  • operations such as repeated halving (ardhaccheda) and repeated squaring, whose rules resemble those of logarithms and exponents;

  • counting combinations (bhaṅga, vikalpa) of philosophical positions, senses or karmic states;

  • the geometry of circles needed for a cosmos of concentric continents and oceans, using the value \(\pi \approx \sqrt{10}\).

A word of caution is needed at the outset. Popular accounts often claim that Jain texts “anticipated” Cantor’s transfinite numbers, Napier’s logarithms, modern set theory or even the place-value system itself. These claims do not survive a reading of the sources. What the texts contain is interesting enough on its own terms, and this chapter describes it without such comparisons except where a modern analogy is clearly marked as an analogy.

docs.title: 10.2 Sources and Their Dates
docs.text:
The relevant material is spread over texts of very different ages. The Śvetāmbara canonical texts were transmitted orally for centuries and received their final redaction at the council of Valabhī in the fifth century CE (Chapter 8); individual passages may be much older, but no part of the canon can be dated securely to a particular century BCE (Dundas 2002). The Digambara works are post-canonical by definition and can be dated somewhat more precisely (Table 10.1).

Table 10.1. Principal Jain texts with mathematical content Text Date (approx.) Mathematical content Sthānāṅga (Ṭhāṇaṃga) canonical; redacted at Valabhī, 5th c. CE List of ten topics of calculation (saṅkhyāna); numerical classifications Vyākhyāprajñapti (Bhagavatī) canonical; redacted 5th c. CE Counting of combinations (bhaṅga) Sūryaprajñapti, Jambūdvīpaprajñapti canonical; redacted 5th c. CE (older astronomical content) Calendar astronomy; circle measures with \(\pi\approx\sqrt{10}\) Anuyogadvāra early centuries CE; redacted 5th c. CE The 21-fold classification of number; time-units; large numbers Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya c. 4th–5th c. CE (attributed to Umāsvāti) Rules for chords and arcs of a circle Lokavibhāga (Sanskrit, by Siṃhasūri) based on a Prakrit original dated 458 CE Cosmology using place-value word numerals Tiloyapaṇṇatti (Yativṛṣabha) composite, c. 5th–8th c. CE Cosmography; measures of the loka; grades of number Dhavalā (Vīrasena) on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama completed 816 CE Rules for ardhaccheda and related operations; large numbers Gommaṭasāra, Trilokasāra (Nemicandra) c. 10th c. CE Quantitative karma theory; cosmography Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha (Mahāvīra, the mathematician) c. 850 CE General arithmetic, algebra and geometry

The last entry deserves notice. Mahāvīra (or Mahāvīrācārya), a Digambara Jain who worked at the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I, wrote the Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha, a comprehensive textbook of arithmetic, algebra and geometry. Unlike the canonical material, it belongs to the mainstream of Indian mathematics and was used well beyond the Jain community (Plofker 2009); a selection of Indian mathematical texts in translation, with commentary, is given in Plofker’s sourcebook chapter (Plofker 2007). Its nine chapters run from terminology and the basic operations through fractions, miscellaneous problems, the rule of three and “mixed” problems (interest, partnership and the like) to plane geometry, excavations and shadows. Among its notable rules are a general rule for the number of combinations of \(n\) things taken \(r\) at a time and the explicit statement that a negative quantity, not being a square, has no square root. Its opening verses praise calculation as necessary to every worldly and religious pursuit, and its problems are often framed with Jain imagery, but its methods are those shared with the astronomer-mathematicians of the period.

docs.title: 10.2.1 The Ten Topics of the Sthānāṅga
docs.text: The Sthānāṅga, which arranges its material in numbered lists from one to ten, includes a list of ten topics of calculation (saṅkhyāna). Datta interpreted them as: fundamental operations (parikamma), determinations or practical problems (vavahāra), geometry (rajju, literally “rope”), mensuration of heaps (rāsi), fractions (kalāsavaṇṇa), simple equations (jāvaṃ tāvaṃ, “as much as”), squares (vagga), cubes (ghaṇa), fourth powers (vaggavagga) and combinations (vikappa) (Datta 1929). The list is terse and its interpretation partly conjectural, but it shows that by the time of the canon’s redaction calculation was recognised as a field with recognised sub-topics.

docs.title: 10.3 The Classification of Number
docs.text: The best-known Jain contribution is a classification of all quantities (saṅkhyā) that appears in the Anuyogadvāra and is elaborated in later Digambara works such as the Tiloyapaṇṇatti and the Dhavalā.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Three Kinds and Twenty-One Grades
docs.text:
Quantities are first divided into three kinds:

  1. Saṅkhyāta (numerable): finite quantities that can in principle be counted. The lowest is two, since one was not regarded as a “number” in the sense of a counted plurality.

  2. Asaṅkhyāta (innumerable): quantities beyond the highest numerable.

  3. Ananta (infinite): quantities beyond the highest innumerable.

Each kind is then graded. The numerable has three grades: lowest (jaghanya), intermediate (madhyama) and highest (utkṛṣṭa). The innumerable and the infinite are each divided into three orders — parīta (“limited”), yukta (“joined”) and the “innumerable-innumerable” (asaṅkhyāta-asaṅkhyāta) or “infinite-infinite” (ananta-ananta) — and each order again has a lowest, intermediate and highest grade. The full scheme therefore has \(3 + 9 + 9 = 21\) grades of number (Table 10.2 and Figure 10.1) (Datta 1929; Plofker 2009).

Table 10.2. The twenty-one grades of number in the Anuyogadvāra scheme Kind Orders Grades Saṅkhyāta (numerable) — lowest (two), intermediate, highest: 3 grades Asaṅkhyāta (innumerable) parīta, yukta, asaṅkhyāta-asaṅkhyāta each lowest, intermediate, highest: 9 grades Ananta (infinite) parīta, yukta, ananta-ananta each lowest, intermediate, highest: 9 grades

docs.title: 10.3.2 How the Grades Are Defined
docs.text:
The boundaries between grades are fixed by constructions rather than by abstract definition. The highest numerable is reached through a famous thought-experiment. One imagines a series of enormous cylindrical pits (palya), each as wide as Jambūdvīpa (100,000 yojanas) and filled with mustard seeds; seeds are dropped one by one into successive continents and oceans, new and larger pits are formed as each is emptied, and further pits keep tally of the operations. The number of seeds involved, less one, is the highest numerable; adding one gives the lowest innumerable. Higher grades are then generated by operations such as raising a quantity to the power of itself.

Two points follow from this. First, saṅkhyāta is finite: it covers every number that can be reached by counting, however large. Second, the lower grades of “innumerable” and even of “infinite” are themselves produced by finite (if enormous) operations on finite quantities. In modern terms they are very large finite numbers to which the tradition assigned a special status, not infinities in the sense of modern set theory. Only the highest grade of the “infinite-infinite” is treated as genuinely unlimited; the Dhavalā associates it with the content of omniscient knowledge (kevala-jñāna).

The categories were put to work in Jain doctrine. The number of space-points (pradeśa) in the inhabited universe (loka) is said to be innumerable; the number of souls, of material atoms and of the moments of time is said to be infinite; the number of souls fit for liberation (bhavya) is infinite, so that the world will never be emptied of souls. These statements are doctrinal claims about the cosmos expressed in the vocabulary of the classification.

Scholarly Note: On comparisons with Cantor

It has often been asserted that the Jain grades of the infinite anticipate Georg Cantor’s transfinite cardinals. The comparison is misleading. Cantor’s achievement was to define infinite sets precisely, to compare their sizes by one-to-one correspondence, and to prove that some infinite sets (such as the real numbers) are strictly larger than others (such as the natural numbers). The Jain texts contain neither the definitions nor the proofs; their “infinite” grades are produced by finite operations and ranked by construction. What they do show is a willingness to reason about quantities beyond counting and to treat “the infinite” as something with internal distinctions — a striking feature of the tradition that can be appreciated without claiming priority over modern mathematics (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 10.4 Large Numbers and Measures of Time
docs.text:
Jain cosmology and karma theory require immense spans of time and space, and the texts provide names for them. The Anuyogadvāra lists time-units that rise by fixed multiples (many by 8,400,000) up to the śīrṣaprahelikā, which on its reckoning is the twenty-eighth power of 8,400,000 — a number of 194 digits. Beyond the countable lie units defined by analogy. A palyopama (“pit-comparison”) is the time needed to empty a pit one yojana across, packed with the finest hairs, if one hair is removed every hundred years; a sāgaropama (“ocean-comparison”) is \(10^{15}\) (ten koṭākoṭi) palyopamas. A complete cycle of cosmic time, made up of a descending and an ascending half (see Chapter 11), lasts twenty koṭākoṭi (that is, \(2\times10^{15}\)) sāgaropamas (Jaini 1979).

Such units are not measurements in any empirical sense. They express the conviction that the cycles of rebirth are, by human standards, practically endless, and they allow the texts to state the life-spans of gods and hell-beings in a fixed vocabulary.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Raising a Number to Its Own Power
docs.text: The Digambara commentaries describe an operation called vargita-saṃvargita, in which a number is raised to the power of itself. Applied to 2, it gives \(2^2 = 4\); applied again, \(4^4 = 256\); applied a third time, \(256^{256}\), a number of more than six hundred digits. The operation is used in constructing the higher grades of the innumerable and the infinite (Datta 1929). It is a vivid illustration of how quickly repeated exponentiation outruns any counting, and it is sometimes compared with modern notations for very fast-growing functions; the comparison is a useful teaching analogy, no more.

docs.title: 10.5 Repeated Halving and Related Operations
docs.text:
The Dhavalā and related works use several operations that count how many times a quantity can be reduced in a given way:

Ardhaccheda (“half-cut”) the number of times a quantity can be halved before reaching one. For a power of two, \(2^k\), the ardhaccheda is \(k\). Trikaccheda (“third-cut”) the number of times a quantity can be divided by three before reaching one. Vargaśalākā the number of times two must be squared to reach the quantity: for \(2^{2^k}\) it is \(k\).

For powers of two, ardhaccheda behaves exactly like the logarithm to base two, and the texts state rules that correspond to familiar properties: the ardhaccheda of a product equals the sum of the ardhacchedas of the factors, and that of a quotient equals their difference (Plofker 2009). These rules were tools for comparing the enormous quantities of cosmology and karma theory. They were not developed into a general method of computation, as Napier’s logarithms were in the seventeenth century, and there is no historical connection between the two. It is accurate to say that the Jain operations have properties analogous to logarithms; it is not accurate to say that the Jains invented logarithms.

docs.title: 10.6 Combinations
