docs.text:
Counting arrangements and selections (bhaṅga, vikalpa) was a recurrent Jain concern. The Vyākhyāprajñapti works out, for instance, how many ways a set of philosophical positions or of entities can be taken one, two or three at a time, giving the correct numbers for small sets (Plofker 2009). Later karma theory, as in Nemicandra’s Gommaṭasāra, enumerates the possible combinations of karmic states.

A simple example is found in Jain logic itself. The seven-fold predication (saptabhaṅgī, Chapter 9) is generated from three basic predicates — “is”, “is not” and “is inexpressible” — taken singly, in pairs and all together. There are \(2^3 - 1 = 7\) non-empty selections from three items, which is exactly the number of modes. Whether or not the Jain logicians thought of it in these terms, the structure is combinatorially exact.

General rules for combinations and permutations were later stated by mathematicians outside the Jain tradition as well, notably in prosody (Piṅgala and his commentators) and in the astronomical-mathematical treatises; the Jain material is one strand in this wider Indian interest in combinatorics (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 10.7 The Geometry of a Circular Cosmos
docs.text: Jain cosmography describes the Middle World (madhya-loka) as a series of concentric ring-shaped continents and oceans surrounding the circular continent of Jambūdvīpa, whose diameter is 100,000 yojanas. Describing such a world required formulas for circles and their segments.

docs.title: 10.7.1 The Value π ≈ √10
docs.text:
Jain texts take the circumference of a circle as \(\sqrt{10}\) times its diameter, and its area as one quarter of the circumference multiplied by the diameter:

\[C = \sqrt{10}\,d, \qquad A = \tfrac{1}{4}\,C\,d = \tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{4}\,d^2 .\]

Applied to Jambūdvīpa, the first formula gives a circumference of about 316,228 yojanas, and the texts state the figure to fractions of a yojana. The value \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.162\) is less accurate than the \(3.1416\) given by Āryabhaṭa (499 CE), but it was widely used in India and had the advantage of reducing circle calculations to square roots (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 10.7.2 Chords and Arcs
docs.text:
For a segment of a circle of diameter \(d\) cut off by a chord, with height (arrow, iṣu) \(h\), texts associated with the Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya give the chord \(c\) and the arc \(a\) as

\[c = \sqrt{4h(d-h)}, \qquad a \approx \sqrt{6h^2 + c^2}.\]

The first is exact; the second is a serviceable approximation. Such rules allowed the cosmographers to give the dimensions of the bow-shaped regions (kṣetra) into which the mountain ranges divide Jambūdvīpa (Datta 1929).

docs.title: 10.7.3 The Rajju
docs.text: Distances in the universe as a whole are measured in rajju (“rope”), a unit defined in various ways, some of them in terms of innumerable yojanas. The universe (loka) is fourteen rajju high. Its width is seven rajju at the base, narrows to one rajju at the level of the Middle World, widens to five rajju in the upper world and narrows again to one at the top. Digambara texts such as the Tiloyapaṇṇatti compute its volume as 343 cubic rajju (Caillat and Kumar 1981).

docs.title: 10.8 Place-Value Numerals in the Lokavibhāga
docs.text: The Sanskrit Lokavibhāga of Siṃhasūri is a cosmological work that presents itself as a version of a Prakrit original by Sarvanandin, completed on a date equivalent to 458 CE. It expresses numbers with “word-numerals” (bhūta-saṅkhyā) arranged by place value, using a word for “sky” or “void” for zero. If its date is accepted, it is among the earliest datable texts to use decimal place-value with a zero (Plofker 2009). The date has been questioned, and in any case the place-value system was a pan-Indian development whose earliest evidence comes from several sources; the Lokavibhāga is a witness to it, not its origin.

docs.title: 10.9 Mathematics in the Service of Doctrine
docs.text:
The Jain material shows mathematics embedded in a religious worldview. Cosmography required the geometry of circles and the arithmetic of very large distances; karma theory, which counts the types, durations and intensities of karmic bonds, required combinatorial reasoning and the comparison of large quantities; and the doctrines of an uncreated universe, an infinite number of souls and omniscient knowledge required a vocabulary for the innumerable and the infinite.

In this respect the Jain tradition resembles the wider Indian tradition, in which gaṇita (calculation) developed in close contact with astronomy, ritual and other disciplines. The Jain contribution is real and distinctive — above all the systematic attention to grades of the innumerable and infinite, and the long tradition of cosmological geometry — and it is best appreciated without the exaggerated claims that have sometimes surrounded it. Its later history, from Mahāvīra’s Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha to the fourteenth-century works of Ṭhakkura Pherū and Mahendra Sūri, is traced in Chapter 12; the wider history of Indian mathematics is the subject of Volume 11 of this series (Gaṇita).

Figure 10.1. The classification of quantities in the Anuyogadvāra and later Jain works.

docs.title: 11.1 The Jain Universe: Loka and Aloka
docs.text: Jain cosmology is unusually systematic and quantified (Caillat and Kumar 1981; Jaini 1979). Unlike the Buddhist and the Brahmanical (Purāṇic) cosmologies, which describe world-systems that are periodically destroyed and re-formed, it holds that the universe (loka) is eternal, uncreated and indestructible. It exists within an infinite expanse of empty space (aloka-ākāśa), and its structure is described in precise numerical detail.

docs.title: 11.1.1 The Shape of the Universe: Lokapuruṣa
docs.text:
The Jain universe is conceived as having the shape of a cosmic person (lokapuruṣa) standing with arms akimbo, hands on hips and elbows out. In the standard diagrams the person is reduced to the outline of the universe itself. The lower world spreads like the legs and skirt of a standing figure; the narrow middle world, where humans live, is its waist; the widest part of the upper world marks the elbows; and the abode of the liberated is at the crown of the head. Manuscript and temple paintings often fill this outline with a human body, sometimes with the continents drawn across the waist; Figure 11.1 gives the outline with the proportions stated in the texts.

Figure 11.1. The Lokapuruṣa — the Jain cosmic person whose body represents the structure of the entire universe. The upper world (Ūrdhva Loka) houses the celestial realms and the abode of liberated souls at the apex. The middle world (Madhya Loka) contains the human realm. The lower world (Adho Loka) contains the seven hell realms. The proportions follow the textual measurements in rajju. Painted versions fill this outline with a standing human figure, arms akimbo; the drawing gives only the outline.

docs.title: 11.1.2 The Three Worlds
docs.text:
The upper world (ūrdhva loka) contains the heavens, arranged in ascending order of refinement. Lowest are the kalpa heavens — twelve in Śvetāmbara texts and sixteen in Digambara texts, from Saudharma and Īśāna up to Acyuta — whose gods still live in a society of ranks, kings and servants. Above them lie the nine Graiveyaka (“neck”) heavens and the five Anuttara (“unsurpassed”) heavens, whose gods are all equal. At the apex is the crescent-shaped Siddhaśilā, also called Īṣatprāgbhārā, above which, at the very top of the loka, the liberated souls (siddha) dwell in omniscience and bliss. Rebirth even in the highest heaven is still bondage; only the Siddhas have left the cycle.

The middle world (madhya loka) is the most elaborately described region of the Jain cosmos. At its centre lies Jambūdvīpa, the “Island of the Rose-Apple Tree”, a circular continent surrounded by concentric rings of oceans and continents, extending outward in ever-larger circles (Table 11.1).

Table 11.1. The concentric continents and oceans of the Madhya Loka Ring Continent Ocean Notes 1 Jambūdvīpa — Central continent; 1 lakh yojanas in diameter 2 — Lavaṇa-samudra Salt ocean 3 Dhātakīkhaṇḍa — Second continent 4 — Kālodadhi Black-water ocean 5 Puṣkaradvīpa — Third continent (half accessible to humans) \(\vdots\) (continuing outward with innumerable concentric rings)

At the centre of Jambūdvīpa stands Mount Meru (Sumeru), the cosmic axis. Six mountain ranges divide Jambūdvīpa into seven regions (kṣetra), with Bharata-kṣetra, the land of India, in the south. Humans live only in the two and a half innermost continents, and only in some regions of these can Tīrthaṅkaras appear and liberation be attained.

The lower world (adho loka) contains seven hells (naraka), each darker and more painful than the one above (Jaini 1979). Their names describe a progressive dimming of light, from the “gem-lustred” (Ratnaprabhā) through the pebble-, sand-, mud- and smoke-lustred hells (Śarkarā-, Vālukā-, Paṅka- and Dhūmaprabhā) to the hells of darkness (Tamaḥprabhā) and great darkness (Mahātamaḥprabhā). At the base of the universe, and in fact throughout it, are the nigoda, the simplest beings, which share bodies in clusters and from which, in Jain doctrine, souls first emerge into the wider cycle of rebirth.

docs.title: 11.2 Cyclic Time: Utsarpiṇī and Avasarpiṇī
docs.text:
Jain cosmology conceives of time as eternal and cyclical. Jain authors call the cycle of cosmic time the kālacakra, “wheel of time” — the same word, in a quite different sense, as the title of the late Buddhist tantra described in Chapter 6. Each turn of the wheel consists of two half-cycles:

Utsarpiṇī (Ascending Half-Cycle) A period of progressive improvement in human virtue, happiness, lifespan, and physical stature. It consists of six aras (spokes or epochs), moving from the worst to the best conditions (Table 11.2). Avasarpiṇī (Descending Half-Cycle) A period of progressive decline. Currently, according to Jain tradition, we are in the fifth ara of the descending half-cycle — an age of increasing moral and physical decline. Table 11.2. The six Aras (epochs) of each half-cycle Ara Name Characteristics (Descending Cycle) 1 Suṣama-suṣamā (“very happy”) Extreme happiness; wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) provide for all needs 2 Suṣamā (“happy”) Great happiness; long lifespan; tall stature 3 Suṣama-duḥṣamā (“happy-unhappy”) Happiness mixed with sorrow; at its end Ṛṣabha, the first Tīrthaṅkara, introduces civilisation 4 Duḥṣama-suṣamā (“unhappy-happy”) Sorrow mixed with happiness; the other twenty-three Tīrthaṅkaras appear 5 Duḥṣamā (“unhappy”) Sorrow predominates; decline (the present age, which began shortly after Mahāvīra’s death) 6 Duḥṣama-duḥṣamā (“very unhappy”) Extreme sorrow; collapse of religion and society

The duration of each complete cycle (ascending + descending) is twenty koṭākoṭi sāgaropamas (\(2 \times 10^{15}\) “ocean-measures”, each itself an unimaginably long period; see Chapter 10). The figure is finite but far beyond any human measure, expressing the practically endless round of rebirth.

docs.title: 11.3 Jain Ethics: A Comprehensive Framework
docs.text: Jain ethics is highly systematic, setting out graded duties for mendicants and for lay people. Grounded in the metaphysical conviction that every living being possesses an eternal soul (jīva) with the potential for infinite knowledge and bliss, Jain ethics extends moral consideration to all sentient beings — and indeed to the entire natural world.

docs.title: 11.3.1 The Ethical Framework for Laypeople
docs.text: While the five great vows bind mendicants, Jain teachers set out a graduated discipline for lay men and women (śrāvaka, śrāvikā). The lists of subsidiary vows vary between texts; a common arrangement has twelve (Jaini 1979; Williams 1963). The five “lesser vows” (aṇuvrata) are limited forms of the mendicant’s vows: the householder renounces intentional harm to mobile beings, lying, stealing, sexual relations outside marriage and the accumulation of possessions beyond a chosen limit. Three “strengthening” vows (guṇavrata) limit the directions and distances of one’s travel (digvrata) and the things one consumes and uses (bhogopabhoga-parimāṇa), and forbid purposeless harm (anarthadaṇḍa-viramaṇa). Four “vows of training” (śikṣāvrata) bring the householder for limited periods close to the mendicant’s life: periods of equanimity meditation (sāmāyika), further temporary limits on movement (deśāvakāśika), fasting and quasi-monastic observance on holy days (proṣadhopavāsa), and giving to mendicants and guests (atithi-saṃvibhāga). The structure is characteristic: the lay life is defined not as a separate ideal but as a partial and progressive approach to renunciation.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Ahiṃsā in Practice: Jain Vegetarianism and Beyond
docs.text: The commitment to non-harming shapes everyday life in visible ways. Jains abstain from meat, fish and eggs, and many also avoid root vegetables such as potatoes, onions and garlic, which are held to harbour innumerable minute beings (they are “infinite-bodied”, anantakāya) and whose harvesting destroys the whole plant; honey, alcohol and certain figs are also avoided. Mendicants and devout lay people strain water before use, and mendicants sweep the ground before them. Many Jains do not eat after sunset, so as not to consume insects drawn to food by light. Non-harming has also shaped occupations: Jain texts forbid trades that involve great harm — butchery, fishing, and dealing in weapons, poisons or animal products — which helps to explain the concentration of Jains in commerce, although Jains have also served historically as ministers and generals.

docs.title: 11.3.3 Jain Environmental Ethics
docs.text:
Modern Jains and scholars have drawn out ecological implications from these teachings. The recognition that earth, water, fire, air and plants contain living beings (jīva) means that much of the natural environment is ensouled and deserving of moral consideration. Scholars caution, however, that classical Jain non-harming was aimed at the purification of the individual soul rather than at the protection of ecosystems; “Jain environmentalism” is a modern reinterpretation, though a well-grounded one (Chapple 2002; Cort 2001).

Modern Jain writers have stated these implications as principles: that the elements and plants possess souls and are morally significant; that unnecessary harm to any of them generates karma; and that non-possession (aparigraha) implies restraint in consuming natural resources. The Tattvārthasūtra’s phrase parasparopagraho jīvānām, “souls render service to one another” (5.21), adopted as a motto by the Jain community in 1974, is read today as an ethics of mutual dependence; in its original context it states, more neutrally, that souls affect one another, for good or ill.

docs.title: 11.4 The Six Obligatory Duties (Āvaśyaka)
docs.text:
Every Jain monk and nun, and devout laypeople to a lesser degree, are expected to perform six obligatory daily observances (āvaśyaka; Table 11.3).

Table 11.3. The six obligatory duties (Āvaśyaka) in Jain practice No. Duty Description 1 Sāmāyika Equanimity meditation; a period of 48 minutes devoted to contemplative stillness and the cultivation of inner peace 2 Caturviṃśati-stava Hymn of praise to the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras 3 Vandana Reverential salutation to the spiritual teacher (ācārya) 4 Pratikramaṇa Confession and repentance for transgressions committed during the day or night 5 Kāyotsarga Abandoning the body — standing in motionless meditation, detaching from physical sensations 6 Pratyākhyāna Renunciation — taking a vow to abstain from certain foods, activities, or possessions for a specific period

The Pratikramaṇa is of particular significance. This daily practice of confession and repentance embodies the Jain ideal of moral self-examination. The practitioner reviews all actions of the day, identifies any violations of the vows, and seeks forgiveness from all beings who may have been harmed. A central verse of the pratikramaṇa rite is the khāmemi savva-jīve — “I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me”:

Khāmemi savva-jīve, savve jīvā khamantu me; mittī me savva-bhūesu, veraṃ majjha na keṇai.

I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all beings and enmity with none.

— Vandittu Sutta (the lay pratikramaṇa text) 49

docs.title: 11.5 Jain Festivals and Observances
docs.text:
The Jain calendar includes several important festivals and observances that reinforce the community’s ethical and spiritual commitments (Table 11.4).

Table 11.4. Major Jain festivals and observances Festival Time Significance Paryuṣaṇa Parva Aug–Sept (8 or 10 days) The most important Jain festival; fasting, meditation, confession, and mutual forgiveness Mahāvīra Jayantī Caitra (Mar–Apr) Birthday of Mahāvīra Dīvālī Kārttika (Oct–Nov) Commemorates Mahāvīra’s attainment of nirvāṇa Mahāmastākābhiṣeka Every 12 years Grand anointing ceremony of the Bāhubali statue at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa Saṃvatsarī (Śvetāmbara) / Kṣamāvaṇī (Digambara) End of Paryuṣaṇa / Daśalakṣaṇa Universal forgiveness; Jains seek forgiveness from all beings for any harm done Akṣaya Tṛtīyā Vaiśākha (Apr–May) Commemorates the first Tīrthaṅkara Ṛṣabhadeva’s breaking of his first fast

The Paryuṣaṇa Parva (also known as Daśalakṣaṇa Parva among Digambaras) is the principal festival of the Jain calendar. During these eight or ten days, Jains intensify their spiritual practice through fasting, meditation, scripture reading, and acts of charity. The festival culminates in a day of mutual forgiveness (Saṃvatsarī for Śvetāmbaras, Kṣamāvaṇī for Digambaras), when Jains ask forgiveness of all beings and of one another.

docs.title: 11.6 The Jain Theory of Perspectives Applied to Ethics
docs.text:
The implications of Anekāntavāda for intellectual humility, tolerance and the avoidance of one-sided views (ekānta) were set out in Chapter 9. Applied to ethics, they add two further ideas: that understanding another’s moral perspective is itself a moral act, calling for patience (kṣānti) and friendliness (maitrī); and that dogmatism, ridicule and contempt for others’ views are a form of verbal and mental violence, and so a breach of ahiṃsā.

This ethical reading of Anekāntavāda is largely the work of modern Jain thinkers and of scholars interested in religious pluralism and inter-cultural dialogue. Classical Jain logicians used the doctrine above all in debate, to show that the rival systems each grasped only part of the truth; the extension to a general ethic of tolerance is a modern development, though one with roots in the tradition (Dundas 2002; Long 2009).

docs.title: 11.7 The Jain Community: Social Organisation
docs.text:
The Jain community (saṅgha) consists of four constituent groups: monks (sādhu/muni), nuns (sādhvī/āryikā), laymen (śrāvaka), and laywomen (śrāvikā). This fourfold community (caturvidha-saṅgha) mirrors the Buddhist pariṣad and provides the institutional framework for the preservation and practice of the Jain dharma.

The relationship between the monastic and lay communities is symbiotic: the monastics provide spiritual guidance, teaching, and the living example of renunciation, while the laity provides material support (dāna) in the form of food, clothing, shelter, and medicine. The Jain laity, particularly in the mercantile communities of Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka, and Maharashtra, is known for its philanthropy, endowing temples (Figure 11.2), manuscript libraries, schools, hospitals and animal shelters (Cort 2001; Babb 1996).

Table 11.5. The eleven stages of lay spiritual progress (pratimā), in the Digambara list Stage Name Description 1 Darśana Right faith; acceptance of the Jain worldview 2 Vrata Observance of the five aṇuvratas (minor vows) 3 Sāmāyika Regular practice of equanimity meditation 4 Proṣadhopavāsa Fasting on the holy (parvan) days, the 8th and 14th of each lunar fortnight 5 Sacitta-tyāga Abstaining from eating raw vegetables and fruits 6 Rātri-bhojana-tyāga Abstaining from eating after sunset 7 Brahmacarya Sexual abstinence; celibacy 8 Ārambha-tyāga Abandoning business and worldly occupations 9 Parigraha-tyāga Renouncing possessions and attachments 10 Anumati-tyāga Withdrawing consent for family members to act on one’s behalf 11 Uddiṣṭa-tyāga Accepting only food that has not been specially prepared for oneself

The eleven stages (Table 11.5) apply to the householder the same logic as the vows: each adds a further renunciation, until at the eleventh the layman lives almost as a mendicant while not yet taking initiation. In practice few lay people go beyond the first stages, and the scheme serves as much to define the ideal as to describe what people do.

docs.title: 11.8 Sallekhanā: The Voluntary Spiritual Death
docs.text:
One of the most distinctive and controversial aspects of Jain ethics is Sallekhanā (also called Santhārā) — the voluntary, religiously sanctioned death by gradual fasting at the end of one’s life. This practice is understood not as suicide (which involves passion and attachment) but as a peaceful, meditative withdrawal from the body, undertaken when death is imminent and further life would serve no spiritual purpose (Dundas 2002; Jaini 1979).

The texts surround the vow with conditions. It may be undertaken only when death is near, through terminal illness, extreme old age or calamity; it requires the permission and guidance of a spiritual teacher; food, then water, and possessions are given up by degrees; and the dying person is to remain in meditation and equanimity, often listening to the recitation of the Namokāra mantra. The memorial inscriptions of Karnataka show that monks, nuns and lay men and women undertook it in the medieval Deccan (Chapter 13).

The practice has been the subject of legal and ethical controversy in modern India. In 2015 the Rajasthan High Court held that santhārā could be prosecuted as attempted suicide; the Supreme Court of India stayed that judgement within weeks, pending further hearing. Jain authorities insist that the vow is a religious discipline undertaken without passion when death is approaching, and is therefore distinct from suicide; critics, including some within the community, worry about social pressure on the elderly.

Figure 11.2. The Ādinātha (Caturmukha) temple at Raṇakpur, Rajasthan (front view), built in the fifteenth century under the patronage of the merchant Dharaṇā Śāh; its marble halls are famous for their many carved pillars. Photo: Ingo Mehling, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: Chapter 12: Jain Learning: Language, History and Literature
12.1 Learning in a Mendicant Tradition
docs.text:
The preceding chapters have treated Jain philosophy, mathematics, cosmology and ethics. They do not exhaust what Jain authors wrote. Over some fifteen centuries Jain mendicants, and later Jain laymen, produced grammars and dictionaries, treatises on poetics and metre, works on astronomy and coinage, histories of their own lineages and of the kings who patronised them, and a large narrative and poetic literature in Prakrit, Sanskrit, Apabhraṃśa and the regional languages. Much of this writing was addressed to a readership far wider than the Jain community, and some of it became standard in Indian learning as a whole (Winternitz 1933; Dundas 2002; Jacobsen et al. 2020).

Several features of Jain religious life explain this breadth. Jain mendicants were the teachers of lay communities, and from the early medieval period those communities were dominated by merchants and royal servants who needed literacy, arithmetic and a command of the courtly languages. Mendicants moved between towns and stayed for the rainy season wherever a lay community invited them (Chapter 13), and many of them spent long periods at royal courts — of the Gaṅgas and Rāṣṭrakūṭas in the Deccan, of the Caulukyas in Gujarat, and later of the Delhi sultans and the Mughals. The copying and gift of manuscripts was a religious act, and the libraries (bhaṇḍāras) that resulted preserved Brahmanical and Buddhist works as well as Jain ones (Chapter 8, Section 8.5.2). The Digambaras, finally, gave secular learning a place in their classification of scripture. Of their four “expositions” (anuyoga), one, the prathamānuyoga, comprises narrative and universal history, and another, the karaṇānuyoga, cosmography and calculation; the others treat conduct (caraṇānuyoga) and the categories of reality (dravyānuyoga).

docs.title: 12.2 Grammar and Lexicography
docs.text:
Jain grammarians wrote within the Pāṇinian tradition rather than against it, but they produced independent systems that were shorter, easier to teach and free of the Vedic rules that Pāṇini had included (Scharfe 1977). The earliest is the Jainendra-vyākaraṇa of the Digambara Devanandin, better known as Pūjyapāda, who probably wrote in the fifth or sixth century and is also the author of the Sarvārthasiddhi, the standard Digambara commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra. His grammar survives in two recensions, a shorter one that is probably original and an expanded one. In the ninth century the Yāpanīya monk Pālyakīrti, known as Śākaṭāyana, composed a new grammar with his own commentary, the Amoghavṛtti, named after his patron, the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I.

The best-known Jain grammar is Hemacandra’s Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana, written in the 1130s or 1140s for the Caulukya king Jayasiṃha Siddharāja of Gujarat; according to the later Prabhāvakacarita, the king commissioned it after his conquest of Mālava so that Gujarat would have a grammar to match the one associated with King Bhoja of Dhārā. Its first seven chapters, with Hemacandra’s own commentaries, cover Sanskrit. The eighth is a grammar of the Prakrits — Māhārāṣṭrī, Śaurasenī, Māgadhī, the Paiśācī dialects and Apabhraṃśa — and remains a basic source for the history of the Middle Indo-Aryan languages, not least because its rules on Apabhraṃśa are illustrated with verses that survive nowhere else. Hemacandra also wrote a long poem, the Dvyāśraya (“having two supports”), whose Sanskrit cantos narrate the history of the Caulukya kings while illustrating, in order, the rules of his grammar; its Prakrit continuation, the Kumārapālacarita, does the same for the Prakrit rules (Dundas 2002; Winternitz 1933).

Lexicography was a Jain speciality. The poet Dhanapāla of Dhārā compiled the Pāiyalacchī Nāmamālā, a Prakrit dictionary of synonyms, in 972 or 973, one of the earliest Prakrit lexicons. Hemacandra again produced the most complete set of tools: the Abhidhānacintāmaṇi, a dictionary of Sanskrit synonyms arranged by subject; the Anekārthasaṅgraha, on words with several meanings; the Nighaṇṭuśeṣa, on the names of plants; and the Deśīnāmamālā, a list with his own commentary of “regional” (deśī) words that could not be derived from Sanskrit. The last is one of the few pre-modern Indian works to treat non-Sanskritic vocabulary as worth recording for its own sake. Hemacandra’s Kāvyānuśāsana and Chandonuśāsana, on poetics and metre, completed a curriculum through which a student could learn the whole apparatus of literary composition from Jain textbooks; Indian poetics more generally is the subject of Volume 8 (Kāvya Kalpalatā), and grammar of Volume 10 (Śabda Vidyā).

docs.title: 12.3 Astronomy, Calculation and the Sciences of Trade
docs.text:
Jain astronomy began as part of cosmography. The canonical Sūryaprajñapti and Candraprajñapti and the later Jyotiṣkaraṇḍaka describe a Jambūdvīpa lit by two suns and two moons, which take turns to cross the sky as they circle Mount Meru, and they reckon time in a five-year cycle (yuga) of lunar and solar months that closely resembles the calendar of the Vedic Jyotiṣa (Plofker 2009). The geometry needed for this cosmos, and the mathematics of Mahāvīra’s Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha, are described in Chapter 10.

Later Jain authors took part in the mathematical astronomy of their time. Two cases from the fourteenth century show Jain expertise put at the service of new rulers. Ṭhakkura Pherū, a Śvetāmbara layman who served in the mint of the Khaljī sultans of Delhi, wrote short Prakrit handbooks on arithmetic (Gaṇitasārakaumudī), astrology, architecture, gemstones and — unusually — on the coins that passed through the mint, with their weights and silver content (Dravyaparīkṣā). The Śvetāmbara monk Mahendra Sūri, at the court of Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq, wrote the Yantrarāja (1370), the first Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe, an instrument he learned of from the Islamic astronomers of the court (Plofker 2009). Astronomy as a whole is treated in Volume 12 (Khagola Jyotiṣa).

docs.title: 12.4 Jain Historical Writing
docs.text:
Jain authors kept careful records of their own lineages. The list of elders (sthavirāvalī) at the end of the Kalpasūtra names the teachers and branches of the early community, and the Mathurā inscriptions show that some of its names were real (Chapter 8, Section 8.8). The later gacchas kept lists of their successive heads (paṭṭāvalī), which give names and dates of initiation and death. These are sectarian documents, but they amount to a continuous chronology of Śvetāmbara monastic history from the early medieval period onwards.

Hemacandra’s Pariśiṣṭaparvan (“Appendix”), written as a supplement to his universal history of the sixty-three illustrious persons, tells the lives of the Jain elders after Mahāvīra. It includes the stories of Bhadrabāhu and of the Maurya emperor Candragupta and his minister Cāṇakya, and is a principal source for the Jain tradition of Candragupta’s conversion (Hemacandra 1998). From the thirteenth century Śvetāmbara monks in Gujarat also developed a distinctive genre of historical anecdote, the prabandha. Prabhācandra’s Prabhāvakacarita (1277/78) tells the lives of twenty-two great teachers who “illuminated” the faith. Merutuṅga’s Prabandhacintāmaṇi (“Wishing-Stone of Narratives”), completed at Vardhamāna (Wadhwan) in 1305, gathers stories of the kings of Gujarat and Mālava — Bhoja of Dhārā, Jayasiṃha Siddharāja, Kumārapāla — and of their poets and ministers (Merutuṅga 1901). Rājaśekhara’s Prabandhakośa (1349) continues the genre. Jinaprabha Sūri’s Vividhatīrthakalpa, completed about 1333, is a different kind of work: a guide to more than fifty pilgrimage sites, from Śatruñjaya and Girnār to Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra, recording local traditions, the history of their temples and their destruction and restoration.

Historians treat these works with caution. The prabandhas were written to instruct and to honour the faith; their stories are often anecdotal, sometimes legendary, and are usually set down a century or more after the events. Merutuṅga himself says that he collected stories that were current in his time. Yet for the history of Caulukya Gujarat and Paramāra Mālava they are among the few narrative sources that survive, and much of what is told about Bhoja’s court, or about the rivalries of poets and ministers, comes from them (Dundas 2002).

docs.title: 12.5 Jain Scholars under the Delhi Sultanate
docs.text: The Turkish conquests of the late twelfth and thirteenth centuries, which ended the great Buddhist monasteries of the east (Chapter 7), also brought destruction to Jain temples in the west; Jain sources record, for example, the sack of the temples on Śatruñjaya in 1313. Jain communities nevertheless adapted to the new order, and Jain sources describe a series of negotiated relationships with the sultans of Delhi. Jain accounts relate that Samarā Śāh, an Osvāl merchant in the service of the governor of Gujarat, obtained permission to restore the main temple at Śatruñjaya in 1315. Jinaprabha Sūri, of the Kharatara Gaccha, is said in Jain sources, including sections of his own Vividhatīrthakalpa, to have been received with honour at the court of Muḥammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325–1351), to have obtained an order (farmān) protecting Jain pilgrims and temples, and to have recovered a sacred image that had been carried off to Delhi (Dundas 2002). The details come from Jain writers and cannot all be checked; but together with the careers of Ṭhakkura Pherū and Mahendra Sūri they show Jain merchants, officials and monks finding a place in the Sultanate state more than two centuries before Hīravijaya Sūri’s better-known meetings with Akbar (Chapter 14, Section 14.7).

docs.title: 12.6 Narrative Literature in Prakrit and Sanskrit
docs.text:
Jain authors built up one of the largest narrative literatures of pre-modern India, much of it intended for the sermons in which mendicants taught the laity. Its organising frame is a universal history of the sixty-three “illustrious persons” (śalākāpuruṣa) of each half-cycle of time: the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, twelve universal emperors (cakravartin), and nine each of the Baladevas, the Vāsudevas and their adversaries the Prativāsudevas. The scheme is told most fully in the Digambara Mahāpurāṇa of Jinasena and Guṇabhadra (9th century) and in Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacarita (Jaini 1979; Dundas 2002).

Within this frame Jain poets retold the epics. Vimalasūri’s Prakrit Paümacariya, of disputed date but perhaps from the early centuries CE, is the earliest Jain Rāmāyaṇa, and the Harivaṃśapurāṇa of a Jinasena of the Punnāṭa lineage (783 CE, not the author of the Mahāpurāṇa) gives a Jain version of the Kṛṣṇa story. These versions rationalise the epic narratives — Rāvaṇa, for example, is a learned vidyādhara rather than a demon, and it is Lakṣmaṇa, the Vāsudeva, not Rāma, who kills him — and recast them in terms of Jain ethics, so that Rāma ends his life as a Jain mendicant and attains liberation. The epics and Purāṇas are treated in Volume 7 (Itihāsa–Purāṇa).

Alongside universal history stands a wide range of prose and verse fiction. Saṅghadāsa’s Prakrit Vasudevahiṇḍī, composed before the seventh century, is a Jain adaptation of the lost Bṛhatkathā. Haribhadra’s Samarāiccakahā follows two souls, one virtuous and one consumed by hatred, through nine successive births, and his Dhūrtākhyāna (“Tales of the Rogues”) satirises the improbable stories of the Purāṇas. Uddyotana Sūri’s Kuvalayamālā, completed at Jābālipura (Jalor) in 779 CE, is a Prakrit romance celebrated also for a scene in which merchants from eighteen regions of India speak, and are characterised by, their own languages. Siddharṣi’s Sanskrit Upamitibhavaprapañcā Kathā (906 CE) is an allegory in which the passions and virtues appear as persons, and Dhanapāla’s Tilakamañjarī, written at the court of Bhoja, is a Sanskrit prose romance in the manner of Bāṇa. Story collections (kathākośa) supplied preachers with exempla for every vow and virtue, and many Indian folk tales are first recorded in them (Granoff 1990; Winternitz 1933).

docs.title: 12.7 Apabhraṃśa and the Regional Languages
docs.text:
From the late first millennium Jain poets wrote extensively in Apabhraṃśa, the literary form of the late Middle Indo-Aryan vernaculars, and they are the chief reason why an Apabhraṃśa literature survives at all. Svayambhū’s Paümacariu, a Rāma epic of perhaps the ninth century, and the Mahāpurāṇa that Puṣpadanta composed at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa capital Mānyakheṭa in the 960s, are its major works; the Bhavisattakaha of another Dhanapāla is a popular romance of a merchant’s son (Winternitz 1933).

Jain writers also stand at the beginning of several regional literatures. In Kannada the treatise on poetics Kavirājamārga (c. 850), associated with the court of Amoghavarṣa I, is the earliest extant literary work, and the first great poets were Jains: Pampa (Ādipurāṇa and Vikramārjunavijaya, a retelling of the Mahābhārata, both 941), Ponna (Śāntipurāṇa, c. 950) and Ranna (Ajitapurāṇa, 993, and the Gadāyuddha), remembered together as the “three gems” (ratnatraya) of Kannada literature. The Cāmuṇḍarāyapurāṇa (978) of Cāmuṇḍarāya, the minister who commissioned the Bāhubali colossus at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, is the earliest surviving work of Kannada prose, and Nāgacandra’s Jain Rāmāyaṇa (c. 1100) continued the epic tradition. These poets wrote in courtly as well as religious genres, and their works are still read as classics of the language (Desai 1957; Dundas 2002).

In Tamil, Jain authors produced the Cīvakacintāmaṇi of Tiruttakkatēvar (9th–10th century), a long epic of a prince who ends as a Jain ascetic; the Nālaṭiyār, an anthology of four hundred moral quatrains traditionally ascribed to Jain monks; the Nīlakēci, a polemical poem in which a Jain heroine refutes rival schools; the treatises on prosody of Amitacākarar (11th century); and Pavaṇanti’s grammar Naṉṉūl (c. 13th century), still the standard traditional grammar of Tamil. In western India, Jain monks composed the earliest substantial works in Old Gujarati, the narrative poems called rāsa, among which Śālibhadra Sūri’s Bharateśvara-Bāhubali-rāsa (1185) is often counted the first; and in north India the merchant Banārasīdās wrote the first autobiography in Hindi (Chapter 13, Section 13.6.6). The Buddhist share in Indian literature, and the two traditions’ contributions side by side, are discussed in Chapter 14 (Section 14.6).

docs.title: 12.8 Jain Learning in Perspective
docs.text: It would be wrong to treat this literature as a separate “Jain science”. Jain grammarians worked within the Pāṇinian tradition, Jain lexicographers and poeticians drew on Brahmanical predecessors, and Jain astronomers learned from Islamic colleagues. What distinguishes the Jain contribution is its continuity and its social base. Because learning was carried by wandering mendicants and by lay merchant communities rather than by a few great monasteries, it did not depend on the survival of any single institution, and it was preserved in libraries that the community itself maintained. That pattern, explored for religious practice in Chapter 13, is one reason why so much of the history of medieval western and southern India is known from Jain texts, and why the Jain share in Indian knowledge is larger than the size of the community would suggest.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Monks, Nuns and Householders: Religious Life in Practice
13.1 Renunciants and Householders
docs.text:
The earlier chapters of this volume have dealt mostly with doctrine: the teachings of the Buddha and Mahāvīra, the canons that preserve them and the philosophical schools that grew from them. This chapter turns to practice — to how monks, nuns and lay people actually lived these religions. Its subjects are the daily discipline of mendicants, the history of the orders of nuns, and the gifts, rites, pilgrimages and festivals through which lay people took part. These matters were not marginal. The great majority of Buddhists and Jains have always been householders, and both traditions survived or failed in each region according to how well their mendicants and their lay followers sustained one another.

Both traditions describe themselves as a fourfold community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen (Chapter 2, Section 2.14, and Chapter 11, Section 11.7). In both, the relationship between renunciants and householders rests on an exchange. Lay people give food, robes or cloth, lodging and medicine. Mendicants give teaching, an example of the religious life and, above all, an occasion for merit: in the standard Buddhist recollection of the Saṅgha, the community of disciples is called the unsurpassed “field of merit” (puññakkhetta) for the world, the soil in which a gift bears the richest fruit. Jain writers likewise praise the gift to a worthy recipient (supātra-dāna), and the Jain lay vows include giving to mendicants and guests (Chapter 11, Section 11.3.1).

The two traditions nevertheless regulated the exchange very differently. A Buddhist monk might accept an invitation to a meal cooked for him, and the Vinaya allows robes and lodgings to be given to particular monks. A Jain mendicant may not accept food prepared specially for him, because cooking involves harm to living beings and he must not be the cause of it. The Jain mendicant is therefore dependent on households that know and observe the rules, and the lay community must be trained to give correctly. As the final section of this chapter argues, this difference had large consequences.

Much of what follows draws on the work of scholars who have studied practice directly — in inscriptions, in monastic law codes read as working documents, and through fieldwork among living communities — rather than in doctrinal texts alone (Gombrich 1971; Schopen 1997; Cort 2001; Laidlaw 1995; Babb 1996).

docs.title: 13.2 The Buddhist Monastic Life
docs.text: The structure and rules of the Vinaya and the categories of the Pātimokkha have been described in Chapter 3 (Section 3.2.2), and the Saṅgha’s procedures of collective decision in Chapter 2. This section describes how the rules shaped a monk’s life, chiefly on the basis of the Pāli Vinaya, noting where the other traditions differ (Gethin 1998; Harvey 2013).

docs.title: 13.2.1 Going Forth and Higher Ordination
docs.text:
Entry into the order takes place in two stages. The first is the “going forth” (pabbajjā) from home into homelessness. The candidate’s head and beard are shaved, he puts on the ochre robes, takes the three refuges and undertakes ten precepts (dasa sikkhāpada): the five precepts of the laity, with chastity in place of the avoidance of sexual misconduct, together with abstention from food after midday, from dancing, music and shows, from garlands, perfumes and ornaments, from high and luxurious beds, and from accepting gold and silver. He is then a novice (sāmaṇera). The Vinaya allows boys to be made novices at fifteen, and younger boys if they are old enough, in its phrase, to scare away crows.

The second stage is higher ordination (upasampadā), which makes the novice a full monk (bhikkhu). According to the Mahāvagga, the earliest disciples were admitted by the Buddha’s own words, “Come, monk”, and others for a time by the going for refuge; the Buddha then laid down that ordination must be conferred by the Saṅgha itself. The candidate must be at least twenty years old (a year counted, by an allowance of the Vinaya, from conception), must have a preceptor (upajjhāya), and must possess a bowl and robes. In the assembly he is questioned about “obstructing conditions”: whether he suffers from certain diseases, whether he is a human being, a man, a free man, free of debt and not in royal service, and whether his parents have given permission. The ordination itself is a formal act of the Saṅgha in which a motion is followed by three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha-kamma); if no one objects, the candidate is ordained. A quorum of ten monks was required in the “Middle Country” of the Ganges valley; the Vinaya relates that the elder Mahākaccāna, finding too few monks in Avanti, obtained permission for ordinations in the border regions with a quorum of five, one of them an expert in the Vinaya.

Immediately after ordination the new monk is told the four “resources” (nissaya) on which the life of a monk depends — food gathered on the alms round, robes made of discarded cloth, lodging at the foot of a tree, and fermented urine as medicine — with the reminder that better gifts may be accepted when they are offered; and he is told the four things that must never be done, which are the four pārājika offences. He then lives under the guidance of his preceptor or a teacher (ācariya) for at least five years.

Ordination in the Buddhist sense is not a vow for life. A monk who finds that he can no longer keep the rules may leave the order by formally renouncing the training, and this is not a sin. In Myanmar, Thailand and Laos it became customary for young men to spend a period, sometimes only a few weeks, as novices or monks before marriage; in Myanmar the novice ordination of a boy (shinbyu) is one of the great family festivals.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Robes, Bowl and the Daily Round
docs.text:
The monk’s possessions are few. The commentarial tradition lists eight requisites: the three robes, the bowl, a razor, a needle, a waist-band and a water-strainer. The three robes (ticīvara) are an inner robe (antaravāsaka), an upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and a double-layered outer cloak (saṅghāṭī). The Vinaya relates that the Buddha asked Ānanda to make robes in the pattern of the rice-fields of Magadha, and the patchwork of strips and borders sewn into a monk’s robe still preserves that pattern. Robes were to be dyed with dyes made from roots, stems, bark, leaves, flowers and fruit, which gave them their ochre, brown or saffron colour. The bowl was to be of iron or of clay.

In the early morning the monk walks through the village on his alms round (piṇḍapāta), silently accepting whatever food is placed in his bowl. The Pātimokkha forbids solid food between midday and the following dawn, so the main meal is taken before noon. Meat is not forbidden in the Theravāda Vinaya, provided the monk has not seen, heard or suspected that the animal was killed for him. Devadatta’s demand that vegetarianism be made compulsory is one of the five demands the Buddha is said to have refused. East Asian monks, by contrast, became strict vegetarians, on the authority of Mahāyāna sūtras such as the Laṅkāvatāra and of the bodhisattva precepts, and with the support of the Liang emperor Wu in the early sixth century.

The rule against accepting gold and silver, and so money, caused difficulty from the start. Tradition holds that the Second Council at Vaiśālī (Chapter 3) was called because monks there accepted money from lay people. The Vinaya allows a lay steward (kappiyakāraka) to receive and manage funds on the monks’ behalf, an arrangement that, in many later monasteries, made the rule largely nominal.

The Vinaya also regulates lodging. It permits five kinds of dwelling, from a simple hut to a multi-storeyed building and a cave. Its best-known story of a gift is that of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, who bought the Jeta Grove at Sāvatthī from Prince Jeta by covering its ground with coins and gave it to the Saṅgha; a relief on the railing of the Bharhut stūpa shows carts unloading the coins, with an inscription naming the scene. The wandering life of the first disciples gave way, within a few centuries, to settled monasteries, and the cave monasteries of the Western Ghats and the brick vihāras of the Ganges plain are the visible result (see Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa).

docs.title: 13.2.3 The Monastic Year
docs.text:
The life of a monastery follows the lunar calendar. On the full-moon and new-moon days (uposatha) the monks within a monastic boundary (sīmā) assemble to recite the Pātimokkha; before the recitation, each confesses to a fellow monk any minor offence he has committed, so that the assembly is “pure”. Lay people come to the monastery on these days and on the quarter-moon days, take the eight precepts and listen to sermons.

The three months of the rains (vassa), beginning the day after the full moon of Āsāḷha (June–July), are spent in one residence. A monk may be absent for up to seven days for specified purposes, such as caring for a sick person, but otherwise must stay. A monk’s seniority is counted in “rains”, that is, in the number of retreats completed since his ordination. At the end of the retreat each monk, at the ceremony of “invitation” (pavāraṇā), invites the community to point out any fault it has seen, heard or suspected in him. In the following month comes the kaṭhina: lay people present cloth to the community, which must agree to give it to one monk and must cut, sew and dye it into a robe within a single day. The kaṭhina ceremony has become one of the main lay festivals of Theravāda countries, and the giving of the cloth is regarded as an especially meritorious gift.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Vinaya Lineages and the Monastery as an Institution
docs.text:
Six complete Vinayas survive. Besides the Pāli Vinaya of the Theravāda, four were translated into Chinese in the early fifth century — those of the Sarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Mahāsāṃghika and Mahīśāsaka schools — and the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda survives complete in Tibetan, partly in Chinese (translated by Yijing) and in substantial Sanskrit portions among the Gilgit manuscripts found in 1931. A Sanskrit Vinaya for nuns of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda was among the manuscripts photographed in Tibet by Rahul Sankrityayan in the 1930s (Hirakawa 1990; Clarke 2014). The codes agree closely on the most serious offences and differ mostly in the number and detail of minor rules: the Dharmaguptaka code has 250 rules for monks and 348 for nuns, against 227 and 311 in the Pāli. These differences still matter. East Asian monks and nuns are ordained according to the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Tibetans according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda, and the Theravāda countries according to the Pāli; each lineage must be traced back through valid ordinations to the Buddha (Chapter 4, Section 4.9.1).

For a long time scholars took the Vinaya’s ideal of the propertyless wanderer as a description of Indian monastic life. Gregory Schopen has challenged that picture by reading the Vinayas, especially the very large Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, alongside the inscriptions and the excavated remains of monasteries (Schopen 1997, 2004). The inscriptions at Bharhut, Sanchi and the western Indian caves show monks and nuns making substantial donations of their own, which presupposes that they had money. The Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya has rules for lending monastic funds at interest with written contracts, for the inheritance of a dead monk’s belongings and for monks’ funerals and memorial stūpas. Permanent endowments, whose interest paid for robes and other needs, are recorded in inscriptions such as Uṣavadāta’s deposit with the weavers’ guilds at Nasik (see Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra). In the Gupta period and after, kings and wealthy donors granted whole villages to monasteries, as the Maitraka copper plates of Valabhī and the Nālandā grants show (Chapter 7). Shayne Clarke has argued that Indian monastic law codes did not require monks and nuns to sever ties with their families, as was long assumed, and that several of them envisage contact with, and even support of, relatives (Clarke 2014).

Scholarly Note: Texts and practice

Schopen’s work changed the study of Indian Buddhism, but it has its critics. The Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya on which he relies most is a north-western compilation of the early centuries CE or later, and it may describe the large, well-endowed monasteries of its own time and region rather than Indian Buddhism as a whole. The broader point is widely accepted: the Vinayas are working legal codes for institutions that owned property and dealt with the world, not only statements of an ascetic ideal (Schopen 2004; Clarke 2014).

docs.title: 13.2.5 Monastic Life beyond the Theravāda
docs.text:
The Mahāyāna never produced a Vinaya of its own. Mahāyāna monks and nuns were, and are, ordained under one of the older Vinayas, and in India they lived in the same monasteries as their non-Mahāyāna brethren. Yijing, writing in the late seventh century, observed that the two groups kept the same discipline and differed only in that Mahāyāna monks worshipped the bodhisattvas and read the Mahāyāna sūtras (Yijing (I-tsing) 1896). What the Mahāyāna added was a second set of commitments, the bodhisattva vows. The chapter on morality in the Bodhisattvabhūmi, part of the Yogācāra compendium attributed to Asaṅga, describes a threefold morality: restraint from wrongdoing, which includes the monastic or lay precepts; the cultivation of wholesome qualities; and action for the benefit of beings. It lists offences against the bodhisattva vow that are distinct from those of the Vinaya, such as refusing to teach or to give when asked (Williams 2009). In Tibet a monk came to hold three sets of vows at once — the monastic vows of the Vinaya, the bodhisattva vows and the vows of tantric initiation — and their relation became a subject of scholastic debate.

In East Asia, a set of bodhisattva precepts in the Fanwang jing (Brahmajāla Sūtra), a text probably composed in China in the fifth century, with ten major and forty-eight minor precepts, was taken by monks, nuns and lay people alike, emperors among them; it is the source of the strict vegetarianism of Chinese monasticism. In Japan the Tendai founder Saichō (767–822) argued that these precepts alone sufficed for the ordination of monks, and permission for such ordinations on Mount Hiei was granted just after his death. Japanese Buddhism moved further from the Vinaya model: the clergy of the Pure Land school of Shinran (1173–1263) married, and a government decree of 1872 permitting monks to eat meat and marry made a married, often hereditary, temple clergy the norm for most Japanese schools.

Tibetan monasticism took the opposite direction, towards very large celibate communities organised around scholastic study. The monastic colleges of the Gelug school built their curriculum on five Indian treatises: Maitreya’s Abhisamayālaṃkāra on the Perfection of Wisdom, Candrakīrti’s Madhyamakāvatāra, Dharmakīrti’s Pramāṇavārttika, Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa and Guṇaprabha’s Vinayasūtra, studied over many years through memorisation and debate (Chapter 7). Alongside the monks, Tibetan religion also had non-celibate tantric practitioners, hereditary lineages of lamas such as the Khön family who lead the Sakya school, and, from the thirteenth century, the distinctive institution of recognised reincarnate teachers (tulku, sprul sku), of whom the Karmapas and later the Dalai Lamas are the best known (Samuel 1993). In the Kathmandu valley, the Newar Buddhists of the old monastic castes undergo a monastic initiation as boys and then return to lay life as married householders, the vajrācāryas among them serving as hereditary priests — a form of Buddhism that preserves the outward forms of the Indian monastery within a householder community (Gellner 1992).

Reformers in every Buddhist country have periodically protested against the wealth and worldliness of settled monasteries. In Sri Lanka the division between village-dwelling (gāmavāsī) and forest-dwelling (araññavāsī) monks became an enduring feature of the Saṅgha, and modern forest movements in Sri Lanka and Thailand present themselves as returns to the discipline of the early order.

docs.title: 13.3 The Order of Nuns in History
docs.text:
The founding of the order of nuns, the eight “weighty rules” and the questions they raise for the place of women are discussed in Chapter 2 (Section 2.14.2) and Chapter 14 (Section 14.8.2). This section follows the institution itself through its history (Figure 13.1).

Figure 13.1. The ordination lineage of Buddhist nuns: its transmission from India and Sri Lanka to China, its survival in East Asia, and the modern attempts to restore it in the Theravāda countries using the East Asian lineage.

India. Nuns are well attested in early Indian Buddhism. They appear in large numbers among the donors named in the inscriptions of Bharhut and Sanchi (2nd–1st centuries BCE), and some describe themselves as learned in the scriptures: Kuṣāṇa-period inscriptions name the nun Buddhamitrā as “knower of the three baskets” (trepiṭikā) (Schopen 1997). A nun’s higher ordination required a “dual” procedure: she was ordained first by a quorum of nuns and then by a quorum of monks. The survival of the order therefore depended on a continuous succession of ordained nuns, and once the succession was broken in a region, it could not be restored there from within. Nuns are much less visible in the inscriptions of the later first millennium, and the order seems to have disappeared in India with the monasteries.

Sri Lanka. According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, Aśoka’s daughter Saṅghamittā brought a branch of the Bodhi tree to the island and ordained Queen Anulā and her companions. The Dīpavaṃsa lists generations of nuns who taught the Vinaya at Anurādhapura, and nunneries are mentioned in the chronicles and inscriptions for many centuries. References to nuns cease after the tenth century. The order did not survive the disorders of the Chola occupation in the eleventh century; when King Vijayabāhu I restored the monks’ ordination with monks from Burma, the nuns’ lineage was not renewed.

China and East Asia. The first Chinese nuns, in the fourth century, were ordained by monks alone. A full dual ordination became possible only when Sri Lankan nuns reached China by sea. The Biographies of Nuns (Biqiuni zhuan), compiled by Baochang in the early sixth century, records that a first group of Sri Lankan nuns arrived at Nanjing in 429, and that when more arrived a few years later, led by a nun named Tessarā, they ordained several hundred Chinese women, together with a chapter of monks, in 433 or 434 (Tsai 1994). From China the lineage passed to Korea and Vietnam, and it has continued without break; in Taiwan today nuns outnumber monks.

Southeast Asia and Tibet. Inscriptions of Pagan appear to mention nuns as late as the thirteenth century, but no Theravāda nuns’ lineage survived into the modern period. In Tibet, the full ordination of nuns was never established, since the dual procedure required nuns of the Mūlasarvāstivāda lineage who were not available; Tibetan nuns have been novices (śrāmaṇerikā) only.

Renunciant women without full ordination. In the absence of the order, women in the Theravāda countries created other forms of renunciant life: the ten-precept mothers (dasa sil mātā) of Sri Lanka, whose movement dates from the early twentieth century, the white-robed mae chi of Thailand, keeping eight or ten precepts, and the pink-robed thilashin of Myanmar. Their status is ambiguous: respected as renunciants but without the standing, the support or the formal role of monks.

Revival. From the late twentieth century, Buddhist women and their supporters have sought to restore full ordination using the East Asian lineage, on the argument that it descends from the Sri Lankan nuns of the fifth century. At Sarnath in 1996, ten Sri Lankan women were ordained with Korean nuns and monks as preceptors; in 1998 an international ordination at Bodhgaya, organised by the Taiwanese order Fo Guang Shan, was followed by ordinations within Sri Lanka itself. In Thailand, where a Saṅgha decree of 1928 forbade monks to ordain women, Chatsumarn Kabilsingh received full ordination in Sri Lanka in 2003 as the nun Dhammananda. The revival remains contested. Conservative authorities in Thailand and Myanmar do not recognise these ordinations, arguing that a lineage once broken cannot be revived from another school’s Vinaya; and the ordination of four nuns in Western Australia in 2009 led the Thai forest monastery of Wat Nong Pah Pong to expel the abbot who had organised it from its network. In the Tibetan tradition, the Dalai Lama has supported research and international conferences on the question (Hamburg, 2007) but has said that a decision requires consensus among senior monks (Harvey 2013; Salgado 2013). The anthropologist Nirmala Salgado has pointed out that many Sri Lankan ten-precept mothers do not regard full ordination as the measure of their religious life, and that the debate has sometimes been framed in terms drawn from outside their own practice (Salgado 2013). The modern debate is also summarised in Volume 24 (Samanvaya).

docs.title: 13.4.1 Refuge, Precepts and Merit
docs.text:
A person becomes a lay follower (upāsaka, upāsikā) by going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, in the formula quoted in Chapter 1. The suttas describe the good lay follower as one who has faith (saddhā), keeps the five precepts, is generous (cāga) and has wisdom. On the observance days devout lay people take eight precepts, adding to the five the abstentions from food after noon, from entertainments and adornment and from high beds, and replacing the avoidance of sexual misconduct by chastity. For a day and a night they live much like novices. The Sigālovāda Sutta sets out the householder’s duties to parents, teachers, spouse, friends, servants and religious teachers (Chapter 3, Section 3.7.3).

The organising idea of lay practice is merit (puñña): wholesome action that brings happiness in this life and a good rebirth. The canon names three “grounds for making merit” — giving (dāna), moral conduct (sīla) and meditation (bhāvanā) — and the commentaries extend the list to ten, adding respect, service, sharing merit, rejoicing in the merit of others, listening to the teaching, teaching it and correcting one’s views. Of these, giving has always been the most widely practised. The Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta (MN 142) grades gifts by the worth of the recipient and teaches that a gift to the Saṅgha as a whole surpasses any gift to an individual, even to the Buddha himself.

Lay patrons and exemplars. The canon remembers particular lay followers as models. In the Aṅguttara Nikāya’s lists of disciples who were “foremost” (etadagga) in some quality, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika is foremost among laymen in giving and the householder Citta in teaching the Dhamma; among laywomen, Visākhā is foremost in giving and Khujjuttarā, a servant of Queen Sāmāvatī who repeated the Buddha’s sermons to the women of the palace, foremost in learning (Bodhi 2012). Citta is also shown in debate with the Jain leader Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (SN 41.8), a reminder that the two communities competed for the same patrons. Uma Chakravarti’s analysis of the early texts shows that the Buddha’s best-known lay supporters were drawn largely from the propertied householders (gahapati), merchants and nobles of the new towns of the Ganges valley (Chakravarti 1987). The early inscriptions widen the picture. At Sanchi a panel of the southern gateway records that it was carved by the ivory-workers of Vidiśā, and the great hall at Kārlā names as its donor a banker (seṭṭhi) from Vaijayantī; the cave inscriptions of the Western Ghats also record gifts from yavanas, people of Greek or western origin, and from many women.

Richard Gombrich’s study of village Buddhism in highland Sri Lanka showed how this system worked in practice: villagers understood the doctrine of karma well, and their rituals of giving, chanting and observance were shaped by it, even where practice also drew on local gods and protective rites (Gombrich 1971). He also showed how the “transfer” of merit to others, which strictly contradicts the doctrine that each person reaps the fruit of his own deeds, was reconciled with it: the recipient gains merit by rejoicing in the good deed (anumodanā), and so earns his own reward.

docs.title: 13.4.2 Relics, Stūpas and the Presence of the Buddha
docs.text:
According to the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16), the Buddha’s remains were divided after his cremation into eight portions among eight claimants — King Ajātasattu of Magadha, the Licchavis of Vesālī, the Sakyas of Kapilavatthu, the Bulis, the Koliyas, a brāhmaṇa of Veṭhadīpa, and the Mallas of Pāvā and of Kusinārā. The brāhmaṇa Doṇa, who made the division, received the vessel, and the Moriyas, arriving late, received the embers, so that ten stūpas in all were built. In the same text the Buddha tells Ānanda that a stūpa should be raised for a Tathāgata at a crossroads, as for a universal monarch, and that those who honour it with garlands, perfume or paint, or make their hearts serene there, will benefit for a long time. He also tells Ānanda that the monks should not occupy themselves with the “honouring of the body”; Schopen has argued that this refers to the funeral rites, which were the business of lay people, not to the later worship of relics, in which monks took a full part (Schopen 1997; Walshe 1995).

Later tradition, preserved in the Aśokāvadāna, relates that Aśoka opened the original stūpas and redistributed the relics among 84,000 new ones. The number is legendary, but relic deposits are among the oldest Buddhist remains in India. A casket found at Piprahwa, near the Nepal border, in 1898 bears an inscription that many scholars read as recording the enshrinement of relics of the Buddha by the Sakyas, though its reading and date are debated. At Sanchi, Alexander Cunningham found in 1851 caskets inscribed with the names of Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna; taken to England, they were returned and re-enshrined at Sanchi in 1952. The stūpa was not only a memorial. Inscriptions, Vinaya rules and the plans of monasteries suggest that the Buddha was treated as present in his relics and images, a living resident of the monastery: monastic texts speak of his “perfumed chamber” (gandhakuṭī), and some inscriptions record property given to the Buddha himself (Schopen 1997; Strong 2004). Architecture of the stūpa is described in Volume 16 (Vāstu–Śilpa).

Later Buddhist classification distinguished bodily relics, objects used by the Buddha such as his bowl, and commemorative objects such as images. The Mahāyāna added the relic of the teaching: several Perfection of Wisdom texts say that a place where the sūtra is recited or a copy of it is kept becomes like a shrine (caitya). The relic of the Buddha’s tooth, brought to Sri Lanka according to the chronicles in the fourth century and seen in procession at Anurādhapura by the Chinese pilgrim Faxian around 410, became the palladium of Sinhala kingship; it is now kept in the Temple of the Tooth at Kandy and carried in procession each year in the month of Esala (July–August) (Trainor 1997; Strong 2004).

docs.title: 13.4.3 The Festival Year
docs.text: The lay Buddhist year is marked by full-moon festivals that recall events in the life of the Buddha and of the community. In the Theravāda countries the greatest is the full moon of Vesākha (April–May), which commemorates the Buddha’s birth, awakening and final passing together. The full moon of Āsāḷha (June–July) recalls the first sermon and marks the beginning of the rains retreat; its end, three months later, is followed by the kaṭhina season. Each country added festivals of its own: Sri Lanka celebrates Poson, the full moon of June, as the anniversary of Mahinda’s arrival, and Thailand and its neighbours observe Māgha Pūjā, recalling a spontaneous assembly of 1,250 arahants at which, according to tradition, the Buddha recited the summary of his teaching known as the Ovāda-pātimokkha. In Tibet the month of the Buddha’s awakening and passing (Saga Dawa, sa ga zla ba) is a period of intense merit-making. In China and the lands of Chinese Buddhism, the festival of the seventh month (Yulanpen, “Ghost Festival”), based on the story of the monk Maudgalyāyana rescuing his mother from torment through offerings made to the Saṅgha at the end of the rains retreat, joined the Buddhist calendar to the family’s duty towards its ancestors (Teiser 1988). In modern India, the anniversary of Ambedkar’s conversion at Nagpur has become a major Buddhist festival of its own (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 13.4.4 Pilgrimage, Protection and the Dead
docs.text:
The Mahāparinibbāna Sutta names four places that a faithful person should visit with a sense of religious urgency (saṃvega): where the Tathāgata was born, attained awakening, first taught and passed away; it adds that those who die with a serene heart while on pilgrimage to these shrines will be reborn in a heaven. The sites, their later expansion to eight, and the long history of pilgrimage to them, from Aśoka’s visit to Lumbinī to the Chinese, Burmese and Tibetan pilgrims, are described in Volume 21 (Bhūgola). Aśoka’s pillar inscription at Lumbinī records not only his visit in the twentieth year of his reign but a practical benefit for the place: the village was exempted from the bali tax and required to pay only an eighth share of its produce.

Protective chanting (paritta) is among the most widespread Buddhist practices. Texts such as the Ratana Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta and the Karaṇīya Metta Sutta (Chapter 2), collected in the Khuddakapāṭha, and the longer Āṭānāṭiya Sutta (DN 32), are chanted by monks to protect households from illness, misfortune and harmful spirits, often while a thread held by the monks and the listeners is passed round and later tied on the wrist. The commentarial tradition relates that the Ratana Sutta was first recited to end a plague at Vesālī. The Milindapañha already discusses why such chanting sometimes fails. In Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Buddhism the same need was met by dhāraṇī spells; in Nepal a collection of five protective texts, the Pañcarakṣā, was among the most frequently copied of all Buddhist manuscripts.

Buddhism also took responsibility for the dead. The Tirokuḍḍa Sutta (Khp 7) describes departed relatives waiting outside the walls of their former homes and teaches that they are helped when food is given to the Saṅgha and the merit is dedicated to them; the Petavatthu is a collection of stories about such “departed ones” (peta). Donative inscriptions from the earliest period onwards dedicate gifts “for the honour of mother and father” or “for the welfare and happiness of all beings” (Schopen 1997). In the Theravāda countries monks preside at funerals and at memorial offerings for the dead, chanting and accepting a cloth offered in the name of the deceased (Gombrich 1971). Marriage, by contrast, remained largely outside the monks’ ritual responsibility in India and in most Theravāda societies, and this is one reason why historians have described Indian Buddhist lay life as thinly ritualised (Chapter 7, Section 7.11.2).

docs.title: 13.5.1 Initiation
docs.text:
Initiation as a Jain monk or nun (dīkṣā) is understood as a final renunciation, modelled on the renunciation of the Tīrthaṅkaras, and is intended to be for life (Dundas 2002; Vallely 2002). Among Śvetāmbaras it is preceded by days of celebration in the initiate’s home town. In a great procession the candidate, dressed in fine clothes and jewels like a bride or bridegroom, rides through the streets scattering coins and gifts, re-enacting the year of giving that, according to tradition, every Tīrthaṅkara performs before renouncing the world. At the ceremony itself, the candidate exchanges these clothes for the plain white garments of a mendicant, receives from the presiding teacher the whisk and the other equipment of the order and a new religious name, and has the hair pulled out by hand (keśaloca), as Mahāvīra is said to have done. The plucking of the hair is repeated at intervals throughout the mendicant’s life.

Among Digambaras, a man may advance by stages: first as a kṣullaka, who wears two pieces of cloth, then as an ailaka, who wears only a loincloth, and finally as a naked muni. Digambara women may become kṣullikās and āryikās, the latter wearing a single white sari. Since Digambaras hold that full renunciation requires nudity, an āryikā’s great vows are regarded as great vows only by courtesy (Jaini 1991).

docs.title: 13.5.2 The Discipline of Daily Life
docs.text:
The five great vows (Chapter 8, Section 8.3) are protected by eight further disciplines that the Śvetāmbara canon calls the “mothers of the teaching” (pravacana-mātṛkā).

The five carefulnesses and three controls

The Uttarādhyayana (ch. 24) and the Tattvārthasūtra (9.4–5) list five kinds of carefulness (samiti) and three controls (gupti) (Jacobi 1895; Umāsvāti 1994):

  1. Īryā-samiti: care in walking, looking ahead so as not to tread on living things;

  2. Bhāṣā-samiti: care in speech, avoiding what is false, harsh or harmful;

  3. Eṣaṇā-samiti: care in seeking and accepting alms;

  4. Ādāna-nikṣepa-samiti: care in picking up and putting down one’s belongings;

  5. Utsarga-samiti: care in disposing of excreta and waste in places free of life;

  6. Mano-, vāg- and kāya-gupti: restraint of mind, speech and body.

The Digambara tradition summarises the discipline of a naked monk in twenty-eight “root qualities” (mūlaguṇa): the five great vows, the five carefulnesses, the restraint of the five senses and the six obligatory duties (Chapter 11, Table 11.3), together with seven particular practices — plucking the hair, nudity, not bathing, sleeping on the ground, not cleaning the teeth, eating standing and eating only once a day.

The equipment of the mendicant is meant to serve non-harming. Śvetāmbara mendicants carry a soft woollen whisk (rajoharaṇa) with which to brush away small creatures before sitting or lying down, and a mouth-cloth (muhpattī), held in the hand by image-worshipping mendicants and tied over the mouth at all times by Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs; they carry wooden bowls for alms. Digambara monks carry only a whisk of peacock feathers (piñchī), shed naturally by the birds, and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

Alms are collected in a manner the Śvetāmbaras call gocarī, “grazing like a cow”: a little food is taken from each of several households, so that no family is burdened and no food has to be cooked again. The first chapter of the Daśavaikālika, whose opening verse is quoted in Chapter 8, compares the mendicant to a bee that takes a little nectar from many flowers without harming them. The food must be free of a long list of faults — the Śvetāmbara tradition counts forty-two — of which the most important is that it must not have been prepared, bought or set aside for the mendicant. A Digambara monk takes one meal a day, standing, from his cupped hands. He sets out having privately resolved to accept food only if a certain condition is met; householders who wish to feed him wait outside their doors with the appropriate ritual objects and invite him in with set words of welcome. If he finds a hair or an insect in the food, he stops eating for the day.

Jain mendicants travel only on foot and do not use vehicles, so that the order is constantly on the move between towns and villages. During the four months of the rains (cāturmāsa), from the middle of Āṣāḍha to the middle of Kārttika, they stay in one place, usually in a hall maintained by the lay community (upāśraya among Śvetāmbaras). A town that hosts a prominent teacher for the rainy season treats it as a great event: the mendicants preach daily, many lay people undertake fasts, and the festival of Paryuṣaṇa falls within this period (Chapter 11, Section 11.5).

docs.title: 13.5.3 Orders, Lineages and Ranks
docs.text:
Jain mendicants are organised in lineages under teachers. Among the Śvetāmbara image-worshippers the head of a lineage is an ācārya (with the title sūri), assisted by an upādhyāya who teaches the scriptures; intermediate ranks such as gaṇi and panyāsa mark seniority and learning. Groups of nuns are led by senior nuns (pravartinī, mahattarā). The Terāpanthī order is unusual in having a single ācārya, who alone initiates mendicants and appoints his successor, and who governs the order under a written code laid down by its founder Ācārya Bhikṣu (Vallely 2002).

The Śvetāmbara gacchas (Chapter 8, Section 8.8.1) took shape in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries, in a period of conflict over monastic discipline. Many monks of the time lived permanently in temples, which they managed and from which they drew an income; their critics called them “temple-dwellers” (caityavāsī) and demanded a return to the wandering life and to residence in lodgings provided by the laity. The Kharatara Gaccha traces its origin and its name (“the keen”) to a debate in 1024 at the Caulukya court of Aṇahilapāṭaka in which, according to its own tradition, Jineśvara Sūri defeated the temple-dwellers; the Tapā Gaccha takes its name from the title “the austere” (tapā) said to have been given in 1228 to its founder Jagaccandra Sūri by the ruler of Mewar for his austerities. The tradition speaks of eighty-four gacchas, a conventional number (Dundas 2002; Deo 1956).

Over the centuries the problem recurred. By the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries much Śvetāmbara religious authority lay with yatis, settled clerics who owned property, practised astrology and medicine and presided over the rites of lay families, much as the Digambara bhaṭṭārakas did. The fully wandering “world-fearing” (saṃvegī) mendicants who dominate the Mūrtipūjaka orders today are the product of a nineteenth-century revival, in which teachers such as Vijayānanda Sūri (Ātmārām, 1837–1896), himself first initiated as a Sthānakavāsī, reorganised the Tapā Gaccha (Cort 2001; Dundas 2002). The Digambara revival of naked monks under Ācārya Śāntisāgara in the twentieth century (Chapter 8) is a parallel movement.

Women have always formed the larger part of the Jain mendicant community. The Kalpasūtra’s figures for Mahāvīra’s own community (Chapter 8, Section 8.2.4) are traditional, but in the Śvetāmbara orders of modern times nuns have consistently outnumbered monks by a wide margin. They preach, teach, write and travel as monks do, though they remain formally junior to monks. The tradition remembers individual nuns with honour: the eighth-century philosopher Haribhadra called himself the spiritual son of the nun Yākinī, whose recitation of a verse he could not understand led him to become a Jain mendicant (Dundas 2002). Anne Vallely’s study of Terāpanthī nuns describes how they understand their discipline not as self-denial but as the cultivation of the soul’s own nature (Vallely 2002).

Table 13.1. Mendicant discipline in the Buddhist (chiefly Theravāda) and Jain traditions Buddhist monks and nuns Jain monks and nuns Entry Going forth as a novice; higher ordination at twenty by a formal act of a quorum of monks (and, for nuns, of nuns) Initiation (dīkṣā) by an ācārya; Digambara men pass through grades before full nudity Possessions Three robes, bowl, razor, needle, belt, water-strainer Śvetāmbara: white garments, wooden bowls, whisk, mouth-cloth; Digambara monks: peacock-feather whisk and water-pot only Food Alms round and invitations to meals; meat allowed if not killed for the monk (Theravāda); no solid food after noon Food must not be prepared for the mendicant; taken from several houses; nothing after sunset; Digambara monks eat once a day, standing, from the hands Residence and travel Early wandering gave way to settled monasteries; rains retreat of three months Constant travel on foot, without vehicles; four-month rainy-season halt (cāturmāsa) Confession Before the fortnightly recitation of the Pātimokkha Daily pratikramaṇa; annual rite at the end of Paryuṣaṇa Leaving the order Permitted without fault; temporary ordination common in mainland Southeast Asia Intended to be lifelong; leaving is regarded as a serious lapse Women Order of nuns continuous in East Asia, lapsed in Theravāda lands, never fully established in Tibet; contested revival Nuns outnumber monks among Śvetāmbaras; Digambara āryikās wear a white sari

Table 13.1 sets the two disciplines side by side. The resemblances reflect a shared Śramaṇa background (Chapter 1); the differences — above all in food, travel and the permanence of the vow — reflect the stricter demands of Jain non-harming.

docs.title: 13.6.1 Worshipping a Liberated Teacher
docs.text:
The Tīrthaṅkaras are liberated souls, free of passion, who dwell at the summit of the universe and do not respond to prayer or intervene in the world (Chapter 11). Why, then, do most Jains worship their images? The answer given by Jain teachers is that worship of the Jina is not an exchange with a deity but an act of self-transformation: by honouring a being who has attained liberation, the worshipper calls to mind the qualities of the soul and turns towards them. Lawrence Babb called the resulting ritual culture one of an “absent lord” (Babb 1996).

Among Śvetāmbara image-worshippers the standard daily rite is the “eightfold worship” (aṣṭaprakārī pūjā), performed in the temple after bathing and dressing in unstitched clothes, with a cloth over the mouth.
